description:
This course aims to provide students with an introduction to the legal practice of banking and finance. In particular, this course is designed to give students a flavour of what life is like as a transactional lawyer working on a general banking transaction. 

Over the weeks, students will be walked through the lifecycle of a fictitious watered-down financing transaction. As the transaction progresses, students will gradually be introduced to the various financing legal documents (eg, term sheets, loan facility agreements, corporate authorisations) and their key clauses. Crucially, students will also step into the shoes of lender’s counsel and be given several opportunities to “hold the pen” – students will be tasked to take instructions from their clients and draft/review certain financing legal documents. Finally, students will participate and lead an all-parties call to iron out the outstanding issues blocking the transaction from closing.

Through this course, students will have the opportunity to both gain insights on transactional lawyering, as well as learn practical skills that will better prepare students to transition to their upcoming lives as practice trainees and junior associates. Moreover, while this course is conducted in the context of banking and finance, the practical skills taught in this course will nonetheless be largely applicable to other fields of transactional law, including but not limited to mergers and acquisitions, investment funds, capital markets etc.
longName: Banking and Finance in Legal Practice

This course provides an overview to financial crime compliance with a specific focus on concepts such as anti-money laundering (AML), countering the financing of terrorism (CFT), Corruption, Anti-Scam and Sanctions compliance. The course will address legal and regulatory requirements/expectations under the laws of Singapore for each of these five concepts.
This course will take a closer look at the Financial Action Task Force’s recommendations/standards and better understand how these recommendations/standards impact the Singapore regime. This course will also provide a brief introduction to international legal cooperation across countries, investigations processes and procedures, and cooperation with Singapore law enforcement authorities.
This course will examine the global impact of compliance, through sanctions imposed by the highest international body – the United Nations and other international sanctions regimes imposed by the US Department of Treasury Office of Foreign Assets Control, UK HM Treasury, and the European Union. Finally, this course will address some emerging risks and criminal typologies (such as the risks associated with virtual currencies and De-FI).

description: The module has two general aims. First, to develop an understanding of two apparently competing regulatory paradigms (law, on the one hand, and technological management, on the other); and second, to consider some possible consequences of a transition from the legal regulatory paradigm to the technological management paradigm. This transition is claimed already to be in train in many common law jurisdictions – it is ‘the direction of regulatory travel’ – and the technological management regulatory paradigm now seems particularly salient in light of myriad advances in computation and AI. Drawing and interrogating the contrast between the two paradigms will allow us to see and evaluate the assumptions and benefits of each as well as their disadvantages. We will examine the contrast both in general terms, in our early classes, and then in particular contexts, such as private law and the practice of adjudication, in later classes.
name: The Death of Law

In an era where AI and large language models are transforming legal research, understanding how to effectively find, verify, and use legal information is more crucial than ever. How do we ensure AI-powered legal research tools are reliable? How can we combine traditional legal research expertise with modern retrieval technologies?

You’ll learn:
•	How lawyers think about and search for information
•	Why legal search remains challenging even with AI
•	How modern retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems work
•	What makes AI-powered legal research tools effective and trustworthy
•	How to evaluate and improve legal search systems

Why Take This Course?
•	Learn how RAG systems for legal applications are built
•	Understand the unique challenges of legal information retrieval
•	Learn why simple LLM approaches often fail for law
•	Gain practical experience with modern retrieval techniques
•	Add cutting-edge legal tech projects to your portfolio
•	Master both traditional and AI-powered research strategies
•	Understand the capabilities and limitations of AI legal tools
•	Learn to effectively verify and validate AI-generated results
•	Develop technical literacy crucial for modern practice
•	Stand out with legal technology expertise

What Makes This Course Different?
•	Work with real legal documents and modern AI tools
•	Build practical systems combining traditional and AI approaches
•	Learn to balance automation with necessary human oversight
•	Understand both technical and legal perspectives

Join us to explore how traditional legal research meets modern AI and help shape the future of legal information systems. Learn to build tools that augment, rather than replace, legal expertise.

No prior AI knowledge required – just bring your curiosity and critical thinking skills!

description: International Humanitarian Law, previously known as the Law of War and now also known as the Law of Armed Conflict are the international legal rules that apply to belligerents during times of armed conflict. These may be International Armed Conflicts (IAC) or Non-International Armed Conflicts (NIAC). IHL is not concerned with the cause of the armed conflict but applies when armed conflict occurs in order to mitigate the suffering which such conflicts invariably give rise to. IHL is a subset of Public International Law (PIL). But unlike PIL, its rules are enforced against individuals, not states. Breach of IHL can result in the offender being punish by domestic or military courts; international tribunals or the International Criminal Court.
longName: International Humanitarian Law: Principles and Practice
name: International Humanitarian Law

description: We like to think of ourselves as rational beings, making decisions based on facts and sound principles. Such critical thinking skills are integral to many vocations, including the legal profession in which advice is rendered based on rigorous analysis of law and facts. However, research from social and cognitive psychology has shown the illusion of rationality in human choices. Our decision-making is routinely affected by cognitive distortions including biases, judgment shortcuts, memory distortions and perception limitations. Consequently, many disciplines, including economics and policy making, have acknowledged that we are not as rational as we would like to believe.Whether you are a future lawyer, business consultant or someone who will need to solve problems in your career, you will benefit from understanding the impact of cognitive distortions on decision-making. Harnessing psychological insights will make you more effective in risk prediction, weighing and choosing between solutions, and interacting with clients and other professionals.Drawing from the instructors’ experience in psychology, neuroscience, law and dispute resolution, this course offers a robust evidence-based framework to understand the impact of the illusion of rationality on decision-making within the legal profession. Key insights from psychology will be applied to different contexts in the legal profession, including dealing with clients, giving legal advice, assessing chances of success in litigation, dealing with high-conflict situations, and engaging in negotiations.
longName: The Illusion of Rationality in Decision-Making: Insights from Psychology
name: The Illusion of Rationality

description:
This course examines the operation of the rule of law in Singapore – the approach, the application, and the development of an autochthonous legal system. The rule of law has been critical to Singapore’s survival and prosperity. Simply put, the rule of law embodies the fundamental principle that every person and institution is subject to the same set of laws. It also regulates and moderates power, especially in the public sphere. 

Moreover, since independence, Singapore has also conscientiously evolved its own approach to governance with the rule of law, itself adapted to fit local needs and priorities, and yielded commendable outcomes including for the economy and business, the social fabric (including housing, healthcare and social safety nets), racial and religious harmony, law and order, international relations and more. This non-ideological, outcomes-based approach interacts with concepts such as constitutionalism, the separation of powers, and judicial review. 

The course will also consider criticisms of Singapore for its manner of observance of the rule of law, which the Government steadfastly maintains that there is no universal under¬standing of what the rule of law is and requires. It insists that the rule of law is subject to the social, economic and security imperatives facing Singapore. 

The course will examine how the rule of law in Singapore supports a rules-based order in emerging areas such as artificial intelligence, climate challenges, and online harms.
longName: Rule of Law in Singapore: Approach, Application, and Autochthony
name: Rule of Law in Singapore

description:
Antitrust, competition or anti-monopoly laws aim to prevent or discourage businesses from engaging in anticompetitive behaviour. From the enactment of the Sherman Act (1890) in the United States until the 1970s, competition laws existed only in a handful of industrialized countries. In the last few decades, however, many countries around the world have adopted competition policies and established independent competition authorities. Over 130 jurisdictions have adopted competition laws. The OECD observed that Asia-Pacific region witness an increase in the importance of competition policy and law over the past 20 years.

This course aims to introduce students to the competition policy and law landscape in Singapore. Students will gain an understanding of the three main prohibitions of Singapore's Competition Act 2004 namely, the anti-competitive agreement prohibition, the abuse of dominance prohibition, and the merger prohibition. The course will also refer to Singapore's seminal competition law cases issued by the Competition and Consumer Commission of Singapore, as well as the Competition Appeals Board. Students will also be given an overview of sectoral competition law regimes in Singapore administered by the Infocomm Media Development Authority, and the Energy Market Authority.
name: Singapore Competition Law

Sports law is increasingly being recognised as a distinct and sperate field of law, with its complexities and unique sets of regulations and jurisprudence. description: Taxation is a key consideration for virtually any form of commercial activity or private wealth structuring, making it crucial for practitioners to understand the broad principles of tax law. From choosing between asset sales or share sales, and the choice of business vehicles, to decisions on whether to raise capital through debt or equity and the constant threat of anti-avoidance rules; commercial and private wealth lawyers must at least be aware of the tax implications. This course will also provide a strong foundation for those intending to specialise in tax practice. Focusing on the Income Tax Act 1947 (ITA), this course gives students a solid grounding in the core principles of income taxation in Singapore. description: A good command of dispute resolution remedies is essential for legal practice, whether as a litigator or transactional lawyer, whether in litigation or international arbitration.Knowledge of dispute resolution remedies will inform a party as to what are the benefits and risks that the litigation or arbitration process can present; and what are the objectives that can be secured in litigation (and what other objectives may need to be achieved via mediation or some other form of alternative despite resolution).This course is intended for students who intend to pursue a meaningful and rewarding career in legal practice. Students who have taken this course have gone on to private practice in top law firms, in-house counsel positions in leading multi-national companies, as well as public service (Justices’ Law Clerks; etc). This is therefore a practical, hands-on course to remedies. This course will guide students in practical aspects of remedies by reference to actual litigation and arbitration cases which the course instructors themselves have argued successfully. Students will study and compare the different remedies used in different cases and learn to assess why they were selected.  For example: when is a freezing Mareva Injunction available as a pre-emptive strike? When can you obtain an injunction for breach of restrictive covenants? What if a defendant is insolvent? These are some of the questions which a litigant may ask counsel, and which students will explore.Students will also explore the rapidly developing and exciting new area of cryptocurrency. We will explore remedies for cryptocurrency hacks and “persons unknown” cases, including pre-action discovery / interrogatories, ancillary disclosure orders, self-identification orders, and the use of Mareva and proprietary injunctions to these cases.Through case studies, students will assume the role of counsel to understand the tactical advantages and strategic considerations that counsel face – including evidential issues, assessment of damages, burden of proof, selection of defendants and impact of the defendants’ insolvency. As noted above, knowledge of effective remedies are the bedrock of any legal practice career. Students will gain practical knowledge for a head start in legal practice, whether in private practice, as in-house counsel or in the public sector.

description: The historical evolution of international investment law can be traced to the commercial and political expansion of dominant states from the seventeenth through the early twentieth centuries. Elements of these origins continue to resonate in today’s approaches to international investment law. The current regime, which emerged in the post-war period, was designed as a framework aimed at promoting and protecting cross-border investment through treaty-based commitments and arbitration mechanisms. Over time, it has developed into one of the most prominent and contested areas of international economic law. Investment treaties and investor–State dispute settlement (ISDS) now generate significant debates concerning regulatory autonomy, sustainable development, and the legitimacy of adjudicatory processes.This course explores the origins of international investment law, its key features, and protection standards, and considers how arbitration has shaped and consolidated the substantive and procedural frameworks that govern international investment disputes. Students taking this course are encouraged to critically examine the evolution, function, and contested role of arbitration in shaping this area of international economic law.The course has four main parts. Part 1 examines the historical origins and the economic and political rationales of international investment law. It addresses the costs and benefits of investment treaties for investors, states, and other stakeholders, as well as why developed and developing countries concluded investment treaties. Part 2 examines substantive standards of investment protection such as fair and equitable treatment and non-discrimination. It also examines the host state’s right to regulate and the interaction of international investment law with other areas of international law such as international environmental law. Part 3 looks at investor-state arbitration, including remedies, the annulment, and enforcement of awards. Part 4 examines the broader questions about the regime’s functioning and legitimacy. It discusses ongoing reform efforts, including both substantive reforms that incorporate sustainable development objectives and procedural reforms of ISDS.
name: Intl Investment Law & Arb

description: Corporate law, securities regulation, and financial markets are the architecture of modern economies — determining how businesses are built, how capital moves, and how risk and reward are allocated among those with a stake in the outcome. This course offers a deep examination of that architecture by exploring why the relevant rules exist, how they shape economic relationships among competing stakeholders, and whether they succeed in achieving their underlying economic and ethical objectives.An understanding of these dynamics is essential because effective business lawyers often need to move beyond the mechanical application of legal doctrine and exercise strategic judgment and creative problem-solving. By engaging with the economic logic and normative considerations embedded in corporate, finance and business law, students develop the ability to identify what truly matters in complex transactions, to distinguish structural issues from surface-level detail, and to craft innovative legal solutions. These skills are developed through economic analysis, case studies, and rigorous doctrinal and ethical reasoning.The course is designed primarily for law students and is also open to students of economics, business, finance, and accounting seeking a understanding of the mechanics and purposes of corporate, finance, and business law.

description: This course will explore the legal system of Taiwan, officially known as the Republic of China (ROC), as well as its external relations with key trading partners such as ASEAN countries. Taiwan was ceded to Japan by the Qing Dynasty under the Treaty of Shimonoseki in 1895. The ROC was established in 1912 following the overthrow of the Qing Dynasty. According to the Cairo Declaration, the ROC resumed control of Taiwan after the Second World War. In 1949, following its defeat in the civil war by the Chinese Communist Party, which established the People’s Republic of China (PRC), the ROC government relocated to Taipei. In 1971, United Nations General Assembly Resolution 2758 transferred China’s seat from the ROC to the PRC, contributing to Taiwan’s unique status under international law.Taiwan’s legal system is based on the ROC Constitution promulgated in 1947. The ROC implemented the Chinese legal system in Taiwan, which had been influenced by Japan during its administration. Germany and the United States have also significantly influenced Taiwan’s legal development, particularly in constitutional, civil and commercial law. The Legislative Yuan (Parliament) is Taiwan’s unicameral legislature. The Constitutional Court of the Judicial Yuan holds the power to interpret the Constitution. The Executive Yuan serves as the executive branch, with the Premier appointed by the President, who is elected every four years by universal suffrage. Today, Taiwan ranks among the largest Asian economies and operates as a vibrant democracy under a two-party system.In this SMU-X course, students will examine various aspects of Taiwanese law and explore Taiwan’s legal relationships with China, the EU, Singapore and the United States. They will gain practical experience by working with lawyers and legal counsel to address real-world legal challenges.Please note: Supported by the Taiwan Studies Project Grant from the ROC Ministry of Education, this course does not include an overseas trip and does not fulfil SMU’s global exposure requirement. However, students will interact and engage in projects with legal and policy experts specialising in EU–ASEAN law and relations. The course will also incorporate SMU’s blended learning approach, which may include some online sessions.
name: ASEAN–Taiwan Law and Relations

description: Contracts are the foundation of commercial life.  This course aims to equip students with a firm appreciation of the unique character of contracts as a form of voluntary undertakings. This course begins by examining the concepts relating to the formation of contract, the establishment of the parties’ obligations (i.e., the contents of the contract), as well as the construction of the contractual document. It then examines the various methods by which a contract may be discharged. Contract Law 1 will be followed in the second semester by LAW102 Contract Law 2, which will go on to look at issues relating to defects in intention, formalities and capacity, what sort of remedies are available when a contractual obligation is breached, as well as certain issues relating to contracts for the sale of goods. Over the two courses, students will be sensitised to the role of the law in facilitating commerce, respecting legitimate expectations, and guarding against unfair exploitation of economic or social weakness. The study of the subject will also provide students with an excellent opportunity to observe, evaluate and critique developments in the law as it responds to the fast-changing and dynamic environment of the world of commerce.

description: Under Singapore law, there are different ways in which businesspeople may organise commercial activities with a view to maximising operational efficiency and minimising exposure to personal risk. Most, however, will opt to incorporate a company for the purpose. This is however no indication that the company is a simple structure. On the contrary, as the company is effectively a web of different interests, rights and obligations, it is a highly complex structure. As such, the corporate form is fittingly the most regulated of all business entities. In this course, we will examine how a company is formed, the consequences of incorporation, how it is managed and controlled, what responsibilities are visited upon those who exercise control over a company’s assets, how a company transacts with third parties, and how it raises capital. The course will also expose the student to issues relating to shareholder rights and to creditor protection mechanisms. In addition, the student will be introduced to corporate rescue and insolvency laws, as well as to corporate finance.

description: This course aims to introduce students to the basic principles of common law and equity as applied to property, both immoveable and moveable including intellectual property. Beginning with an exploration of what ownership of land means, this course will consider how land can be dealt with at common law and in equity, before taking a look at how some of these complexities have receded, given the adoption and universal application of the Torrens registration system in Singapore. In the middle part of this course, the question of ownership and transfer of moveable property at common law and in equity will be considered with particular attention to the difficulties posed by intangible moveable property in the form of intellectual property rights as well as other choices in action. The final part of the course examines the creation of security interests over immoveable and moveable property and the problems relating to determining the priorities of competing security interests. Comparisons may be drawn with alternative systems of property law, e.g. the scheme of security interests set out in the Uniform Commercial Code and the treatment of property generally in the American Restatement on Property.

This course is generally concerned with how law, institutions and norms promote good governance, how political power and public law functions are legitimated, how abuses of public power are prevented or remedied, and the relationship between the individual and the state.

In what ways do ideals of justice and morality underlie the law? Are unjust laws law? How can laws be properly justified? In a pluralist society in which people do not share the same views on moral questions, when is the constraint upon the liberty of an individual justifiable? Is adjudication a rational practice: do legal rules determine cases, or is law really politics? The examination of these questions will be related to live issues in current contexts. Where relevant, issues raised by disruptive technologization in society will also be discussed.

description: This course provides an overview of the fundamental principles and methodologies of the conflict of laws (also known as private international law), with focus on their application in commercial transactions. Cross-border commercial transactions are common in a modern globalised era. The conflict of laws addresses three large questions: (1) in which country should the case be tried? (2) which country’s law should be applied to resolve the dispute? (3) What should be the legal effect in one country of a judgment given in another? From the perspective of Singapore law, the questions translate into: (1) When would or should a Singapore court hear the case (and sometimes try to stop it from being heard in another country)? (2) Which country’s law would or should the Singapore court apply to resolve the issue before it? And (3) What legal effect would or should a foreign judgment have in Singapore? This is a course on Singapore conflict of laws, with focus on Singapore legislation and case law, but references and comparisons will be made from time to time to international instruments and the laws of other countries.

The objective of this course is to introduce students to the jurisdiction and principles of equity originally developed by the courts of equity, and which are now applied and implemented within our \"fused\" system of common law and equity.  Students will be acquainted with the historical development of equity in England, as well as modern-day developments and application of equitable concepts, institutions and remedies in various jurisdictions such as in Australia and Canada. Selected developments in equity by the Australian and Canadian courts will be compared with the position in England and Singapore.

description:
Participants will be introduced to the many legal issues and problems that arise from and relate to modern developments in Information and Communications Technology. ICT is changing the socio-economic environment and the way we behave and transact on a global scale. Terms such as “the gig economy”, “disruptive innovations”, “big data”, “social media” and “the Internet of Things” describe some of these changes.

In relation to the law in this area, Asia has only more recently begun to catch up on the laws to deal with these issues. For example, Singapore has released many new and amended laws within the last decade alone that relate to infocomm developments. More recent amendments include changes to the Electronic Transactions Act of 2010 relating to e-contracts, e-signature and intermediary liability; the enactment of the Personal Data Protection Act in 2012 relating to data protection, the do-not-call registry and the Spam Control Act; changes to content regulations, specifically the class licensing regulations in 2013; the Protection from Harassment Act of 2014 and amendments to the Copyright Act in 2014 and 2016. In 2018, the Singapore legislature is expected to produce more new laws to deal with the fake news phenomenon and electric payment systems as well as in the areas of cybersecurity, electronic transactions and data protection.

Other than the legal changes in Singapore, the latest trends and developments in other jurisdictions, with a focus on the Asian region, will be considered where relevant.

description: This is an introductory course designed to help business students acquaint themselves with the framework of Singapore’s legal system and to understand the legal environment within which businesses operate. A substantial part of the course is dedicated to the study of contractual principles as the making and performance of contracts form the rudiment of all businesses. Apart from the law of contract, students will learn about various types of legal liability (criminal, tortuous and statutory) which may arise in the conduct of business, basic concepts relating to the ownership, use and infringement of intellectual property, as well as common forms of business relationships. To ensure that students are equipped to face the challenges and exploit the opportunities presented by the current e-revolution in commerce, the course also requires students to understand and analyse new legal issues arising from the conduct of businesses through electronic media.

description:
This course aims to introduce PLE students to how law operates in Singapore. We will explore the role of law in Singapore in the management of both public power and the sphere of private dealings between persons. This will be done through a study of the various sources of law and their nature; the legal institutions and the relations between them; and foundational principles and values.

We will begin by exploring the concept of law and the ideals of constitutionalism, democracy, the rule of law, and the separation of powers – all of which pertain to the ways in which power is defined and limited by law. Besides studying what law is, we will study tools and concepts which have some degree of formality but are not law, such as policies and decisions by those who hold discretionary powers.

Having inquired into these ideas, we will go on to explore the various institutions of the state and their roles, as well as the values that animate them. This is important because law does not put itself into action; legal institutions breathe life into laws by interpreting them, executing them, and serving as sites of contestation as to how they are to be interpreted and executed. We will discuss matters such as different modes of lawmaking and their relative advantages and disadvantages; the role of the state in controlling its own power; and the limits to law as a means of governing society. Finally, we will apply all this knowledge by focusing our attention on a few discrete areas of law as case studies.

While this course will focus on Singapore, comparisons will be drawn with other legal systems, particularly the UK’s, when appropriate.
longName: Governance Through Law In Singapore: Institutions, Jurisprudence, And Values
name: Governance Through Law In SG

description:
The corporate form is the most widely used legal structure for the operation and conduct of business.  It deals with a web of different interests and the rights and obligations of a number of stakeholders. As such it is a highly complex structure and the most regulated of all business entities. 

This course will cover the main body of laws that regulate the operational aspects of companies embodied in the Companies Act. Where appropriate and relevant, these laws will be considered from the different perspectives of the various interest groups in a corporate structure. The course will also attempt to acquaint the student with the primary issues that are raised in the management of companies. Topics include current issues in corporate governance, the external regulation of corporate matters, the duties of corporate managers, directors and other officers, the law and practice of meetings and legal issues relating to corporate restructuring. The difficulties relating to transactions with other parties, which are peculiar to companies, will also be covered, including corporate contracting and insolvency. The course will also touch upon the ongoing law reform in this area.

Upon the completion of this course, the student should –
 understand the legal framework within which companies operate;
 appreciate the different interest groups within the corporate framework; understand the dynamics of majority control and minority shareholder rights;
 appreciate the extent of and understand the legal duties and responsibilities expected of management; and
 have a basic understanding of issues pertaining to corporate finance and securities regulation.
name: Company Law

description: This course encourages students to reflect on the nature of law and (more importantly) the many roles it plays in the wider society. Amongst the various topics to be discussed are the following. Is law objective? Is law only “a system of rules”? Is there any necessary connection between law and morality? Ought the law to be used to enforce morality? What is “justice”? How does law interact with society? What is the future of law in a postmodern world where subjectivity and relativity appear to be the order of the day? Is there a “third way” between capitalism and socialism? Pre-requisite: LGST101
name: Theories of Law

description:
You are a mid-level manager on the fast track in an MNC based in Singapore. Your boss wants you to relocate abroad to establish a factory to produce and sell certain high technology widgets in a fellow ASEAN country, ASEAN X. The Government of ASEAN X welcomes the proposed investment and is willing to provide funding for your operation if you undertake to export a percentage of the production to Europe as well as sell to an ASEAN X state owned enterprise. Feasibility studies show that the factory to be established will have an over-capacity and it will be desirable to sell a percentage of the production below cost to the U.S. market.  ASEAN X law requires you to form a local manufacturing company together with a local shareholder. The short-list of the local candidates proposed to you are all relatives of the President of ASEAN X. You will be required to sign a joint venture agreement with one of these candidates but you are concerned about the impartiality of the courts in ASEAN X in case you have a dispute with your local partner and have to rely on this joint venture agreement. The technology that you will be introducing carries some risks and should an industrial accident occur, many people of different nationalities will be injured. ASEAN X also has a history of political turmoil and there have been situations where rampaging mobs have destroyed the property of foreigners and the government has taken over the business of foreigners and compensated them with valueless ASEAN X dollars. 

The foregoing is not an untypical account of the range of problems faced by managers who do business overseas or across borders. Accordingly, the objective of this course is to develop an understanding of the major legal principles that shape and affect international business transactions with special reference to foreign direct investment and transborder commercial dispute settlement. In our globalized environment, supply chains run half way across the globe and there is an unprecedented movement of money, people, goods, and services across borders.  Principles of law that provide the context for the negotiations and performance of international business transactions are not only relevant at the basic level of contract formation between international business participants but also have strategic relevance to issues of planning and location. Increasingly, such principles include rules of international law, specific rules on world trade that are overseen by the World Trade Organization, and investment protection treaties. Rather than attempt to cover too wide a range of topics in what would inevitably have to be a hurried and superficial examination, the course will cover certain fundamental legal topics that should be studied by those aspiring to manage international operations.

description:
The law relating to information technology is still developing. By its very nature, this particular area of law touches and is concerned with virtually every other area of law (from contract to tort to criminal law). Its growing importance for doing business and in changing consumer behaviour also entails the consideration of more comparative perspectives than would be the case with regard to more traditional areas of law, and requires that the concerns of businesses and consumers be addressed with as much attention as that of governments and policymakers. As such, this course will challenge students to look beyond the legal rules and consider the role of government, industry and end-users in shaping laws and policies affecting information technology.

Pre-requisite: LGST101

description:
This course examines the role of economic principles in analyzing the law.  The course seeks to provide students with an understanding of the law based on microeconomic analysis.  Under the economic approach to the law, laws are viewed as providing incentives for changing behavior and as instruments for achieving policy objectives.

This course also explores the implications for what the law should be.  The economic approach to law places emphasis on the criterion of efficiency, particularly in analyzing private law (property, contract and tort law).  The course also addresses criticisms of the economic approach to law, in particular, the redistributive approach to private law.

Economic analysis of law is considered from a number of the following perspectives: the Chicago School (Neoclassical Law and Economics); Public Choice theory; New Institutional Law and Economics; and Behavioral Law and Economics.  Economic analysis is applied to some of the following areas of law: property law (including the law of intellectual property); contract law; tort law; corporate law; competition law and consumer protection law; criminal law; and litigation process and alternative dispute resolution.

By the end of the course, students should be able to use microeconomic analysis to address a variety of topics in the law.  Illustrative topics are the ownership of genetic material, enforceability of shrink-wrap licenses, products liability, attorney-client privilege, and the duty to report a crime, to name but a few.  The economic approach to law even lends itself to analyzing such an arcane topic as property interests in sunken treasure.

Illustrative topics are the ownership of genetic material, enforceability of shrink-wrap licenses, products liability, attorney-client privilege, and the duty to report a crime, to name but a few.  The economic approach to law even lends itself to analyzing such an arcane topic as property interests in sunken treasure.
name: Economic Analysis of Law

description: This course seeks to instill knowledge and appreciation of the main principles of tax law in Singapore . As tax is a creature of statute, an understanding of the promulgation and interpretation of statutory provisions is included in the course. The course covers income tax, which forms the bulk of the course topics, property tax, goods and services tax, stamp duties and estate duty. Students will study how tax legislation is applied by the Singapore courts to both corporate and individual taxpayers on specific tax issues, and will be exposed to a variety of case authorities emanating from several jurisdictions with tax laws similar to our own. Having become acquainted with fundamental tax concepts and principles, students are led into the analysis of the decided cases relating to topics in the course. These topics include the taxation of business income of companies and employment income of individuals. In addition to tax issues on income sourced in Singapore , the course devotes a seminar to international taxation, which also touches on tax issues in electronic commerce. For a balanced approach to the study of revenue law, as a complement to the treatment of substantive tax issues, the method and manner of dealing with tax assessments, objections and appeals under our tax system are also dwelt upon. This endeavours to make students familiar with the processes involved in, and procedural aspects of, the resolution of tax disputes. This tax course also seeks to deliver a practical approach on how tax issues arise and are handled in real life, to equip and prepare students for the world of business after completion of their studies.

description:
This course focuses on the legal fundamentals of real estate practice and development in Singapore. While space and the built environment is ubiquitous, real estate remains a unique asset class. The rules relating to its current and future value, how it may be securely transferred from one party to another and its very definition all depend on law. The course is vital for students with an interest in real estate transactions, its development, investment and financing.

The primary topics covered include the nature of real property, contract and property torts, interests in property, development and construction, the rules relating to securitisation and taxes affecting property. It is one of the foundational courses of the Real Estate Track offered in LKCSB and SOE in Singapore Management University.

description: This course aims to provide a basic understanding of the legal aspects of obtaining funds for a business through debt financing, with a particular focus on secured debt financing. As such, it considers the legal issues involved in various forms of extending credit, such as loans, credit cards and hire-purchase. It will also examine the types of assets that may be given as security to raise funds, and the various forms of security interests such as mortgages, charges and guarantees.  The legal issues pertaining to each form of security will be explored.  The course concludes with a consideration of the liabilities of a business and, correspondingly, a creditor’s remedies and priority position in the event of default in repayment.
name: Credit & Security Law

departments.name: Yong Pung How School of Law

description: The objective of the course is to equip students with the knowledge of Consumer and Marketing Law. The course would cover the law relating to the sale and supply of goods and services in Singapore including, among other things, the law of sales, hire-purchase, consumer credit, product liability and e-commerce. Further the course will deal with the law relating to advertising and marketing devises such as multi-level marketing, licensing and franchising. The course will then consider methods of consumer protection including the Consumer Protection (Fair Trading) Act and the roles of agencies such as CASE and the Small Claims Tribunal.
name: Consumer & Marketing Law

description:
This course lays the foundation of knowing the laws that facilitate wealth planning and management. In planning for self as well as the “next generation’, a person has to consider not only preserving, but also growth of, capital; short term as well as long term investments; and how to segregate business wealth from private wealth.  As the size of the wealthbase grows, the scope of wealth planning will go beyond national borders.

This course will build upon the knowledge of the basic business law course, especially contract and tort, and will add to a student’s knowledge by the inclusion of tax law and other generation planning related laws.  This course has an international flavour to it as students will be exposed to basic comparison of the laws of at least two countries.  Furthermore, the emphasis of this course is not on the principles only, but on the application of such laws to wealth planning and management.

description:
It is a truism that the world at large and Singapore in particular has entered the information age where knowledge and new ideas will form the bedrock of the new economic order. This course has the aim of setting out a thorough overview of the rationale  and principles governing  protection of confidential information outside of the statutory intellectual and industrial property rights. The course will also examine a number of areas of current special concern. These include: industrial (commercial) espionage and the balance of rights and obligations of confidentiality as between an employer and employee. Both of these are likely to be of increasing importance in Singapore and the international market place in years to come. The course also has the objective of deepening appreciation of how the common law system works and the overlaps that can arise between different pigeon holes within the law of obligations. By examining the rationale for protection as well as different legal theories by which confidential information can be protected, students should at the end of the course acquire a better awareness of the workings of contract, tort and property law principles. 

Aside from industrial (commercial) confidential information, the course will explore the interface between privacy and confidentiality. In a world where information is a premium and information technology ubiquitous, “informational privacy” or “informational self-autonomy” is likely to become as important as reputational interests and bodily self-autonomy.  This is well illustrated by the recent litigation by Naomi Campbell, Michael Douglas and Catherine Zeta Jones. Discussion of the rapidly developing law in the area will be intellectually challenging and highly topical for Singapore and the international market because of its international importance. The question of protecting informational privacy is more than a matter of personal concern to individuals: adequate safeguards may become increasingly important in the data processing industry.

description:
It is a truism that the world at large and Singapore in particular has entered the information age where knowledge and new ideas will form the bedrock of the new economic order. This course has the aim of setting out a thorough overview of the rationale  and principles governing  protection of confidential information outside of the statutory intellectual and industrial property rights. The course will also examine a number of areas of current special concern. These include: industrial (commercial) espionage and the balance of rights and obligations of confidentiality as between an employer and employee. Both of these are likely to be of increasing importance in Singapore and the international market place in years to come. The course also has the objective of deepening appreciation of how the common law system works and the overlaps that can arise between different pigeon holes within the law of obligations. By examining the rationale for protection as well as different legal theories by which confidential information can be protected, students should at the end of the course acquire a better awareness of the workings of contract, tort and property law principles. 

Aside from industrial (commercial) confidential information, the course will explore the interface between privacy and confidentiality. In a world where information is a premium and information technology ubiquitous, “informational privacy” or “informational self-autonomy” is likely to become as important as reputational interests and bodily self-autonomy.  This is well illustrated by the recent litigation by Naomi Campbell, Michael Douglas and Catherine Zeta Jones. Discussion of the rapidly developing law in the area will be intellectually challenging and highly topical for Singapore and the international market because of its international importance. The question of protecting informational privacy is more than a matter of personal concern to individuals: adequate safeguards may become increasingly important in the data processing industry.
longName: Law of Confidential Information, Trade Secrets & Privacy
name: Law of Confi Info, TS & Pvcy

description: The course examines the process behind the creation of a new nation from a loose confederation of thirteen distinctly different British colonies.  That new nation has gone through a series of “revolutions” that have many of their roots in issues that were apparent even at the time of the original revolution against British rule in the 1770s.  Slavery was the most difficult issue, and the disputes over slavery led to a terrible Civil War in 1861-65.  The nation was re-formed after the Civil War, but almost collapsed again during the Great Depression that began with the stock market crashes of 1929.  The result of government intervention in the economy was the creation of a new concept of the central government as fundamental as that which occurred after 1865.  In the 1950s and 1960s the Civil Rights Movement was a peaceful revolution that ended the last legal vestiges of slavery.  The Constitution has been the fundamental framework and point of reference for all dramatic national changes.  It remains so today, and it also is the matrix for determining the scope of personal, individual rights.  Study of the history of the Constitution, the governing document of the oldest democratic republic in continuous existence, provides an opportunity to analyze and to understand the role of law in creating and maintaining a stable, but flexible, framework for the ordering of a heterogeneous society.
name: US Constitutional Law & Hist

description: This course deals with the law and practice relating to the negotiation, drafting and interpretation of contracts. It begins by looking at the theory and practice of negotiation. It then considers the evidentiary problems of different ways of making contracts, ranging from contracts which are wholly oral to those which are wholly written and signed. Next, the course focuses on how contracts and contract terms are construed and interpreted. Finally, the principles learnt are put into practice through examining standard form contracts and other documents.
name: Cont Nego, Draft & Interpret

description:
Mergers and acquisitions raise legal issues that will affect strategy, deal structure, legal responsibilities and liabilities. An understanding and sensitivity to such issues will be valuable for future business leaders, investment bankers, business consultants and entrepreneurs and will enhance their effectiveness. 
This course examines mergers and acquisitions transactions from the transactional perspective. The topics that would be covered include mechanics of structuring mergers and acquisitions transactions, the preparatory work that is required in connection therewith, the regulatory environment in which mergers and acquisitions take place, duties of participants engaged in mergers and acquisitions (including financial advisers and directors of acquirors and target companies), deal protections, deal tactics for friendly and hostile bids, disclosure obligations, compulsory acquisitions and financing. 
The course aims to provide an understanding of the legal regime under which mergers and acquisitions are regulated in Singapore and the focus is on the acquisition of publicly listed companies. Comparisons with jurisdictions such as United States, Australia, United Kingdom and Hong Kong will be made. 
Case studies, adapted from real life examples, will be used extensively in the course. 

The prerequisites for the course are Business Law and Company Law.
name: Law of Mergers & Acquisitions

description:
Alongside information technology, biotechnology and the life sciences has been
identified as one of the major engines to power Singapore’s industrial and economic growth in her next phase of economic development. Indeed, the life science industry is already highly competitive in the international market place. Established players include, the United States, the European Union (especially the United Kingdom) and Japan. Significant new entrants include: China, India, Malaysia, South Korea and of course Singapore.

This course seeks to provide students with an overview of the interface between life
sciences, biotechnology and the law. The course will commence with lectures and
discussions of the science behind the modern biotechnology revolution. This will set the scene for a teasing out of some of the main areas where legal issues have arisen of late.  What then follows is a discussion in more detail of some specific areas. Whilst the selection of specific areas will vary from year to year, the main areas are likely to be incentive aspects (the need for appropriate intellectual and industrial property rights); public health aspects (access to medicines and the impact of modern patent laws); third world development and environmental aspects (biodiversity and biopiracy issues especially in relation to the interface between TRIPs and the Convention on Biodiversty) and the rights of individuals and genetic information (genetic privacy, genetic research and related matters).

name: Law, Life Sci & Gene Engrg

description:
Negotiation introduces students to fundamental concepts in interest-based negotiation. The 7 elements of interest-based negotiation will provide the participants with a framework for a more structured approach towards preparing for and handling negotiation.

Students will also learn various communication and relationship building strategies. A number of these concepts are from the field of neuro-linguistic programming. The application of such concepts is new and represents one of the latest advances in the field of negotiation.

In addition, students will be provided with a dynamic communication framework for the analysis of negotiations. The focus will be on why some conversations seem to be fraught with difficulty and how a negotiator can have more productive conversations during and even after negotiations.

Fluency in English, both written and spoken is necessary and may impact assessment.

Attendance at ALL classes is crucial and will impact assessment, in particular the 1st two classes as these are foundational classes. Please note that unconfirmed students will NOT be allowed to attend the class.

description:
Conflict Resolution introduces students to fundamental concepts in interest-based conflict management. The 7 elements of interest-based conflict management will provide the participants with a framework for a more structured approach towards preparing for and handling conflict.

Students will also learn the various stages of a mediation session based on the model endorsed by the SMC. There will be discussions about what each stage seeks to achieve and illustrations on how to work towards the goals.

In addition, students will be introduced to various key communication skills which form the basic skills-set required for conflict management. They will learn that effective communications is critical to conflict management. They will also be given practical strategies that they can use to overcome different types of impasse that they are likely to encounter while mediating.

Fluency in English, both written and spoken is necessary and may impact assessment.

Attendance at ALL classes is crucial and will impact assessment, in particular the 1st two classes as these are foundational classes. Please note that unconfirmed students will NOT be allowed to attend the class.

Students will also learn the various stages of a mediation session based on the model endorsed by the SMC. There will be discussions about what each stage seeks to achieve and illustrations on how to work towards the goals.

In addition, students will be introduced to various key communication skills which form the basic skills-set required for conflict management. They will learn that effective communications is critical to conflict management. They will also be given practical strategies that they can use to overcome different types of impasse that they are likely to encounter while mediating.

Fluency in English, both written and spoken is necessary and may impact assessment.

Attendance at ALL classes is crucial and will impact assessment, in particular the 1st two classes as these are foundational classes. Please note that unconfirmed students will NOT be allowed to attend the class.

description:
The results of sale transactions are all around us. Most goods – such as the chair you may be sitting on, the computer from which you may be reading this, and the food you may have recently eaten - have reached consumers and business organizations as a result of sales. The buying and selling of goods is a fundamental aspect of domestic and international business, and Singapore is a well-known centre of trade, as a consumer of both local and foreign goods. Given that sale transactions are a common part of daily life, a sound understanding of the law regulating sales is important for an entrepreneur and for the management of resources in organizations.

This course will provide an overview of the rules that apply to sale transactions, an understanding of major differences between domestic and international sales, common trade terms, and major methods of financing sales and of transporting goods across borders. It will also provide an understanding of the wider national and international environments in which international trade takes place, including product liability laws, major methods of resolving trade disputes, and important regulatory issues, such as WTO rules, and laws on customs, competition, technology transfer and security.
name: Law of International Trade

attributes: TRCK - Finance Major: International Trading Track
college: Yong Pung How School of Law

departments.name: Yong Pung How School of Law

description:
Singapore has been an entrepôt economy and a bustling trade center in Asia ever since Sir Stamford Raffles decided to shift operations from Penang to Singapore. Like most developed countries, Singapore’s economy includes many features of a knowledge economy and a trade in intangible wealth. But the buying and selling of goods continues to be an important part of the economy as evidenced by Singapore’s port with its excellent infrastructure which continues to be one of the busiest in the world. 

Selling of goods across borders involves several more parties and transactions than a domestic sale of goods transaction. The buyers and sellers probably themselves are sellers and buyers of the same goods to other persons. Naturally they would want their rights and duties to be consistent through the string of contracts. Just as a Chinese ideogram will mean the same to Chinese speaking different dialects, common trade terms that possess a common meaning to buyers and sellers from different countries with different languages are needed. A Seller will not want to part with his goods until he is paid and buyer will not want to pay until she has received the goods. Banks will therefore have to pay a critical part to facilitate the deal. Goods have to be carried across borders usually in ships under shipping contracts known as contracts of carriage. Also prudent parties will wish to arrange insurance.

What could be a simple sales transaction in a domestic setting becomes complicated in an international sale of goods transactions because these very same parties now have to also conclude other legal relationships with banks, carriers, and insurers. These multiple legal transactions will be contained a variety of contracts, for example, in a sale of goods contract either governed by a local sale of goods act or by the Convention on the International Sale of Goods. The obligations of the parties about time of payment, shipping, and risk of loss will be captured in trade terms such as CIF, FOB, C&F that will be shorthand understood by trading professionals. Bills of Exchange and Letters of Credit will be used to pay for the goods and marine insurance contracts will be used to protect buyers and sellers. 

The outcome of the course will be to provide the student with a sound grasp of the basic principles underlying these inter-connected subjects. There will be a prescribed text that will be supplemented by readings of some leading Singapore cases and applicable legislation.

description: This elective will introduce students to common sources of business disputes including contract, intellectual property, product liability and regulatory disputes. It will then examine the various forms of methods used to settle such business disputes especially in a cross-border context, as well as dispute avoidance techniques. It will cover the advantages and disadvantages of negotiations, mediation, arbitration, litigation and trade actions available to private business operators, relevance of regional arbitration bodies, ASEAN and other regional trade arrangements, and how business disputes that escalate to State level are resolved at the World Trade Organization and other external fora. The course will be taught interactively through seminars, role-play scenarios and group discussions.

The course will focus on the current practical legal issues related to the above mentioned areas.

description:
This course is designed to familiarize students with the aspects of Chinese Law which are most relevant in the recent development of the Chinese legal system. The course begins by looking at significant historical events and traditional Chinese legal concepts as well as the current legal situation and their impact on the social and economic development of Chinese society. The main emphasis will be on current legislative bodies, the law-making process, the judicial system, the court system and the interpretation of law in China. By the end of the course, students should have a better understanding of the present Chinese legal system and the problems it faces. 
This course will be conducted in Mandarin and students who enroll in this course must be proficient in reading and writing Chinese.
name: Chinese Legal Sys (Mandarin)

departments.name: Yong Pung How School of Law

description:
China’s rapid economic development in the last 30 years has attracted increasing global attention. More than ever before, foreign businesses and businessmen are heading to China to do business or to work. Often, these businessmen encounter culture shock and other problems even though they are able to speak Chinese. This is because of inadequate preparation before going to China. They are often handicapped by their limited knowledge and understanding of China. This course is therefore designed to meet this need. It is aimed at helping to produce bilingual and bicultural professionals who will be better equipped to do business in China. This course will therefore be conducted in Mandarin, and introduce students to important aspects of modern China: its rich and long history; traditional culture, complicated economic development and unique legal system. In the short term, it will help students going to China for internship or Study Missions to enhance their language skills and acquire a general background understanding of modern China. In the long run, it will stand them in good stead in the future when they do business with or work in China.

This course will be conducted in Mandarin. Students should be able to understand, read and write Mandarin. Basically, students who have passed their GCE O-level Chinese examination should be qualified to take this course. Students who come from China and have received education above high school level in China are not eligible to take this course.

description:
Since its establishment in 1994, the World Trade Organization (WTO) has become the most important international organization for business firms across the globe. Its ever expansive rules now cover issues ranging from trade in both industrial and agricultural products, trade in services, labor mobility, investment, free trade agreements, and a wide variety of domestic regulatory regimes. What are these rules? How are these rules made? What are the economic rationales for these rules? What are the impacts of these rules on both international and domestic firms? How can firms use these rules to protect and advance their interests? This course, taught by a former lawyer at the WTO Secretariat, will provide students with an opportunity to examine these issues with a critical perspective.

For those who want to work for international firms, this course is important because it can help you to learn some of the most important international rules governing trade and investment worldwide. Even for those who want to work for Singapore-based firms, this course is important because WTO rules affect many businesses in Singapore, the country with the highest trade to GDP ratio in the world.

name: WTO: Law, Economics & Policy

description: This course is about India’s democracy. Born in 1947, India – both as an idea and as a polity – is uniquely complex and contradictory. With nearly 1.2 billion people, at least 22 official languages, all major religions and hundreds of caste and sub-caste groups, it is a political and social experiment unparalleled in world history.  Understanding India, in large measure, is about understanding the processes of continuity and change – of tradition and modernity – through which she experiences herself. With that objective in mind, this course will introduce students to some of the key debates and conflicts that have shaped modern India.

description: This course will introduce international law theory and practices that concern contemporary global issues, which range from the Palestinian Authority’s United Nations statehood bid, South China Sea disputes to the economic crisis in Europe.  The course is not only designed for students seeking to acquire basic knowledge necessary to pursue a career related to international relations or transnational business, but also for students who wish to understand the in-depth legal and political analysis of real-world situations.  Each class will begin with an introduction to international law principles, followed by case study discussions. The course will cover legal issues such as custom and treaties under international law, the relation between international and domestic law, the determination of statehood and recognition policy, national governments’ jurisdiction and immunity, states’ international responsibility, the role of international courts, and the legal structures of international organizations.  Due to the fast-growing development in international issues in Asia, the course will also focus on practices of Singapore, China, and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN).
name: Intl Law & Global Politics

description: This course will examine the legal and regulatory issues relating (and of concern) to the media and entertainment industry. These issues will straddle various media platforms such as print, music, film and the Internet. The areas of law that will be covered include: Contracts and licensing issues; the role of statutory bodies (i.e. MICA, MDA and IDA) and content regulation (free speech and censorship); relevant torts like defamation, the law of confidence and privacy as well as copyright and trademark issues (including rights clearances and the role of IPOS). The focus will be on the Singapore law and regulatory regime although references will be made, where relevant or necessary, to developments in foreign jurisdictions, particularly US and UK law.
name: Entertainment Law

college: Yong Pung How School of Law

departments.name: Yong Pung How School of Law

description:
There really is no subject matter called Entertainment Law.  Unlike Constitutional Law, Securities Law, Bankruptcy Law and Labour Law, which each deal with a defined area of the law, Entertainment Law is a catch-all phrase that encompasses all the various type of legal issues that attorneys have to deal with in the film, television, music and publishing industries.
This course will examine many of these legal issues, both from a case and transactional viewpoint.  Case law will focus almost exclusively on California and US cases, simply because there are so many more cases decided under these laws, and other jurisdictions tend to look to these decisions when dealing with similar factual and legal issues.  Students who understand the basic legal issues discussed will be able to find the appropriate case law in whatever jurisdiction they are practicing. Issues covered will include: contracts, torts, labour law (mostly collective bargaining agreements), (limited) copyright and trademark issues specific to film/music/publishing, Lanham Act (unregistered trademark law), and both statutory and common law causes of action particular to these industries, including accounting issues in the film industry.  
Mixed into the case studies will be an introduction to a number of common contracts in the film industry—writers, directors, actors, producers, distributors etc.---and students will learn the main deal points and many negotiating strategies surrounding these contracts.
name: Entertainment Law

description:
Law does not exist in a vacuum, and neither do businesses –law provides the backbone upon which businesses operate. Armed with some basic knowledge, entrepreneurs should be able to better structure their businesses, avoid common legal pitfalls, and identify potential problems, and take appropriate actions, both before and after the problems arise. A failure to understand –at least rudimentarily –the impact of the legal landscape and certain legal developments on business transactions often has dire consequences.

This is an introductory course designed to help acquaint students –who may be future business owners or managers –with the legal environment within which businesses operate and the common legal issues one may face when doing business in Asia, with a particular emphasis on Singapore. The course will entail not only classroom teaching and learning, but will also include invaluable sharing sessions guest speakers from various relevant fields, as well as field trips to legal institutions and/or offices in Singapore.

A substantial part of the course will be dedicated to exploring, at a general level, various aspects of laws pertaining to doing business, with an especial focus on business organisations and commercial transactions.

With cross-border business dealings being the norm instead of the exception, an understanding of the implications of contractual clauses in international contracts, and of the avenues for the resolution of international disputes, also become essential.

Because business relationships with commercial parties are primarily governed by contract, an understanding of how contracts work is important. Basic principles of contract law (e.g. the making and performance of contracts), as well as laws applying to specific situations (e.g. the sale of goods and services), will be taught in brief. Students will also be introduced to the law of torts and will, in particular, learn the essentials of the very pervasive tort of negligence, and the often-misunderstood tort of defamation.
longName: The Legal Environment of Business: An Asian Perspective
name: The Legal Env of Business

description:
Initially two obscure projects (The Silk Road Economic Belt and the 21st-century Maritime Silk Road) announced in 2013, the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) has quickly become the centre-piece of China’s economic diplomacy over the past few years. Spanning across Asia, Europe and Africa, the project is often called the “Marshall Plan” of China as it aims to promote the economic development of the
less-developed countries in the three continents.

Taught by an advisor to the WTO and the Chinese government, this course will provide an in-depth analysis for the background for the BRI, the detailed strategy of China in each areas covered such as trade and investment, and how the BRI might result in an alternative economic order led by China.

name: China's BRI: Challenges & Opp

description:
This course will introduce students to key issues in domestic and international financial crime. It begins with the basic principles of criminal law in Singapore. Students will also learn how evidence is obtained in the course of investigations and how that evidence may be used to charge and convict offenders in court. The course will then progress to cover the major types of financial crime, such as: (1) cheating, criminal breach of trust and criminal misappropriation of property; (2) corruption; (3) market misconduct: insider trading and market manipulation; (4) tax evasion; and (5) money laundering and terrorist financing. Efforts to combat international financial crime, e.g. the setting up of the Financial Action Task Force, anti-money laundering procedures, and mutual legal assistance and exchange of information regimes, will also be discussed in this course.

This course will be taught with its main audience in mind, namely, students taking a second major in Financial Forensics offered by the School of Accountancy.

The course will then progress to cover the major types of financial crime, such as: (1) cheating, criminal breach of trust and criminal misappropriation of property; (2) corruption; (3) market misconduct: insider trading and market manipulation; (4) tax evasion; and (5) money laundering and terrorist financing. Efforts to combat international financial crime, e.g. the setting up of the Financial Action Task Force, anti-money laundering procedures, and mutual legal assistance and exchange of information regimes, will also be discussed in this course.

This course will be taught with its main audience in mind, namely, students taking a second major in Financial Forensics offered by the School of Accountancy.

description:
Sustainable development has become a key concept for the 21st century and has been endorsed and recognised in a number of instruments of international law. Problems like global climate change, high pollution levels and depletion of living and non-living natural resources are becoming important restraints on the global economy. These sustainability challenges will reshape the global economy. The transition to a greener, more sustainable economic system will require collective action by governments, international organizations, multinational corporations, and civil society.  

This course reviews the principles and rules underlying the post-war international economic order, in particular with respect to trade, foreign investment and finance, as well as some of its key institutions, such as the World Bank and the World Trade Organization. The course reviews the role of international economic agreements in pursuing sustainable development.

college: Lee Kong Chian Sch of Business
description:
Ethical and socially responsible conduct and good governance are treated with increasing importance and prominence by the corporate world, governments, the public, civil society, and other stakeholders globally. The integrity, reputation and success of organizations and individuals are increasingly and intricately linked with the level of ethical conduct, social responsibility and accountability to a varied range of stakeholders.

It is also increasingly evident that society and governments expect the business world to behave ethically and be socially responsible, with self-regulation and norm-generation being favoured approaches in dealing with the impact of business on various aspects of our lives.

This course aims to sensitize participants to the issues and concerns of business ethics and social responsibility. It seeks to equip participants with the conceptual tools and thinking/ethical processes by which decisions are made and evaluated when businesses/individuals are confronted with ethical and moral dilemmas. It is also hoped that a good understanding of ethics can be applied to the development of frameworks and environments that promote good governance.

Although this is an academic course with real world relevance, it is certainly neither intended to make ‘saints’ out of ‘sinners’, or to propose the merits of a virtuous life. Instead, what it aspires towards is to engage, inform, and sensitize participants in critically evaluating the trends, societal concerns and expectations while encouraging participants to develop a personal perspective about ethics, integrity, personal and corporate responsibility—informed by rigorous and nuanced understanding of the knowledge and theoretical approaches—in business and professional life.

college: Lee Kong Chian Sch of Business
description:
This course aims to give participants a good appreciation of the law as it affects providing financial advice, marketing of financial products and compliance. 

The first part of the course assists participants to understand the law. It will address the regulatory framework imposed by statute and relevant authorities, including the Financial Advisers Act, MAS Notices, Guidelines and other publications. It also discusses tort, contract law, negligence, fiduciary duties of client advisers and consumer rights. It also addresses misrepresentation and non-reliance clauses. Participants will also be introduced to agency law, conflict of laws and the interplay between the regulatory law, tort law and contract law. 

The second part of this course will also provide an ethical and practical approach to compliance and risk in view of heightened regulatory requirements that impact wealth managers. Regulatory framework and regulations such as Anti Money Laundering, Fair Dealing and Tax Oﬀences will be introduced to discuss issues relevant to the wealth management industry, and strategy for Singapore as a wealth centre, private banks and trust companies, and for individuals seeking to make a career in the industry. In addition, different types of risks that can impact the wealth management business, and how such risks can be managed with renewed rigour in areas such as client suitability, enhanced due diligence in client onboarding will be addressed.
