description:
This course addresses the issues of intellectual property (IP) in the pursuit of capturing value. The general order of topics is: 1+2. Introduction to Intellectual Property (IP) Rights I and II; 3. How Firms Can Use IP To Extract Value: Case Study Analyses and Presentations; 4. Legal Perspective I: Different Types of IP-Related Contracts; 5. Legal Perspective II: IP Due Diligence in Corporate Transaction; 6. IP – Value Extraction: An R&D Perspective; 7. IP – Value Extraction: Examples of Value Extraction through Technological Innovation and Commercialisation; 8. Legal Perspective III: IP Management and Litigation. This course will examine the different ways in which value may be extracted from the ownership of intellectual property rights (IPRs) and provide an understanding of the threats and opportunities that IPRs provide to all businesses.

The course will start with a general introduction into intellectual property rights (IPR’s) which are important when considering the development of an effective IP management and valuation cum extraction strategy. We will also look at the legal underpinnings and the proper management of IP rights (IPRs) in the context of their commercialisation. The course will look at ways of exploiting different IPRs and the different challenges they present. We will consider how to and why it is necessary to conduct IP due diligence in corporate transactions, and participants will be taken through some practical steps that should be employed to undertake this effectively. Further, this course will show how technological and business innovations enable creation of sustainable wealth & value and outline strategies for extracting them. In continuation, it will examine practical examples of innovations to understand how they can create remarkable value. Importantly, we will consider the critical role IPRs play in extracting enterprise value. 

Based on various case studies, participants will be guided through the processes, tools and standards through which enterprises can engage in innovation, effective IPR management, commercialisation and, ultimately, value extraction.

The goal of this course is to introduce you to the real, practical considerations and opportunities involved in the management, commercialisation and effective exploitation of IPRs so that you are better able to deal with the issues as they arise and better recognise and manage these when they do.
longName: Business Sustainability, Intellectual Property and Value Extraction
name: Bus Sust, Intel Prop & Val Ext

college: Lee Kong Chian Sch of Business
description:
This course addresses the issues of intellectual property in the pursuit of capturing value. The general order of topics is:

1. Introduction to the different IP rights
2. Ownership and general contractual arrangements.
3. Dealings generally: structure and negotiation of licence agreements/assignments
4. Know-how (or trade secrets)
5. Dealings with copyright
6. IT/IS industry and IP issues
7. IP due diligence in corporate transactions
8. Internet and IPRs
9. Enforcement

This course will examine the different ways in which value may be extracted from the ownership of intellectual property rights (IPRs) and provide an understanding of the threats and opportunities that IPRs provide to all businesses.

The course will start with a short general overview of the various intellectual property rights around the world and the more important differences between particular countries, which are important when considering the development of an international IP strategy.  We will also look at some of the misconceptions about IPRs and their commercialisation.   The course will then turn to look at different ways of dealing with IPRs: assignment or sale, licensing, and joint ventures; and the different challenges they present.  We will look at the type of provisions to be included in assignments and licence agreements of the different IPRs and relate these to the possible commercial goals.  After that, we will first consider how to and why it is necessary to conduct IP due diligence in corporate transactions, what to look for and how to negotiate the documentation.  Then, IP issues in the IT industry will be explained and discussed, as well as those you will come across in relation to using the Internet or setting up an Internet-based business.  Finally, we will consider how the enforcement of IPRs plays a critical role in extracting value. 

The goal of this course is to introduce you to the real-world, commercial issues involved in the international commercialisation of IPRs so you are better able to deal with the issues as they arise and better understand the proper role of lawyers, and your interaction with them, when they do.
name: Intel Property & Value Capture

Yet it is critical for the CFO (and other members of senior management) of a corporation to have a good understanding, and some level of mastery, of the key legal issues and risks in business. The topics covered are: introduction to law (including business model protection), negligence liability, contract law, corporate law (including agency law) and international aspects.

college: School of Economics
description:
This course aims to give participants a good appreciation of the law as it affects giving financial advice and selling financial products. It provides an overview of the subject and focuses on the key legal principles, the pertinent issues and problems and the measures that may be adopted. 

A vital part of this regime is the regulatory framework imposed by statute and by the relevant authority (in Singapore, the Monetary Authority of Singapore [MAS]). The labyrinth of regulation formed by the statutes (primarily the Financial Advisers Act), the subsidiary legislation (in particular the Financial Advisers Regulations) and the MAS Notices, Guidelines and other publications) is a comprehensive and complex framework which financial advisers  must understand, comply with and leverage upon. The course aims to give participants a good snapshot of this framework.

The counterpart to the regulatory regime is the civil liability regime, which has two main parts: tort law (primarily the tort of negligence) and contract law. As regards negligence, participants in the financial advice industry have rights and liabilities towards each other. The law of negligence is vast; in this course, we take a summary look at the tort of negligence and consider its application to financial advisory activity. 

As regards contract law, the course gives a quick overview of contract law and focuses on some of the more important issues and concepts pertinent to financial advisory work, such as misrepresentation and non-reliance clauses. 

In addition to tort law and contract law, participants will be briefly introduced to  fiduciary duty and international legal aspects. 

Participants are encouraged to ask freely any questions about the law in general or financial advisers law in particular.
name: Financial Advisors and the Law

description:
This course is an introduction to intellectual property rights (IPRs), and their relationship to the knowledge economy. In a world where everything from songs to seeds, and colours to shapes, can be protected (and copied), a basic understanding of IPRs is essential. This course examines the various categories of rights, and the different threats and opportunities that they present for businesses. It also considers the extent to which IPRs can foster or hinder creativity and innovation.

During this course, we will differentiate the types of IPRs (such as patent, copyright, and trademark), and understand their strategic value in a commercial context. We will demystify basic terminology and debunk the key misconceptions and myths that exist. We will also explore diverse conceptual frameworks and approaches to thinking about ownership vs. licensing, proprietary vs. open source, and offense vs. defense. It is often said that IPRs can be both sword and shield: we will consider practical examples that demonstrate this duality, as well as the related tactical considerations for start-ups as well as established enterprises. 

The goal of this course is to introduce you to core concepts and practical considerations involved in the creation and management of IPRs, so that you are better able to deal with potential issues as they arise. It should help you ask important questions and weigh in on IP policies and approaches at your workplace.
name: Intel. Property, Data & Innov.

description: Linguistics is the study of language in all its aspects. The purpose of this course is to acquaint students with some general principles of human language based on the fact that our capacity for language sets us apart from other species. The course will describe the structure of human languages (the heart of Linguistics), their history and the ways in which they evolve. The course will also cover the major branches of the discipline including phonetics and phonology, syntax, morphology, semantics, pragmatics and students will be introduced to the principles of applied linguistics such as sociolinguistics, psycholinguistics, neurolinguistics and second language acquisition.

Calculus primarily deals with change and the rate of change, although, the basic concepts of Calculus have not changed for the past few hundred years. description: The traditional understanding of the term “entrepreneurship” focuses on the creation of new ventures. Entrepreneurship can be practiced within existing for-profit and not-for-profit organisations, large and small. This process is known as corporate entrepreneurship.  Many organisations practice corporate entrepreneurship as a way of constantly rejuvenating itself, evolving to stay relevant to new trends and technologies, and to enter a new industry sector.  This course trains students to become more entrepreneurial in large corporations. It examines theoretical models and practical manners through which organisations practice corporate entrepreneurship. Students will study the entrepreneurial process from examples including nascent corporate new ventures and the eventual spin-off of such ventures.

description: Large, established corporations face fundamentally different innovation challenges than new or young small firms. The routinization of practices, obsolescence of such routines and dominant logic that may be misaligned with changes in the environment subject large firms to great difficulties in innovating. Further, revenue cannibalization with existing products and the politics of allocating scarce resources away from established, competing product divisions afflict how new ventures are created within large corporations.  These issues have few parallels in new, small firms.  In view of typically bureaucratic hierarchies in large corporations, it is important for students to understand how to design and manage innovation systems for large corporations, as well as how to lead corporate entrepreneurship.
name: Corporate Entre. & Innovation

description:
This course aims to introduce students the evolving body of knowledge known as Complex Adaptive Systems (CAS), the technology movement and mindset that has replaced the outdated Newtonian machine-like mindset of the past. Nurturing this new mindset is highly crucial in a knowledge-intensive and fast changing environment.  It will also introduce students to technological/scientific concepts/systems such as autopoiesis, self-organization, rugged landscape, genetic algorithm systems, biodiversity systems and horizon scanning systems. It will illustrate the new encompassing strategic thinking / planning using CAS technology (known as the intelligence strategy).

The course will be interactive and will also cover the complex adaptive dynamics of the human thinking systems and their organizations, the nonlinearity of intelligence, and the significance of nonlinear strategic thinking. Further, important concepts like 
Chaos theory and complexity theory such as consciousness, complexity, connectivity, dissipation, emergence and dialogue will be discussed to show how they can be better exploited by human organizations.  The course will illustrate to you the characteristics and significance of the edge of chaos, the butterfly effect, the red queen race, and their relationships with innovation and creativity.
name: Intelligent Organisations

attributes: TRCK - Public Policy, Devt, & Mgt Track (Business)
college: Lee Kong Chian Sch of Business

departments.name: Lee Kong Chian School of Business

description: This course introduces to management students the concept of organising around intelligence (a new organisation form known as intelligent organisation), and the intelligence strategy (a new form of leadership and management philosophy/theory). It is a fresh mindset that perceives human organisations as composite complex adaptive systems with human beings as their interacting agents. Such a mindset is vital for survival in the knowledge intensive environment. The topics covered in this course include Introduction to Intelligent Organisation Theory, Basic Properties/Characteristics of Chaos and Complexity Theory, Complex Adaptive Systems and the Edge of Chaos, The Human Thinking System and Physical Symbol System, Intelligence and Its Nonlinear Characteristics, Intelligent Organisations and their Structure and Collective Intelligence, Organisational Learning and Knowledge Management, Innovation and Creativity, Evolution and Co-evolution, Intelligent Information and Knowledge Networks, The 3C-OK Framework, Deliberate and Emergence Strategy, and The Intelligent Person Model.
name: Intelligent Organisations

college: Lee Kong Chian Sch of Business

description: The course aims to introduce to interested students some basic concepts of Chaos, Complexity Theory (Complex Adaptive System)and Evolution Theory such as consciousness, complexity, connectivity, dissipation, emergence, autopoiesis, self-organization, biodiversity, rugged landscape and dialogue, and how they can be better exploited by human/business organizations to increase their competitiveness in a knowledge-intensive and fast changing environment. The complex adaptive dynamics of the human thinking systems and their organizations, the nonlinearity of intelligence, and intelligence management will also be discussed. The concept of organizing around intelligence and the significance of nurturing an intelligent organization with a biotic structure that encompasses an intense intelligence source (orgmind) will also be studied (intelligent organization theory). Additional significant and critical CAS properties such as the edge of chaos, the butterfly effect, the red queen race, smarter evolvers and their relationships with risk-taking, sustainability, and innovation and creativity will be explained. Ultimately, the course will illustrate to you the new and more holistic thinking/planning, such as the integrated deliberate and emergent strategy, and the intelligence leadership and management theory.

Enterprise development is the process involved in managing the various stages in an enterprise with focus on the early phases of its life cycle, including the factors that contribute to its survival. 

This course will provide students with experiential learning opportunities in order to acquire the relevant knowledge and skills in running and growing a new business.

description:
Enterprise development is the process involved in managing the various stages in an enterprise with focus on the early phases of its life cycle, including the factors that contribute to its survival.

This course will focus on development of online businesses, which often attract entrepreneurs with their low capital requirements, ease of experimentation, high profile successes, and possibilities of achieving scale. Existing brick and mortar businesses also can relate to the opportunities as they seek growth and innovation potential in the online economy.

But online start-ups face distinctive managerial challenges, eg that most are often grounded in network effects, requiring the mobilization of many users to deliver value. It is noted that key online platforms are already in control of powerful incumbents, how can upstarts find opportunities?

The following are some of the questions that will be addressed:
a)	What do enterprises need to do during their mobilization phase?
b)	What are the key elements they need as they scale up?
c)	How do they compete against others and keep themselves afloat?
d)	What are practical issues related to technical implementation and how risks are mitigated?
e)	What are monetization and Market Design strategies to create a well functioning online ecosystem?
Students will be given opportunities to discover theory constructs of research of online businesses and to relate their perspectives to their potential business/ ideas to ensure the success of a new enterprise.

This course is designed to equip students planning entrepreneurial ventures in online businesses or those interested in careers as managers, investors or consultants with focus on online businesses.

description: This course examines these issues and challenges faced by family businesses. Family businesses play a significant role in many economies. They have proven to be resilient over generations. While their unique features as families in business have enabled many family businesses to sustain their growth over time, these same qualities can prove to be hindrances to their competitiveness. The success of family businesses also depends on successful intergenerational transfer. For continued growth, there may be a need to introduce professional management in the form of practices and professional personnel. The introduction of modern management into family businesses is needed yet this is an area that family businesses have great difficulty with particularly with the introduction of professional managers who are not family members. Family businesses require governance structures that can accommodate both the business and family relationships.

description:
Family businesses are the most prevalent form of business in the world. It is also an emerging and vibrant area of interest today among academics, practitioners and students of management. This course explores the unique challenges and opportunities involves in ownership and management of family businesses. Key family, ownership and management issues relevant to the management and continuity of these enterprises will be covered. Topics in this course include the uniqueness of family business, succession, governance, working with non-family managers, communication, strategy and continuity. 

This course will be useful to students from business-owning families. As most of the business organizations in Asia are family-owned, this course will also benefit students who may work for a family business in the course of their future career. Students who wish to enter the private banking, wealth management, corporate banking and consulting industry will find knowledge gained in this course helpful to their work. Anyone who thinks the interaction of two somewhat mutually exclusive systems – the family and the business - difficult will find this course fascinating.

description:
In knowledge economies for firms to succeed and grow the entrepreneurial behaviour has to shift from opportunity seeking to opportunity creation. description: The primary topic of this course is strategic management in the Chinese context, including that of both local Chinese companies and foreign companies operating in China, but with a somewhat greater focus on the former. The course has two primary features. First, it broadly encompasses three levels of strategies of companies competing in the Chinese context: business strategies, corporate strategies, and cross-border competitive strategies. Second, in analyzing the strategies of companies competing in the Chinese context, the course will take a comparative perspective. The key frameworks in strategic management are mostly developed in the West. Since there are fundamental differences in macro national environment, competitive industry, and firm strategic issues between China and the West, whether the existing frameworks are applicable to the Chinese context is thus a key concern. We shall discuss throughout the course the similarities and differences between strategic management issues in the West and in China.

description:
The course provides an introduction to environmental and human sustainability (i.e., human development) issues, and the means of solving such problems. Environmental sustainability, and more generally, sustainability, has become increasingly important to developed and developing nations alike. The typical issues include resource scarcity and polluted environments, but the more recent issue of climate change has become a major issue. In contrast, sustainability issues in poorer regions usually involve human development concerns, such as reducing poverty and improving health and fulfilling other basic needs. Nearly half of the course will be on managing such issues of human development issues (and indirectly, their intertwined nature with environmental problems). Where possible, we will show the links between environmental sustainability and poverty. While solutions to these problems may require the involvement of the private sector (firms), the public sector (government) and the community, firms are increasingly called on to reduce their negative impacts on the environment and humans alike. The course will focus in particular on how business can address sustainability issues. Sustainability issues often consist of complex interactions between human activity and the environment. The course will apply several academic perspectives to characterizing these problems and their possible solutions. 

The course first examines how particular patterns of economic and social development are manifested in past practices and developmental paths, such as unsustainable patterns of urbanization and industrialization. The private sector is an integral part of many problems and solutions, and as such, will be the main focus of the course. An important part of addressing sustainability is the use of various frameworks to help incorporate a sustainability perspective into firms’ strategies and operations. These often employ a systems perspective. To help characterize firm’ sustainability and determine appropriate courses of action, the course will cover also specific managerial tools and frameworks that help to characterize sustainability challenges and incorporate them into corporate plans include the Triple Bottom Line, Life-Cycle Assessment, and the Base of the Pyramid approach and its business models. Where necessary, material on and links to concepts of strategy, business models, stakeholder engagement, public policy (in terms of governance), and innovation will be made.

The course covers various policy or “governance”, as well as private sector management, responses to these challenges. Issues and solutions will address a variety of higher level organizing concepts (e.g. risk and resilience), scales of analysis (regional, global issues), sectors (e.g. manufacturing, energy), environmental media (e.g. water), systems perspectives (e.g. material flows and lifecycle perspectives), forms of governance (e.g. economic and regulatory mechanisms), and management issues (organizations and practices). Similarly, the poor in the East and in other developing regions face many of the same issues as seen in other developing and developed regions, and so cross-comparisons between different regions can yield many lessons.

description:
This course provides an introduction to environmental sustainability and human development issues, and the means of framing, analysing and solving such problems. A part of the course will focus on Asia, but given the global prevalence of the issues, and that many of the experiences and concepts derive from other regions, we will also draw from studies on other developed and developing regions.
 
Environmental sustainability, and more generally, sustainability, has become increasingly important to developed and developing nations alike. Typical issues include resource scarcity and polluted environments, but more recently, global climate change has become the primary issue for many. In general, sustainability issues often consist of complex interactions between human activity and the environment. The course will apply several academic perspectives to characterizing these problems and their possible solutions.
 
We will first examine how patterns of economic and social development are manifested in past practices and developmental paths, such as unsustainable patterns of urbanization and industrialization. In contrast, sustainability issues in poorer regions usually involve human development concerns, such as reducing poverty, improving health and fulfilling basic needs. As such, at least one third of the course will address poverty and other human development issues, or issues recognizing the intertwined nature of poverty and environmental problems.
 
The course will focus in particular on businesses’ role in causing and addressing sustainability problems. An important part of addressing the sustainability of firms is the use of various frameworks to help incorporate a sustainability perspective into firms’ strategies and operations. To help characterize firms’ sustainability and determine appropriate courses of action, the course will cover specific managerial tools and frameworks that help to characterize sustainability challenges, including the Triple Bottom Line, Life-Cycle Assessment, the Base of the Pyramid approach, and business models for addressing poverty. The primary focus will be on strategy and business models that operationalize change, but the course will also introduce the roles of various business functions as they relate to the sustainability of the firm, including marketing, supply chains, and financing.
 
Where possible, we also recognize the role of public policy for governance, and the role of innovation. Technology issues covered include the role of information technology in addressing poverty, and solutions that reorganize the industrial system (e.g. renewable energy policies and industrial “ecosystems”, i.e., industrial regions that built on recycling loops). The course will also briefly cover economic concepts, which are used in policy solutions as well as to analyse firm-level outcomes, e.g. risks, costs and benefits to a firm’s actions. Finally, solutions to many sustainability problems may require partnerships between the private sector (firms), the public sector (government) and the community. We will operationalize the analysis of partnerships through business models.
 
While many modern sustainability concepts have a Western origin, because of our location in Asia and the increasing importance of sustainability to the local and regional context, aspects of the course will either include Asian issues or comparisons to Asia.

description:
This course provides an introduction to environmental sustainability and human development issues, and the means of framing, analysing and solving such problems. As environmental and social problems mount around the world, firms have become more attuned to the need to devise new products, services and strategies, and to communicate these to a variety of stakeholders, even as they cooperate with them.

Environmental sustainability, and more generally, sustainability, has become increasingly important to developed and developing nations alike. Typical issues include resource scarcity and polluted environments, but more recently, global climate change has become the primary issue for many. In general, sustainability issues often consist of complex interactions between human activity and the environment. The course will apply several academic perspectives to characterizing these problems and their possible solutions. 

The course will focus in particular on businesses’ role in causing and addressing sustainability problems and on how they moderate their impacts. An important part of addressing the sustainability of firms is the employment of various concepts and frameworks that help incorporate the sustainability perspective into firms’ strategies and operations. To help characterize firms’ sustainability and determine appropriate courses of action, the course will cover specific managerial tools and frameworks. The primary focus will be on strategy and business models that support change and its operationalization, but the course will also illustrate the role that “greening” other business functions play in the sustainability of the firm, including those of marketing, supply chains, and financing. The course will review core management frameworks to help non-business major students become familiar with more sustainability-specific frameworks, practices and concepts to be covered. These tools are not only means for improving a firm’s sustainability performance, but also support its transparent and effective reporting. Representative examples of sustainability measurement standards will be introduced and their potential impacts in advancing corporate sustainability will be discussed. The course will also reflect on the general role of innovation in all of this. Technology issues covered include the role of information technology in addressing poverty, and solutions that reorganize the industrial system (e.g. renewable energy policies, and industrial ecosystems or industrial symbiosis, i.e., industries that incorporate recycling loops at regional levels).

description:
This course provides an introduction to environmental and human sustainability management, and develops an approach for solving sustainability problems by designing new and better solutions. Sustainability is becoming an increasingly important if not critical problem for developed and developing nations alike: typical issues include unsustainable resource extraction, polluted environments, and recently, climate change. Finally, sustainability issues in poorer regions involve human development concerns, such as poverty, health and other basic needs. Firms are increasingly seeking to reduce their negative impact on the environment and humans alike. 

Sustainability is a complicated topic due to the myriad human and economic effects, and people need to be engaged on a different (more sustainable) basis. This requires multiple disciplinary perspectives to identify and solve problems. The course largely adopts the perspective of a design course while covering many of the same topics a traditional sustainability management course would, but this course will focus on creating solutions from a human-centered design perspective, taking into account systems-related (e.g. environmental constraints), firm-level concerns (e.g. economic feasibility, measures of sustainability, and frameworks to be more sustainable), and consumers and stakeholders. 

The primary focus of the course and the course project will be environmental sustainability. The course will examine a range of tools that companies have for characterizing how their production activities affect the environmental system, and for ameliorating their impacts. At the product or service level, this includes lifecycle assessments (evaluating impacts over the total product lifecycle), forming closed loops (i.e. recycling or reusing waste) that reduce pollution, and designing for the environment (using non-toxic or lower-polluting materials). In addition, we cover firm level benchmarking tools that capture the full chain of production, such as the Global Reporting Initiative’s sustainability reporting guidelines and the Triple Bottom Line. 

The class will teach and employ design techniques for assessing users’ needs and wants, so that the projects can generate ideas for prototypical sustainable products and services that are wanted. The projects will be expected to develop at least one way by which these designs can gain better “traction”, such as by better designing the business model (e.g. marketing of the product), the supply chain, or by designing a social influence system or public policy to support this. While most projects are expected to be about the environment, social sustainability problems (e.g. ageing consumers, impoverished farmers in the supply chain) may also be tackled in projects so long as these can be justified to be a primary concern of the firms. Some of the same tools can be used but will have to be augmented by the students’ research. 

The last section of the course will cover approaches for characterizing and solving problems from a human development perspective in developing regions. The last section of the course will examine possible means for helping poorer regions and peoples to “lift” themselves out of poverty by way of engaging with business, organizing their communities, and other institutional solutions. This is known as the “base of the pyramid” perspective. It will also form the basis for the personal essay, but students will be expected to read ahead in order to complete this by the end of the course. 

 
The course employs a variety of pedagogical approaches to learning. 
•	Small cases and articles will be discussed on a weekly basis, along with the main readings. The central text will be supplemented with cases and other readings. The reading will be heavy, and will involve at least three to four chapters, articles and/or cases per week. 
•	For the group projects, in addition to the analysis performed in the ‘small project’, in the ‘main design project’, we will adopt a “lighter” qualitative human-centered design approach to determining basic human (consumer) wants and needs, and where possible, stakeholders’ needs. (This is due to the importance of consumers in “accepting” any solution, and their lifestyles in affecting the environment.) We will use these findings to brainstorm ideas and eventual concept-level solutions to a given company’s product or service, and its environmental impacts. 

Students taking the course should be comfortable with the nature of design thinking (involving a heavy project component and high uncertainty), as well as with a reading-intensive course. While the course covers aspects of design thinking, it does not require design thinking and is different from/complementary to a design thinking elective. The course covers selected design stages in more depth (e.g. understanding consumer needs and more meanings in order to come up with meaningful product ideas), does not cover the full design cycle (e.g. does not cover rapid prototyping or field observational work), and covers systems thinking (for capturing sustainability concerns). Thus, it is not a substitute for design thinking, but applies aspects of design thinking to sustainability problems.

description: This course provides an introduction to environmental sustainability and human development issues, and the means of framing, analysing and solving such problems. As environmental and social problems mount around the world, firms have become more attuned to the need to devise new products, services and strategies, and to communicate these to a variety of stakeholders, even as they cooperate with them.Environmental sustainability, and more generally, sustainability, has become increasingly important to developed and developing nations alike. Typical issues include resource scarcity and polluted environments, but more recently, global climate change has become the primary issue for many. In general, sustainability issues often consist of complex interactions between human activity and the environment. The course will apply several academic perspectives to characterizing these problems and their possible solutions. The course will focus in particular on businesses’ role in causing and addressing sustainability problems and on how they moderate their impacts. An important part of addressing the sustainability of firms is the employment of various concepts and frameworks that help incorporate the sustainability perspective into firms’ strategies and operations. To help characterize firms’ sustainability and determine appropriate courses of action, the course will cover specific managerial tools and frameworks. The primary focus will be on strategy and business models that support change and its operationalization, but the course will also illustrate the role that “greening” other business functions play in the sustainability of the firm, including those of marketing, supply chains, and financing. The course will review core management frameworks to help non-business major students become familiar with more sustainability-specific frameworks, practices and concepts to be covered. These tools are not only means for improving a firm’s sustainability performance, but also support its transparent and effective reporting. Representative examples of sustainability measurement standards will be introduced and their potential impacts in advancing corporate sustainability will be discussed. The course will also reflect on the general role of innovation in all of this. Technology issues covered include the role of information technology in addressing poverty, and solutions that reorganize the industrial system (e.g. renewable energy policies, and industrial ecosystems or industrial symbiosis, i.e., industries that incorporate recycling loops at regional levels).

The last part of the course will examine sustainability in poorer regions as being about addressing human development concerns.

description: To achieve superior performance in an increasingly dynamic and uncertain global business environment, companies in every industry must create internal capability to harness strategic change for sustainable competitive advantage. However, companies that are able to strategically change their entrenched ways of doing things and then reclaim leading positions are the exception rather than the rule. With the industry 4.0 upon us and fast advancement in digital technologies, firms in many industries would find it even more pressing but challenging to build the managerial capabilities to cope with the digital transformation that will reshape the business landscape tremendously for the future. Against this backdrop, this course discusses how companies can effectively manage the strategic change and digital transformation that will significantly impact the way the business is configured for competitive advantage. Besides the internal managerial challenge, the course also emphasizes that companies must cope with strategic interactions with different industry players to create value collectively and continuously. With respect to digital transformation, the course discusses digital concepts and technologies such as omni-channel, platforms, eco-systems, blockchain, IOT, AI, and cloud computing etc. that impose both challenges and opportunities for strategic change management in the increasingly technology-based, internet-based, and data-based business contexts.

description:
This course will explore how ‘play’ can enhance creative design processes to promote innovation and invention. Play was borne out of not only human desires for leisure and frivolity, but cultural and biological needs such as learning and community bonding. Recently, it has been observed that inventors in history have conceived of new ideas and products, even technological inventions, in a playful manner (Johnson, 2016). Playful invention processes could be serious experimental (and risky) efforts, or playfully frivolous ones. The course will analyze and apply creative and inventive processes, with the focus on how the mind can explore more widely and inventively by becoming less self-conscious and critical through play. 

Playful invention facilitates creativity by blending ideas together from different domains, causing ‘forms’ to transcend boundaries, and ultimately, to reshape not only leisure, but other domains and culture itself. This creative blending helps cross-fertilize domains with new ideas. We will examine how inventors ‘playfully created’ in different domains such as narrative, visual arts, space (including architectural space), and games. While most of the cultural domains covered relate to historical and current popular culture, we also pay attention to specific local and ‘globalized national’ cultures.

At least half of the course focuses on the actual practice of techniques that are related to the conceptual study of domains and thinking processes. We will adapt the design thinking process to incorporate additional brainstorming techniques (including domain-specific ideation techniques) and user-centered prototyping while removing the ‘project client’ typically seen in design thinking projects. In addition, we will illustrate and practice how to design using domains as lenses into the design of forms related to those domains. 

A significant part of the course will involve a project to design an innovative experience or other ‘form’ using these creativity and design techniques. In-class (or online) group exercises and projects will be used to demonstrate and practice these techniques, and full class attendance is expected in order to participate in these group exercises and group work.

description:
This course will explore how ‘play’ can shape invention and innovative cultures. Inventors have been observed to be playfully conceiving new product designs and experiences in history as well as in technological innovation. The course investigates this link between play and invention through a broad treatment of the phenomena that examines historical and modern cultural domains (the historical treatment will comprise half or more of the examples). Play was borne out of not only of human desires for leisure and frivolity, but also necessity and cultural purposes, e.g. learning and community bonding respectively. We will broadly construe the forms of play relevant to invention to include not only the creation of playful artifacts, but also the playing around (or playfulness) observed in inventors’ actions, and the passions of inventors.

The course articulates the relationship between play and invention through both, study, and actual practice using creativity tools and design techniques. We illustrate the link between play and invention through studies of inventors’ life experiences, where their “playing” with concepts, technology and even cultural interpretations helped them to foster new ideas and inventions. Such play involves the creative combining of different concepts, which involves crossing boundaries between knowledge domains, and experimentation. In practicing the ‘play-to-invent’ relationship, we will cover creativity tools for ‘ideating’ concepts from diverse sources of knowledge, and design prototyping methods to flesh out and trial the ideas and concepts. In-class exercises and projects will serve as contexts for teaching and demonstrating these techniques. Note that while these techniques originate from the creative thinking and design fields, our goals are not to exercise sheer creativity for creativity’s sake, or to apply the full cycle of user-centered design thinking. 

To reflect on how play is relevant to successful invention, we will cover a range of social scientific concepts for understanding play in theoretical terms, as well as how play has become relevant to culture. We will also contextualize our learning by covering a range of specific creative domains, including the visual arts, fashion, shopping, narrative, visual arts, food, and digital media. Key principles are highlighted in each domain and its designed forms to help understand how invention occurs within that domain, e.g. the nature of narrative in film, and the role of blends in cuisine. We also show how blends have occurred over historical time, such as when inventors made connections across domains as distantly-related as fashion, early London and Paris shopping galleries, American suburban malls and Disney theme parks; and those of early mechanical toys, computers, and musical instruments. Play facilitates creative blending by cross-fertilizing ideas from different domains, allowing ‘forms’ to transcend boundaries, and ultimately, to radically reshape leisure and culture. 

Comparisons will be made between historical and modern ‘forms’, and examples will come from across continents, largely from European and American history. A significant part of the course will be a project to design innovative experiences or other ‘forms’ using the creative and design tools, and by incorporating the students’ understanding of the aesthetics and effects of play.
name: Play in Invention and Culture

description:
This course is about one of the unrecognized roots of innovative cultures: play. The course provides a broad treatment of play in historical and modern culture and society, including digital forms of play such as videogames and social media. The course provides students with concepts and analytical tools to understand play in theoretical terms, the relevance of play to modern life, and the innovative and economic consequences of play. 

The course will illustrate how play was borne out of human instincts for leisure and frivolity, and yet how the play of inventors contributed to and shaped historical ‘forms’ (i.e., designs, products, experiences), technological change, innovations, and economic (consumptive) activity. These effects occurred within and across sectors as variant as the visual arts, fashion, shopping and entertainment experiences, and digital entertainment. One dominant theme drawn from the main text is the set of connections between variant forms, such as that between cotton textiles, London’s and Paris’ earliest shopping galleries, America’s suburban malls and Disney’s theme parks; or that between early mechanical toys, computers, and musical instruments. 

The course will trace how play is a way of helping parts of ‘forms’ to transcend boundaries (e.g. between products or economic sectors), and therefore, to somewhat inadvertently affect mass industrialized forms of leisure and popular culture. To understand how play operates in these itinerant pathways, we will examine the role of various concepts including those of the ‘meaning’ and ‘authenticity’ of the forms (to users), the ‘creativity’ (of inventors), ‘serendipity’, social phenomena such as ‘status’, and the nature and role of technology. In several of the lessons, comparisons will be drawn between historical and modern forms of play. Many of the examples in the textbook are European and American ones, but where possible, comparisons to local cultures of play will be used to form a sense of the local roots of innovative culture. One experimental part of the course will be a project to design a paper prototype of a game that incorporates the students’ understanding of the aesthetics and effects of play.

description:
This course is about one of the unrecognized roots of innovative cultures: play. Play was borne out of human instincts for not only leisure and frivolity but also necessity and culture, e.g. learning and community bonding respectively. The play of inventors has also been premised to have contributed to and shaped historical ‘forms’ (such as the design of products, and experiences), as well as technological innovation and economic (consumptive) activity. The course provides a broad treatment of play and its relation to invention in historical and modern culture, and will touch on both historical and modern forms of play such as games, videogames and social media. 

The course examines the play-to-invent relationship in three ways. First, the course will illustrate through examples of inventors’ life experiences how their “playing” with concepts, technology and even cultural interpretations helped them to foster new ideas and inventions. Second, the course draws on a range of social sciences for concepts and analytical tools to understand play in theoretical terms, the relevance of play to invention, and more broadly, to understand play’s relevance to cultural existence. Third, exercises are used to ensure that students appreciate and can reflect on how these pathways to invention work, through being playful during creative processes. We broadly construe the forms of play relevant to invention to include not only the creation of playful artifacts, but also the playfulness observed in inventors’ acts, and the passions of inventors. 

We will look at a variety of creative domains, including the visual arts, fashion, shopping and entertainment experiences, and digital entertainment. One dominant theme (drawn from the main text) is the connections across different domains, such as that between cotton textile patterns, early London and Paris shopping galleries, America’s suburban malls and Disney’s theme parks; or that between early mechanical toys, computers, and musical instruments. Thus, a playful form of borrowing and blending effects creativity and invention by cross-fertilizing ideas from different domains. In this way, play helps ‘forms’ to transcend boundaries between domains, and ultimately, to shape leisure and culture. 

To understand how play works in inventive pathways, we will examine the role of various factors, including the ‘meaning’ and ‘authenticity’ of the forms (to users), the ‘creative processes’ seen in inventors (including ‘serendipity’), social phenomena that affect consumption of playful forms (such as ‘status’ and means of diffusion), and the nature and role of technology. Comparisons will be made between historical and modern ‘forms’, and examples will be across continents, including Europe, Asia and North America. A significant part of the course will be a project to design an innovative game, experience or other ‘form’ that incorporates the students’ understanding of the aesthetics and effects of play.

description: More and more business organizations are using A.I. technologies such as predictive analytics, deep learning or sentiment / image analysis to identify patterns and trends in vast reams of (big) data, allowing them to make ‘smarter’ decisions (e.g. about loss of customers or the necessary service inspection of equipment) and potentially to become more competitive in real-time. As A.I. technology is already surpassing human decision- making in certain instances, there is growing concern about ‘uncontrolled A.I.’ in business and society, incl. regulatory and ethical-legal challenges. Against this background, this new course aims to equip students with foundational, theoretical and practical knowledge about A.I. driven business applications in selected private and public sector organizations. At the beginning of the course, students will watch Ex-Machina (2015), a psycho- techno thriller film which tells the story of a young programmer invited to the home of a reclusive billionaire to test whether an A.I. can pass itself off as human to assess the difficulties to successfully control and ‘switch- off’ artificial intelligence once created. Besides reconstructing the history of artificial intelligence from the 1960s to the current era (as well as a refresher about the basics of computer science algorithms such as audio and video compression algorithms), we will put emphasis on explaining the A.I. driven business models of several top international and local organizations such as New Relic, Splunk, Trade Desk, Nvidia, MetaMind, DBS, NTUC, Gov Tech Agency of Singapore and the German Research Center for A.I. In order to appreciate the power of A.I. technology, we will take a closer look ‘under the A.I. hood’ to understand what makes machine learning, deep learning, neural networks and image analysis tick. Visits to A.I. powered business organizations engaged in customer service management, finance, marketing, supply chain management or manufacturing will be organised aimed at appreciating both the benefits and downside of A.I. Students graduating from this course will be equipped with critical competencies to solve real-world business problems using A.I. technology while simultaneously casting a critical eye on the morality and ethics of commercialising A.I.
name: Doing Business with A.I.

Participants of this course will have the opportunity to visit and engage in participant observation and interviews of firms, managers and entrepreneurs overseas. The purpose of the course includes exposure to the issues of international business and entrepreneurship in the cities that are part of the study mission. The design of the course encompasses pre-study mission preparatory sessions, development of study mission projects in teams, and background preparation for the projects. Integral to the course is the study mission project that participants are to initiate, plan, develop and execute during the business study mission. The project must meet criteria developed by the course facilitator and the management group area coordinator and be in line with the focus of the business study mission.

description: This course should be useful to students who want to learn about the forces driving change in emerging creative industries such as videogames, as well as how such products are developed, and how those industries come about. Please note that the course has a heavy theoretical basis. This involves building a deeper understanding of how digital media products like games come about and work. We do this by understanding how creativity, culture, technology, and processes (e.g. product development and organizational) are integrated into these media. This will help to appreciate industry and business issues. In particular, the course discusses the central role of creativity in these selected industries, as well as the factors that influence or constrain this creativity. We draw most of our examples from the video game industry, and to some extent, “digital” media such as social media, but we will also make comparisons with other industries such as IT, design, film, and animation. The course is interdisciplinary, and readings and theories will be drawn from the business, social science, and media studies traditions.
longName: The Games and Digital Media Industries
name: The Games & Digital Media Ind

description: The course should be useful to students who want to know how some of the emerging creative industries work, so that they can gain a greater appreciation of working in those industries. The course will help students understand the complex interplay of creativity, culture, technology, and product development processes in the development of the new creative industries. We draw most of our examples from the video game and “digital” or “interactive” entertainment industry, but we will also look at other creative industries such as the industrial design, film, and animation industries. Readings and theories will be drawn from the management, economics, media studies and game studies traditions. Some of these concepts and theories were developed to explain creative industries in general, while others are industry-specific. The course illustrates the central role of creativity in these selected industries, as well as the factors that influence or constrain this creativity. Creativity and the creative acts themselves are therefore the core organizing principles of the course.

description: This course provides an introduction to creative industries, including an understanding of how they develop and function, and how they are managed. Amongst other issues, the course will discuss the motivation of creative individuals, the nature of creativity, the geographic location of creative work, creative product development processes, and institutions that influence the industry. The course should be useful to students who want to know how creative industries work, so that they can work in, manage or finance them with greater appreciation. The course could also help students understand the complex interplay of technology, creativity, political economy and culture in the development of modern industry, and to provide a context for “appreciative management”, that is, developing a management “philosophy” for a system by understanding it from its roots.

description: Since the mid-1980s intra-regional trade and investment links in East and Southeast Asia have expanded rapidly with the shift of production by firms from Japan and newly industrializing countries to lower-cost, neighboring countries. Ethnic Chinese from Hong Kong, Taiwan, Singapore, Malaysia or Indonesia are actively involved in these massive transformation and integration processes. The course will scrutinize their role as well as some of the (culturally biased) misperceptions about their business conduct. The degree, to which their extensive business networks succeed because of ethnic characteristics, or simply because of the sound application of good business practice, is a key issue that will be discussed throughout the course. Based on various corporate case studies and a multi-disciplinary explanatory framework, we will assess the role, characteristics and challenges of Chinese entrepreneurship and business networks in the People’s Republic of China, Vietnam, Malaysia, Singapore and Indonesia in an era of global market expansion.
longName: Entrepreneurial Leadership in Ethnic Chinese Business
name: Entre L'ship in Ethnic Chi Biz

description: This course exposes students to the experiences of entrepreneurs.  It focuses on the implementation of tools and techniques for managing the growth and operations of small enterprises.  Here, the critical issues center on the challenges of survival, opportunity realization and continuous adjustments to the balance between leadership and management.  The course covers such topics as hiring the right people, defining their roles, building the appropriate control systems and structures, and managing their efforts.
name: Exp. in Small Bus. Consulting

attributes: TRCK - Public Policy, Devt, & Mgt Track (Business)
TRCK - Strategic Management Major: Entrepreneurship Track
college: Lee Kong Chian Sch of Business

departments.name: Lee Kong Chian School of Business

description:
With the push for entrepreneurship in Singapore, more and more small businesses are starting in Singapore.  However, small business in Singapore and around the world faces many challenges in the pursuit of growth, in particular lack of resources, in terms of quality, people, systems and capital.  In addition, most small businesses do not conduct sufficient planning.  This course will help students identify the issues of small businesses such as challenges of survival, opportunity realization, execution of their vision, leadership, recruitment of right people, motivation of staff and gathering critical resources such as capital.  Students could then have a real life experience in working with a small business owner to identify a business problem and develop a solution and plan to help the business grow.

This course provides a capstone experience for students using cases and independent work that allow them to understand the issues and challenges as well as environment of Entrepreneurs of small business in managing and growing their business.  Students will integrate their learning experiences by creating a plan project as a role of consultant to identify the challenges and competition faced by entrepreneurs.
name: Exp. in Small Bus. Consulting

description: This course is highlight relevant in the light of Enron and Informatics. The course explores the dynamics of power and control within the corporation. It provides the participants insights into how a corporation is governed as opposed to management at the operational level. Accountability and enterprise and how the tension between these two elements is maintained in corporate governance frameworks are discussed in the context of Singapore's Code of Corporate Governance and corporate law. The other topics include the corporation's officers (board, management and other key officers), board accountability, management and board relations and the role of the company auditor and company secretary. The role of directors, their fiduciary obligations and board performance are some aspects of sound corporate governance examined. The course also examines the role of governance on performance particularly on management behaviour. The differences in international corporate governance are also covered.
name: Corporate Governance

description:
Over the last 5 years, the Asia-Pacific region has experienced a resurgence of economic activity and investments. Such robust performance was underpinned by the combination of a highly favourable external environment, and buoyant domestic demand, in particular as a result of a significant strength in business investment in many economies in the region. Also, the rise of China is deemed by economists, sociologists and other academics alike as one of the pivotal developments in the region. The evolution of the business environment in the Asia Pacific region is the theme of the course.

This course consists of a set of core lectures which will introduce students to: (a) the economic, political and socio-cultural theories and frameworks for understanding the context of business in the Asia Pacific region; and (b) the application of contextual knowledge to the decision-making processes of companies operating in the region. As part of this, course participants are expected to apply the theories and frameworks to assess the business environments of specific Asian economies; specifically, participants are expected to develop country scenarios for given time horizons. As well, course participants are also required to analyze and make presentations about issues and challenges that are relevant to companies operating in countries such as China (including Hong Kong and Macau), South Korea, Taiwan and selected ASEAN economies.
name: Asia Pacific Business

attributes: TRCK - Public Policy, Devt, & Mgt Track (Business)
college: Lee Kong Chian Sch of Business

departments.name: Lee Kong Chian School of Business

description:
The evolution of the business environment in the Asia Pacific region, defined geographically as economies around the Pacific Ocean, is the theme of the course. It covers all economies in the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) including the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN). The rise of Japan, then China is deemed by all as a pivotal drivers of growth and development in the region. More than the traditional flying geese model or Asian miracle as led by Japan, China has further proven its state capitalism in general, and how doing in Asia works, in particular. Equally are added challenges of demography, ageing and environmental sustainability as affecting risks or opportunities for business.

The highlight of this course is for all to be apprised of the geoeconomics and geopolitics in Asia Pacific, a sizeable market by population and middle-income affluence offering both opportunities and challenges. Quintessentially, this is an applied course in International Business focusing on ASEAN and Asia Pacific business.
name: Asia Pacific Business

It covers all economies in the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) including the US and rising China with the rest of the Asian miracle economies led by Japan and its East Asian neighbours as well as the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) a core of 10 ranging in size from Indonesia to Singapore. Over the past two decades, the Asia-Pacific region has experienced a resurgence of economic activity and investment. Such robust performance has been underpinned by the combination of a highly favourable external environment, and buoyant domestic demand, in particular, as a result of a significant strength in business investment in many economies in the region. The rise of China in particular, is deemed by economists, sociologists and other academics alike as one of the pivotal development in the region. More than the traditional flying geese model or Asian miracle as led by Japan, China has further proven that state capitalism and how Asia works can be as successful as the rest of Asia Pacific cases. The added challenges of demography and environmental sustainability as affecting certain countries are as critical, affecting business.
 
This course consists of a set of core lectures which will introduce students to: (a) the economic, political and socio-cultural theories and frameworks for understanding the context of business in the Asia Pacific region with ASEAN for emphasis; and (b) the application of contextual and local knowledge to the decision-making processes of companies operating in the region. Course participants are expected to apply theories and frameworks to assess business environments of specific Asian economies; specifically, participants are expected to analyse and make presentations as case-studies about issues and challenges that are relevant to companies operating in countries such as China (including Hong Kong and Macau), Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, ASEAN and other Pacific constituents in business, commercial and trade relationships.

description:
“In the past decade, the United States’ economy grew by an average of 1.6% a year, the European Union’s by 1.7%, Latin America’s by 4.6%, East Asia's by 5.4% and South-East Asia's by 5.9%. The 21 economies of the largest trans-Pacific grouping, Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation (APEC), account for nearly half of global trade. The region comprises not only the world’s ‘factory floor’ but also its most important sources of services, technology and investments, and final goods markets,” writes Peter Petri, an international trade economist.   Yet despite the much celebrated economic progress of the region and the potential to be reaped from it, there are clear strains and risks resulting from geopolitical and economic trends which impact businesses that operate here. 
 
This course consists of a set of core lectures which will introduce students to: (a) economic, political and socio-cultural theories and frameworks for understanding the context of business in the Asia Pacific region; and (b) the application of international business theories and frameworks to understand the decision-making processes of companies investing in the region. Course participants are expected to apply theories and frameworks to assess business environments of specific Asian economies.  Participants are expected to analyse and make presentations about issues and challenges that are relevant to companies operating in large emerging economies such as China, India, Taiwan, and South Korea but also other economies such as Myanmar, Indonesia, the Philippines, and Vietnam.

description:
Businesses go through continuous, irreversible and unprecedented periods of change. More often than not, the future is already here – it’s just a matter of recognizing it. But while the pace of change accelerates, many organizations remain “under-led” and “overmanaged”. They are either unable or not flexible enough to identify new opportunities, anticipate market trends, address increasing complexities, challenge boundaries and assess risks. Perhaps not surprisingly, two out of three change initiatives fail.

Companies need to strike a fine balance: improving profitability while at the same time, transforming the corporate environment to develop their employees’ capacity to solve continuously arising challenges and align behavioral patterns. This goes beyond improving operational efficiencies and must be applied before it reaches a crisis point.

In this course, students gain an excellent understanding of the “bigger picture” and learn the methods of leading corporate change processes. Concepts revolve around the firm’s most important asset – its employees. Students study how megatrends such as global warming, protectionism, complexity and other environmental drivers redefine corporate values, visions, objectives and leadership styles that subsequently result in modified organizational strategies, structures, systems, communication and culture. Students apply an 8-step corporate transformation process from creating a sense of urgency to anchoring the change and be introduced to the basics of “chaos theory” and change audit. Further, students learn how to leverage intangible resources to boost synergies and discuss the reasons for change resistance and fatigue. Frequent use of videos and actual press clippings as well as case studies and class discussions will help to illustrate the content.

description:
The essential nature of this course is to explore globally relevant concerns that have irrevocable and long-term implications on the way we conduct business in the 21st century. These \"Mega-Trends\" are complex in nature and often overlooked as they may not be immediately visible. Mega-trends span over several years, sometimes decades. The relevance of these trends will be delved into through their implications on businesses, in particular in Asia, as well as the opportunities presented by them. In addition, we will analyze the \"lessons learnt\" from countries that are already affected by such trends. Mega-trends that will be examined include global warming, environmental conservation, market protectionism, global terrorism, population ageing, urbanization, miniaturization & artificial intelligence. 

By investigating the cause and effects of these phenomas, the course aims to stimulate critical thinking and inculcate far-sightedness. Through the combination of lectures, case study analysis, project work, as well as class presentations and discussions, the course will provide evidence for these trends, establish their relevance and present implications and opportunities for businesses. Students are expected to actively participate in class discussions and team activities.

description:
Megatrends describe data within macro-perspectives spanning over 5-30 years that may have profound implications on values, strategies and risk review. Cause & effect relations are often unknown, occur in small doses and are interdependent. Thus, consequences are not immediately evident. This course helps students to understand the importance and developments of globally evolving data patterns in 5 key domains: ecology, society, economy, geo-political and technology.

Opportunities, complexities and uncertainties are discussed in a business context. We will contrast findings, practices and lessons learnt when analyzing the effects of resource scarcity, environmental and societal stress, demographic change, diversity, globalization and the economic system. Further, we will explore developments in key technology areas (artificial intelligence, big data, biotech, nanotech, ITC, internet security and space technology) and debate implications on Singapore’s transition into a knowledge- and innovation-based economy. Special topics on “Closed & Finite System Thinking”, “Non-linear Behavior”, “Culture” and “Risk Mitigation” complement the course. Trends are internalized through examples and a research project to ascertain a solid understanding of ongoing debates. Interest in the discussion of current world affairs and a passion for creating a better future are pre-requisites to succeed.

description: This course examines how Asian industrial competitiveness (and therefore, economic success) came about and continues to be sustained. The course reviews the past and recent Asian experience of industrial development to develop lessons for the continuing strategic interaction of Asian countries and firms with one another and with the world. We adopt the industry and firm as our units of analysis, developing an understanding of selected keystone industries of particular countries, and case studies to root this industry-level understanding in specific firms’ experiences and strategies. There is a diversity of industrial developmental models in Asia – sharing common features with one another as well as differences. We will focus on the technological industries, but cover selected of the newer sectors such as services, software and digital entertainment. We will apply tested frameworks and concepts to understand how Asian firms developed their competitiveness, and how they interact with competitors and their strategies in the global playing field. These frameworks include conventional theories used in international business and strategy (e.g. those of competitive advantage), but we will also utilize other theories and concepts, such as ones involving clustering, networking, institutions and public policy, and innovation, to help illustrate how particular Asian industries’ models vary from those in other regions, as well as from one another.

We will focus on the technological industries, but cover selected of the newer sectors such as services, software and digital entertainment. We will apply tested frameworks and concepts to understand how Asian firms developed their competitiveness, and how they interact with competitors and their strategies in the global playing field. These frameworks include conventional theories used in international business and strategy (e.g. those of competitive advantage), but we will also utilize other theories and concepts, such as ones involving clustering, networking, institutions and public policy, and innovation, to help illustrate how particular Asian industries’ models vary from those in other regions, as well as from one another.

description:
For their long-term survival, all organisations need to innovate their product and/or service portfolios, as well as how they organise their processes. Innovation is often a continuous process. Sometimes organisations have a breakthrough product, but more often innovation is a continuous sequence of smaller improvements, recombining existing technologies into a new approach, and re-positioning existing solutions into new business models - all to enhance the value proposition for the customer in a significant way. 
Innovation and product development require creativity and imagination, but also hard work in the form of project management under uncertainty, improving the productivity of R&D, finding the best way to organise for speed and quality of the development cycle, profit management, etc. Being an innovator requires talent. 
This course will not transform you into an innovator, but will help you hone your skills in managing the product development and innovation process. This course will familiarise you with how organisations manage the process of innovation and how they develop successful products, services and systems. The focus will be on innovation and product development in existing organisations. While we may touch on the topic of corporate entrepreneurship, this course is not about the start-up of new companies, nor is it a course on marketing of new products. The course is most valuable for those who want to work in industrial firms or do consulting work.

Please take note of the timings for the site visits and guest seminars indicated in the course outline.

description:
Corporate governance is about the relationship between the managers/executives of a firm and its various stakeholders including shareholders, employees, and larger community. Different countries have different systems of capitalism and deal with this relationship in very different ways.  Because of these differences, specific systems and practices of corporate governance differ greatly around the world and in Asia. These differences, however, have been under pressure, as capital, management, and business practices become more global. Indeed, many Asian countries have revised their corporate governance system that is more consistent with global rules and expectations of investors who invest globally.   

This course aims to make participants aware of the key issues that are related to corporate governance in especially the Asian context by examining corporate governance practices in various Asian countries and comparing them with non-Asian models, specifically the US and Germany.  Participants will be equipped with the conceptual frameworks and tools to understand and analyze the issues that are pertinent to corporate governance practices as well as their impacts on other issues such as firm performance, business ethics, and firm strategy.

description:
This course introduces the fundamentals of technology entrepreneurship, as pioneered in Silicon Valley and in the Boston-MIT regions, and today it is spreading across the world. You will learn the process technology entrepreneurs use to start companies.  It involves taking a technology idea and finding a high-potential commercial opportunity, gathering resources such as talent and capital, figuring out how to sell and market the idea, and managing rapid growth.

Here in Singapore, the government has greatly invested in our research and development facilities for the last 20 years. Our first National Technology Plan (NTP) was formulated in 1991, with a budget of $2bn to kick-start Singapore’s strategy in harnessing research and technology to grow our economy. The current Research, Innovation and Enterprise (RIE 2015) is the 5th plan in the series. It has a budget of $16.1bn, and reflects the government‘s commitment to consolidate its effort in remaking SGP economy. One key emphasis in the current plan is the initiative in commercialization.

The course demonstrates the entrepreneurial mindset ... when others see insurmountable problems, people look for opportunities in technology and business solutions. The class will spend time understanding the research and technology innovation landscape in Singapore, learn skills in formulating business ideas to commercialize the research success, working with researchers to build business enterprises. A technology entrepreneurial perspective is also a wonderful way of thinking in order to tackle new opportunities in social entrepreneurship, whether it is in government or NGOs.
name: Technological Entrepreneurship

description:
At the core of the course is the process of developing low-cost, quick consumer experiments, mostly simultaneously, to learn about the market potential for different variants of new products or services, which will be iterated multiple times until an attractive variant of the new business idea is identified or an avenue to an adjacent space is explored. The course also familiarises students with how best to present their market validation information and the initial outlines of their business and revenue models on social platforms and to early-stage investors.

The course will guide students in the process of developing and market-testing new venture ideas. Students will work in teams, and each team will receive a grant of $1,000 towards prototyping and market testing their new venture idea. Also, each student team will be assigned a mentor(s) to give the team feedback on their market testing process. A panel consisting of faculty instructor, industry experts, and entrepreneurs will select the teams for the course based on their one-page new business idea outline.

The student team business idea should be scalable, i.e., the aspiration of the student team should be to have at least 10 employees or $1 million in revenue within five years.
