description:
At the end of 1945, the areas bordering the Straits of Malacca were facing recovery from wartime destruction and the sharp decline of colonial rule.  Indonesia, the largest and most geographically widespread, in 1945 was the first to become independent.  Formed in 1948, the Federation of Malaya became independent in 1957.  The city state of Singapore broke off from Malaya and became independent in 1965.  At this point, these three post-colonial countries were at somewhat similar levels of development (although the British had treated Singapore as an urban center and a major port -- not an agricultural resource).  All three were low income countries with per capita GDP ranging from $56 in Indonesia, $333 in Malaysia to $516 in Singapore.  Indonesia and Malaysia possessed significant natural resources, whereas Singapore (now cut off from Malaysia) was bereft even of water.  Over the past fifty years, the political and economic choices made in the three countries have varied, and their growth trajectories diverged.  Today, per capita GDP varies greatly:  Indonesia, $3,491; Malaysia, $11,307; and Singapore, $56,284 (World Bank data).

These three countries have pursued different pathways which to some extent can be explained by economic drivers, but also by government policy choices with regard to inclusive growth.  The course will consider this in the context of business in Indonesia, Malaysia and Singapore, and will study it from multiple perspectives:  government, corporate/family business, and social impact. To examine this in a one-week timeframe, we will focus on the development of infrastructure, real estate (housing), education and health care.
 
Resource-rich environments attract investors, but managing today in countries such as Malaysia and Indonesia where governments are sensitive to issues of competitive and strategic sustainability, raises challenges.  Having moved from low income status to low middle-middle income status, Indonesia and Malaysia face the challenge of avoiding the “middle-income trap,” the situation where developing economies’ convergence to the development frontier comes to a halt once their income per capita reaches a middle-income level.  In contrast, Singapore surmounted that challenged, but now as an advanced market economy, it faces the challenge of a small, high wage country (5.5 million): the need to innovate to remain competitive at this level.
longName: Sustainable Growth in ASEAN: Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia
name: Sustainable Growth in ASEAN

description:
This course, South China Visit Program (Pearl River Delta), is designed to develop students’ appreciation of the nuances of doing business in (South) China. Doing Business in China explores the various unique aspects of China’s history, culture, society, value system, business practices, and its implication to doing business in this emerging economy.

The course seeks to understand the knowledge and behaviours necessary to successfully meander through China’s business environment, encouraging the student to take a truly local perspective in dealing with dynamic management issues in this diverse eco-system. It emphasizes how the variables of politico-socio-cultural practices interact with other national and international factors to affect managerial processes and behaviours, and illustrates current developments and trends. In addition, the growing competitive influence of e-commerce will also be considered. The highlight of the course is its emphasis on experiential education – interaction with government representatives and business practitioners.

The scope of the coursework includes assessing China’s unique business eco-system (political, economic, legal), appreciating China’s leadership, understanding various aspects of doing business in China, learning Chinese etiquette, fostering successful relationships (the importance and the art of relationships), and getting a glimpse of China’s economic future development.
Throughout the course, the students are expected to apply what they have learned in the course and assess the relevance of these factors in doing business in China.
name: Doing Business in China

description: The Capstone course allows students to apply a cross-disciplinary approach while considering both business model architecture and the formulation of business solutions. It prepares students for the complex business environment of today by emphasising the application of academic knowledge accumulated from a range of prior core courses to solving real world problems. The course develops in students an ability to: strategically position the client and its challenge within an environmental context; appropriately scope the challenge of the client; develop and execute a workplan to address the challenge; and develop solutions by establishing a fact-base through directed primary and secondary research, drawing out relevant insights through analytic review, and engaging in abstract idea generation. The course exposes students to the uncertainties and ambiguity that exists within real-world business landscapes and organisational environments of industry clients, as well as, the challenges with engaging busy business executives and convincing them and their organisation of innovative solutions that have been devised by the students that address the client’s real-world challenges.

It will examine issues including state and corporate governance, work and organizations, gender, inequality and religious beliefs, and evaluate the trade-offs Asian societies make between individual liberty, national progress, regional imperatives and global capitalism.

We pursue the search for meaning in modern life through a reading of selected texts and the portrayal of life’s dilemmas in classic films. description:
This new elective is designed to help students develop an in-depth understanding and analysis of strategic business opportunities in ASEAN relating to China’s Belt and Road Initiative (BRI). It will introduce key concepts in strategic management and involve students in a real-life strategic business challenge proposed by PIL Logistics.
 
Under the third Sino-Singapore flagship project, Singapore and China are collaborating on the Chongqing Connectivity Initiative - New International Land-Sea Trade Corridor (CCI- ILSTC) as part of the BRI partnership. The CCI-ILSTC links the Belt (the overland Silk Road Economic Belt) and the Road (the 21st Century Maritime Silk Road) via rail and sea, which makes Singapore a key node on the BRI. CCI-ILSTC will reduce the time taken for goods travelling from Singapore to Chongqing from four weeks to about a week. 
 
This elective will feature a visit to Lanzhou & Dunhuang to understand the agricultural produce in Gansu Province, and to have a comprehensive understanding of the broader CCI-ILSTC project which is potentially a new high-growth opportunity for Singaporeans. Participants will have the opportunity to engage business leaders, entrepreneurs and government officials in project discussions.

description: The traditional model of one company engaging in the product conceptualization, detailed design, engineering, manufacturing and distribution is rapidly giving way to a host of new modes of operation. For virtually all facets of operation, companies nowadays need to decide whether or not to undertake an activity in-house or via a third-party, and in each case, the activity can be conducted either in the same locality, elsewhere within the same country, or in an entirely new country. Essentially where the theory on the boundary of the firm meets the firm-specific perspective on international business, this course is designed to explore these complex in-sourcing versus out-sourcing, as well as on-shoring or off-shoring decisions that face large and small companies these days. The additional management decisions and activities that follow an out-sourcing/off-shoring decision to a previously in-sourced/on-shored activity will be discussed. Assessment will be based on a combination of paper reviews, course project(s) and/or final examination.

description:
The SIE6011A-MGMT340 Understanding Chinese Culture and Business Environment program comprises some of the most economically significant Chinese cities located in the southern parts of China. This program is designed to develop students’ appreciation of the nuances of China’s business practices in the Greater Bay Area (GBA) and the Shantou Special Economic Zone (SEZ) in South China. It explores the various unique aspects of China’s history, culture, society, value system, business practices, and its implication to doing business in this tectonic economy.

The course seeks to understand the knowledge and behaviours necessary to successfully meander through China’s business environment, encouraging the student to take a truly local perspective in dealing with dynamic management issues in this diverse eco-system. It emphasizes how the variables of politico-socio-cultural practices interact with other national and international factors to affect managerial processes and behaviours, and illustrates current developments and trends. In addition, the growing competitive influence of e-commerce will also be considered. The highlight of the course is its emphasis on experiential education – interaction with government representatives and senior business practitioners.

The scope of the coursework includes assessing China’s unique business eco-system (political, economic, legal), appreciating China’s leadership, understanding various aspects of doing business in China, learning Chinese etiquette, fostering successful relationships (the importance and the art of relationships), and getting a glimpse of China’s economic future development.

Throughout the course, the students are expected to apply what they have learned in the course and assess the relevance of these factors in doing business in China.

description: This course initiative rests on the assumption that there is a powerful synergy between ‘sustainability’ and ‘innovation’ in business and society. The term ‘sustainable innovation’ refers to the creation of new market space, products and services or processes driven by social, environmental or sustainability concerns. Just like general innovation, sustainable innovation goes way beyond incremental improvements of products, services or processes. The challenge is to proactively embrace risk management and sustainability considerations (environmental, social, financial) aimed at aligning (novel) business strategies with the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) to create and capture new value. If managed well by results-oriented, socially aware sustainability leaders, sustainable innovation results not only in greater effectiveness at (intra)organisational levels but also helps to create a cleaner, healthier, fairer (and hopefully more stable) world as envisaged by the circular economy. The urgent need for sustainability has never been greater as evidenced by rapid population growth, pollution, (toxic) waste, plastic accumulating in our oceans, limited natural resources, climate change etc. This course will introduce students to the managerial discipline of innovation management with particular reference to examples of ‘good’ / ‘best’ sustainable innovation practices adopted by both local and international organisations such as City Development Limited (CDL), Banyan Tree, Sustainability Center Freiburg (launched in 2015 by the University of Freiburg in cooperation with five Fraunhofer research institutes), Henkel BeautyCare (whose Social Plastic Ecosystem in partnership with the Plastic Bank social enterprise is aimed at stopping ocean plastic and simultaneously providing opportunities for people in poverty), Procter & Gamble’s Tide Eco-Box (which contains less packaging, 60% less plastic and 30% less water than the current Tide press-tap) and many more.
name: Org Aspects of Sust Innovation

This course is designed to help students develop an in-depth understanding and analysis of strategic business challenges and opportunities in the dynamic and complex environment of Digital Media and Entertainment E-Commerce Ecosystem (DMEEE) in Asia. Value co-creation is an integral performance outcome in digital platform ecosystems. In developing their digital strategies, leading companies in these systems increasingly aggregate and analyze data from both e-commerce activities and media content consumption to gain a multifaceted understanding of their customers, and to develop deep knowledge about media, entertainment and e-commerce. As tech titans like Amazon, Netflix, Alibaba, Tencent, and Bytedance redefine the DMEEE landscape in Singapore and Southeast Asia, other ecosystem players including media firms, entertainment firms, manufacturers and retailers are presented with the challenge of developing their own digital strategies to thrive. This elective will introduce key concepts in strategic management in DMEEE and involve students in a real-life strategic business challenge from Singapore's media and entertainment group, MediaCorp.

Participants will have the opportunity to engage business leaders in project discussions.

description:
Asian entrepreneurs, tycoons, and affluent families are preparing to hand over an estimated S$2.6 trillion of business and wealth assets to the next generation over the coming decade. Many are setting up family offices to facilitate this succession planning and wealth transfer. 

Family offices are privately owned entities that manage the private wealth and other affairs of the family including philanthropy, education, and estate planning. In Singapore, family offices are required to have at least $10 million of assets under management (AUM), with many more than $100 million in AUM. Beyond managing the family wealth, the family office also supports the family’s vision and legacy, and helps to support important transitions in ownership, leadership, and wealth. 

Singapore has gained prominence as the preferred base for family offices, with their numbers doubling to 400 in 2020 as compared to the year before. This trend is expected to continue. Family offices by nature are private, closely held entities. However, with the phenomenal increase in the number of family offices, there is a corresponding spike in demand for professionals familiar with managing the family office. 

The BFI Family Office Management Work-Study Elective is a collaboration with family offices and their advisors that will provide students with the opportunity to undergo a 5-month extended internship programme in a partner company. Most family offices are led by family principals and staffed by small teams of senior professionals with decades of experience. 

Hence, the work-study elective presents valuable opportunities for students to take on a broader range of responsibilities and to learn directly from senior management, compared to junior internships at a larger corporate organization. 

The BFI Family Office Management Work-Study Elective involves an internship locally, where students enrolled will work for at least four days each week at the host company and take courses on campus for up to one day each week for up to five months.

While undertaking this elective, students may enroll in up to 2 course units (CU) of courses, as long as there is no timetable clash with the internship requirements.

This Work-Study Elective is open to all SMU students who meet the pre-requisites.
name: Family Office Management WSE

description:
The importance of entrepreneurship to the economy is intuitive. More formally, numerous independent studies from credible sources have spoken at length about this. A quick search across the internet shows that the benefits of entrepreneurship include but are not limited to the following: accelerating economic growth, promoting innovation, promoting social changes, promoting research and industrial development, and developing and improving existing enterprises. Start-ups and small businesses also have a disproportionate impact on job creation, accounting for 64% of new jobs and contributing to 20 percent of gross job creation. , , , , 

In Singapore, a survey in 2012 as part of a Global Entrepreneurship Monitoring study indicates that 21.4% of people in Singapore intend to start a company in the next three years, ranked second among OECD countries.  This indicates the great interest for entrepreneurship in Singapore alone. Beyond this, the trend for entrepreneurship investment in China, India, and Southeast Asia is also encouraging. Both from the input (number of graduates and family business) as well as from the demand (number of deals and capital invested by angel investors and Venture Capitalists along with the amount that governments invested as limited partners).  

The importance of entrepreneurship, however, goes beyond job creation. It provides an ideal setting to train and equip individuals with skills they need for the future. While the future always seems uncertain, McKinsey, one of the leading management consultant firms in the world, has suggested that cognitive capability, interpersonal skills, and self-leadership are critical part of it. These are all skills that entrepreneurship is rather uniquely positioned to train.
name: Overseas Entrepreneurship WSE

description: Sustainability issues are becoming critical issues in contemporary organisations. The Sustainability Management Work-Study Elective (WSE) will be a collaboration with organisations from the public and private sectors to offer students an opportunity to undertake a five (or more) month extended internship programme in an area of sustainability and its management. With an extended internship timeframe, students will be able to immerse themselves in the functioning of the partner organisation, take on added responsibility, and garner key experiences in managing and solving sustainability challenges. Overall, the WSE will equip students with knowledge and skills that can be transferred to their future workplaces.The Individualized Work-Study Elective (WSE) enables students to integrate a five month internship experience with public or private sector organisations together with academic reflection. While undertaking the extended internship programme, students will develop industry-specific knowledge, professional skills, and critical insight into organizational practices. The course emphasizes structured reflection and the application of management concepts to the student’s work context.This is a 2 CU course, equivalent to two semester-long electives. Students’ primary workload will be the internship itself, complemented by guided reflection and a final report. Faculty supervision is conducted on a light-touch basis (consisting of orientation sessions, mid-term check-ins, and a final review), while recognizing that learning occurs primarily at the worksite.The Sustainability Management WSE involves an internship locally where students will work for at least four days each week at the partner organization, and take courses on campus for up to one day each week. The internship will be for five or more months (e.g., August to December to cover Term 1, or January to May to cover Term 2).

college: Lee Kong Chian Sch of Business
description: Social entrepreneurship examines the process of creating new independent or corporate ventures that pursue the dual primary missions of social benefit and financial return on investment. Hence, the course concerns itself with nonprofit organisations and for profit ventures that have a social mission and aim to be financially self-sufficient or are profit driven. This course is designed as an introduction to the field. It examines the obstacles and constraints faced by social entrepreneurs, a nd surfacing new strategies for them. The course will draw on practitioners as well as on historical and contemporary models to explore the unique range of issues and challenges facing the new social venture. The course invites students to explore solutions to societal problems and to evaluate the market opportunities for social venture creation, the social capital markets and the trade off between social and financial returns, and resource issues. The course will examine the unique management and marketing strategies for the growing social venture. The research seminars will cover the areas of enquiry in nonprofit management and the differences between social entrepreneurship and traditional management and innovation.

college: Lee Kong Chian Sch of Business
description:
This course introduces students to qualitative research methods. Qualitative methods refers to a variety of research techniques that are non-statistical in nature, involve gathering data first hand from “primary sources” (i.e. by observing or interviewing people or organizations), and form a complementary research approach to statistical and other quantitative techniques. Qualitative methods help researchers develop insights into new phenomena, into process, and into complex relationships that are not easily ascertained with other methods. 

The course will introduce qualitative methods from four perspectives. One is by formally studying and practicing the practices of the methods. The second is by studying formative qualitative pieces of research. The third is by understanding the strengths of qualitative research, in studying complex systems with interacting actors or subsystems, and in studying process. The fourth is by examining some of the techniques (as practiced in the real world) in contrast to how they might be practiced (or adapted) to other, specifically virtual, worlds.
name: Qualitative Research Methods

college: Lee Kong Chian Sch of Business
description:
A large proportion of contemporary research on organization, strategy, and management relies on quantitative research methods. This course is designed to provide the statistical background and to familiarize the students with some of the commonly used quantitative research techniques, including ordinary least squares multivariate regression, models for binary outcomes, count models, and pooled cross-section/time series analysis. 

The main objective of this course is to help students understand the relationship between theory, data and statistical methods. This is not a course in statistical theory (i.e. we will not be deriving likelihood functions etc.) but a course on the practical use of statistical techniques to answer management related research questions. We will spend considerable time thinking about theoretical insights that can be translated into testable propositions, and how these propositions are best tested. We will do this through discussions of published papers from leading journals or high quality working papers in management research, and by having you solve statistical problems, work with data and estimate models. At the end of the course, you should be able to use common statistical methods to ask and answer research questions, and have developed critical skills in evaluating others’ research, such that you may apply these skills to your own thesis and other research works.
name: Quantitative Research Methods

college: Lee Kong Chian Sch of Business
description:
The Strategic Management course develops the skills managers need to analyze and improve business performance.  It focuses on competitive advantage and how firms may achieve, sustain, extend and renew it.   Competitive advantage depends on coordinated, mutually reinforcing actions across the entire organization. As a result, the course takes a top management perspective from which the logic of interaction among the functional areas – such as marketing, operations, and finance – may be evaluated and reconfigured.   Both environmental and firm specific sources of performance differences among firms are examined by drawing on a wide body of theory, evidence, and practice.  The course emphasizes the examination of specific cases and the development of practical recommendations as well as communication and persuasion.
This course is a blend of theory and practice where the emphasis is on integrating insights from other functional and core courses to diagnose the reasons for current organizational performance and to develop coordinated actions that will increase future organizational performance by:
1.	Analyzing environmental and structural variables which directly impact organizational performance.
2.	Assessing the motivations and options of competitors.
3.	Evaluating the quality and quantity of available resources. 
4.	Developing plausible resource reconfigurations (strategic options) 
5.	Assessing and choosing among plausible options, taking implementability and projected relevant events into account.
name: Shaping Strategy

college: Lee Kong Chian Sch of Business
description:
Making money is good.  So is reaching out to help impoverished individuals and communities.  It is right to support ‘green’ initiatives and it is right for local business to become an active contributor in the community.  But can we do it all?  Many successful businesses argue that we can.  They argue not only that we CAN invest socially but that we MUST . . .  if we, as corporations, are to maintain our ‘license to operate.’   In this broad survey course, we look at the innovative ways traditional for-profit corporations are reinventing themselves as social leaders.  We also look at the innovative ways not for profits are leveraging business methods to improve their service delivery and enhance sustainability.  We also look at the myriad forms of ‘social’ enterprise that now exist, i.e. at the organization that are neither businesses nor not for profits but something in between.

This course is recommended for all who would like a comprehensive introduction to social enterprise and corporate social responsibility (CSR) and/or for those who would like to understand what the new ‘social mandate’ means for traditional business operations.  The course is especially appropriate for those who aspire to senior leadership positions and who recognize the ‘social’ role they and their companies will be forced to play in today’s demanding market environment.  Collectively, the class will review and debate the various CSR experiments that are underway today, consider the profit impact of these initiatives, and consider their social value and sustainability.  The class will also consider how to create, implement, and assess CSR initiatives that generate strategic synergies with traditional business operations.   As a broad survey, the course will also investigate Bottom of the Pyramid business methods and social enterprise development
name: Doing Good Doing Well

college: Lee Kong Chian Sch of Business
description:
Managing Technological Change examines primarily larger strategic issues in environments altered by technologies. As the range and scale of the impacts of technological change is vast, the course will necessarily be selective. It will be organized around three important and distinct areas which are affected by technological change – the products and services which use new technologies, the competitive markets in which firms compete using the technologies and the organizations which must develop and execute new strategies while taking technological change into account.  These three areas are interdependent in the sense that changes in one can require coordinated changes in the other.  

The first section of the course introduces the idea that technological changes can be very different -- both in their impact on the competitive environment, and in how they affect individual firms.  Different types of technological change place different stresses on firms and some are more difficult to adapt to than others.  For example, the logic of the technology may dictate that some standard be established.  Or, the technology may make existing knowledge of customers and their preferences largely obsolete.

The second section of the course is more centrally concerned with classic strategic issues in product-markets  --- how firms create and capture value and how they build capabilities to compete over the longer term.  For example, if the firm can create value with a new product, can it reap the rewards without control over distribution channels or must it also invest in these? 

The third section of the course considers the organizational variables associated with technological competition. Firms struggle to both extend their existing technologies and product market positions while also creating new businesses. Organizational innovations from internal start-ups to mergers and acquisitions to corporate venture capital must complement, and may lead, an overall technology strategy.
name: Managing Technological Change

description:
Necessity is the mother of invention. One reason for firms to innovate is the necessity to re-invent themselves and get out of stagnation: the industry has either gotten obsolete, or competitors have adopted newer and more efficient business models, and products or services based on more advanced technologies. Innovation is then a necessity as the firm has to innovate or perish, one only has to look at what happened to Blockbuster and Kodak. Blockbuster at one point of time was the leading media rental firm in the world, but they chose to ignore innovation in the way they were delivering their media content to customers. As Netflix gained scale, Blockbuster’s inability to innovate meant that their business model was obsolete, and they had no choice but to file for bankruptcy. Kodak is another famous example: Steven Sasson at Kodak invented the digital camera way back in the 1970s, but rather than developing and commercializing the innovation, Kodak chose to put the new technology on the backburner, as its commercialization would have meant that their existing business model that relied on chemical printing of photographs would have to be cannibalized. However, other competitors jumped on the bandwagon for competitive advantage: hence, if you do not pursue innovation, your competitors will make you obsolete someday, no product or business model has an eternal shelf life. Innovation has many dimensions: it creates value for existing customers, thereby letting you keep your current market share; it creates value for new customers, enabling you to get growth; it enables you to work with new processes to access a lower cost base; supplier innovation enables you to leverage partners’ innovation capabilities to offer value to customers, and capture value for yourself. So the notion of continuous improvement is indeed extendable to continuous innovation, the business world in all sectors moves on a treadmill; the pace of the treadmill is faster in some industries like technology and fashion, and slower in some other industries. Innovation is the lever that enables you to keep pace on the treadmill if you are at the industry average; and enables you to set the pace if you innovate at a faster rate than the industry average. If you stand still on the treadmill or run at a slower pace than the treadmill in a competitive environment, at some stage, you will be thrown off the treadmill.

This course should be of particular interest to people aspiring for a career in designing and managing for innovation, either directly (e.g., V.P. of R&D, R&D Manager) or indirectly (e.g., management consulting). The course will also be useful to SME proprietors and entrepreneurs who intend to serve new markets, or use new technologies, or participants who wish to strategically reposition their offerings in an existing market. The course should also be of interest to people who manage interfaces between innovation and business functions such as finance, marketing, managerial accounting and human resources.
name: Innovation & Growth Management

college: Lee Kong Chian Sch of Business
description:
The emphasis of this course is the dynamic tension between innovation, entrepreneurship and leadership.  A framework is introduced which explains how the creation of value creation (innovation), the pursuit of opportunity (entrepreneurship), and leadership are necessary components in successful innovation and growth management.  

Additionally, we investigate the widely held confusion with regard to innovation and its entrepreneurial roots.  That confusion is based on the view that entrepreneurship is a “founder’s” process driven by only a few unique individuals.  In this course, we expand our understanding of innovation and entrepreneurship to characterize growth management in new ventures as well as in the established enterprise.
name: Innovation & Growth Management

college: Lee Kong Chian Sch of Business
description:
Execution.  It is the essence of management.  It is about getting product out the door.  It is about ensuring excellence in customer service.  It is about ensuring staff are trained and on-board.  In this interactive course, participants will invest in developing the tools and capabilities they need to lead organizations that truly work.  Specifically, students will learn how to develop and use the strategic performance management systems that guide and reward action.  Throughout the course, we will consider not just the technical structures of these systems but how they are used to ensure:  AWARENESS of strategic intent, UNDERSTANDING of how that strategy is implemented, COMMITMENT to that strategy, and ACTION that yield results.
	
Collectively, we will focus on how to translate strategy into actionable measurement systems, how to build and communicate those measurement systems throughout the firm,  how to monitor and ‘refresh’ those systems, and how to motivate employee action by linking personal incentives to realization of specific measured goals.  Again, while much attention will be paid to the technical construction of these systems, this is not a finance or accounting course.   Performance measures have little impact unless they are reinforced by the leaders of the organization.   To ensure effective use of these systems, students will also learn how to anticipate, recognize, and respond to the leadership challenges that arise in complex organizations and how to serve as inspirational figures within their companies.
longName: Execution - The Art of  Performance Management
name: Execution-The Art of  Perf Mgt

college: Lee Kong Chian Sch of Business
description: To study strategic management is one thing, to implement it successfully is another. Strategic games such as this International Strategic Management Simulation are valuable transitional tools for translating business school concepts into the real world. The course simulates the strategy formulation and implementation process of top management teams. Teams will collect many different types of managerially relevant data, analyze it, make decisions, and observe the results in a competitive environment where international rival teams are doing the same. As a group, teams will meet to adjust their plans, expectations and overall strategy in light of their results and their anticipation of future conditions and the actions of their competitors. The course is designed to support SMU’s focus on teaching integrative managerial skills by simulating a more complete business decision-making environment.  Effective management practice requires the effective combination of specialized analysis and information, usually in teams, to make streams of related and ideally, mutually supportive decisions over time.  The simulation will provide a learning experience in which such skills in integrating diverse information and perspectives can be developed.
name: Intl Strategic Mgmt Simulation

The course simulates the strategy formulation and implementation process of top management teams. Teams will collect many different types of managerially relevant data, analyze it, make decisions, and observe the results in a competitive environment where international rival teams are doing the same. As a group, teams will meet to adjust their plans, expectations and overall strategy in light of their results and their anticipation of future conditions and the actions of their competitors. The course is designed to support SMU’s focus on teaching integrative managerial skills by simulating a more complete business decision-making environment.  Effective management practice requires the effective combination of specialized analysis and information, usually in teams, to make streams of related and ideally, mutually supportive decisions over time.  The simulation will provide a learning experience in which such skills in integrating diverse information and perspectives can be developed.
name: Intl Strategic Mgmt Simulation

You will learn to understand the challenges facing MNEs as well as the relevant strategies they employ.

Specifically, the course examines the objectives and strategies by multinationals pertaining to their choices in country locations, market entry, product/service offerings, organizational structure, cross-border R&D and human resource management. The course will also focus on how multinational enterprises manage and control their international subsidiaries.

description:
Perhaps no business subject is surrounded by more interest, mystique, or deification than innovation and its entrepreneurial roots.  Industries and economies are forged by its presence; organizations are obsessed with being associated with it, the world changes when it really happens—and usually in unexpected ways. Truly, to create value where it did not exist prior is a noble pursuit, but is success found only with a few, or only with luck? 

In this course we examine the practice of innovation and entrepreneurship.  We define entrepreneurship more broadly to reflect a more realistic view:  that entrepreneurship is a management practice that can be understood and practiced.  The scope of the discussion includes entrepreneurial views where its participants act as promoters; as well as intrapreneurial views where its participants act as trustees.  Concepts and tools of ideation, innovation and solution development are woven into the practice and leadership of entrepreneurship:

1) The Entrepreneurial Manager 
     a. Role
     b. Behavior
     c. Leadership Attributes 
     d. Promoters v. Trustees
2) Ideation & Innovation
     a. Creative Process
     b. Innovation Process & Diffusion
     c. Solution development
3) Opportunity Assessment & Business Models
4) Managing Uncertainty & Growth

The discussion will be centered on published case studies and instructor developed case material.  Articles and text in support of the theories and frameworks of innovation will be part of the support material.  Tools, simulators and guest speakers will enhance the discussion and learning but it is the student’s perspective and contribution that add the greatest value, and as such, participation is a key learning method.
name: Leading Entre. & Innovation

description: Environmental knowledge is crucial for any business leader today. Climate change, conservation efforts, alternative energies for oil replacement, contingency planning for sea level changes, are just some of the environmental issues reported in the media. But what are the hard scientific data behind the reporting? To make informed decisions, accurate information about the facts is necessary, but the facts are not always easily distilled from media reports that may be biased by advocacy. This course will use data on globally important environmental issues drawn directly from science. We will discuss the data and learn how to interpret them for business decisions. In many areas there may actually be a choice of action with different trade offs depending on the business or policy decisions taken. The goal of the course is to inform future business leaders with factual knowledge about global environmental issues, and to distinguish data from advocacy.
name: World Environmental Issues

college: Lee Kong Chian Sch of Business
description:
Most business leaders try and deliver against various important corporate objectives - driving top line growth, return on investment, cost competitiveness, customer satisfaction etc. Some of these objectives range from tactical moves to inspiring statements, but none of them can stand up to the scrutiny of a governing objective.  

Company resources should be managed to make them worth more than they would be if managed in any other way, by any other firm.

Managing for value or Value based management has been implemented as a governing objective for business strategy implementation by some of the best known FMCG companies – Coke, Pepsi, Cadbury, Unilever to name a few. This is indeed a very demanding objective which continuously drives businesses to weigh options and make choices.

The implementation process is resource intensive, structured and thorough.

This course will provide –

•A comprehensive overview on why MFV is considered one of the most proven and successful governing objective

•How does this principle translate in creation of actual business strategies – strategic position assessment, competitive strategy, participation strategy, pricing and operating strategy

•Through case studies clarify how it is actually implemented in the Industry
longName: Managing for Value - Formulating Successful Business Strategies
name: Managing for Value

college: Lee Kong Chian Sch of Business
description:
Blue oceans are defined by untapped market space, demand creation, and the opportunity for highly profitable growth. Examples of the Blue Oceans are Wii and Yellowtail Winery to name but a few. 

In blue oceans, competition is irrelevant because the rules of the game are waiting to be set. 

In an ever-increasing number of industries, supply exceeds demand. This leads to a highly contested space as rivals fight for limited market share leading to bloody red oceans. Innovative leaders of tomorrow will become more concerned with generating blue oceans than in dominating pre-existing space. 

In this course, students will learn about Blue Ocean theory and Value Innovation methodology. They will:

-	Gain insight into why customer centric philosophies are unlikely to provide significant growth
-	Understand why organizations unwittingly ‘kill’ innovation
-	Discover how the Blue Ocean Strategy approach surfaces unfulfilled demand and uncontested markets
-	Learn how companies apply the Blue Ocean Strategy approach to out-achieve their corporate growth objectives.
longName: Blue Ocean Strategy and Value Innovation
name: Blue Ocean Stgy & Value Inno

college: Lee Kong Chian Sch of Business
description:
Traditional economists argue the central and sole goal of a business is to maximize returns to shareholders. A weakness with this mindset is that it puts profits above all else and thereby ignores that companies are social organizations that serve employees, suppliers, and communities in which they operate. This profit-only mindset can raise significant problems when companies do not view their mission in a wider context, such as illustrated by BP and the oil spill disaster, and at worst be the seed of destruction for amoral firms like Enron. 

This module explores the compelling reasons behind businesses taking on a broader role in developing social value that extends beyond the role of the firm as viewed by traditional economists. The module provides ideas, conceptual frameworks and tools to help students assess approaches to social value alignment and different models of interaction between corporations, governments, intergovernmental organizations, investors, and non-governmental organizations (NGOs). 

This module is practitioner-oriented and intended to provide the participants with a basis for working with and advising business leaders in developing strategic social value alignment, and engage customers through social marketing, and build and understanding of firm level social strategy, dynamics of relationships between companies and stakeholders. Leaders of non-profit and government agencies will also find the module of benefit as it covers public-private relationships and will help identify how to work with business leaders on areas of business responsibility. 

Social issues are wide a varied and include environmental management, health, education, social justice, labour standards, social mobility, climate change, and more. A full treatment of these topics is beyond the scope of this module. Instead, this module will provide broad frameworks and analytical tools for managing social value and stakeholder relationships, and provide illustrative examples though a guest speaker series to bring ideas to life. “Learning by doing” is the centre piece of this course which features a practicum style project where a team will work on realizing greater value for a firm they select to support.
name: Corp Social Responsibility

description:
Strategic Initiative Project is an approach that challenges you to learn through immersion in a real problem. It is a format that develops problem solving strategies and sector knowledge bases and skills by placing you in the active role of problem solvers confronted with an ill-structured situation that simulates the kind of problems you are likely to face as managers in complex organisations.

SIP makes a fundamental shift from a focus on teaching to a focus on learning. The process is aimed at using the power of authentic problem solving to engage you and enhance your learning and motivation. There are several unique aspects that define the SIP approach: Learning takes place within the contexts of currently occurring tasks, issues and problems. That is, these are truly real-world concerns.
name: Strategic Initiative Project

description:
Generally, strategy is defined as a set of choices that managers make in order to increase their firm’s performance relative to competitors. Corporate Strategy in a Global Environment considers strategic choices that managers make in the context of a multi-product, multi-business, multi-location firm. In this course, you will study how successful organizations choose, implement, and evaluate their strategy. The focus will lie on internal and external corporate growth strategies, which have become indispensable for success in today’s economic environment marked by increased globalization, rapid technological change, shortened product lifecycles, and enhanced competition. Tools and techniques for strategy formulation, implementation, and evaluation are discussed. Case studies are used to sharpen your understanding of the importance of strategic decision-making.

Specific areas of focus are:
- Corporate Strategy and Competitive Advantage
- Corporate Scope
- Growth through Acquisitions
- Global Strategy and International Expansion
- Sustaining a Successful Enterprise

college: Lee Kong Chian Sch of Business
description: Alliances among companies have become a fundamental necessity for companies’ competitive and growth strategies. Firms use alliances for a variety of reasons – to share the risks or costs of entering into new products or markets, to access or learn relevant capabilities, to growth etc. At the same time, alliances are very difficult to manage and poorly conceived or managed alliances often create substantial problems for one or more of the alliance partners. Not surprisingly, more than half the alliances formed end up failing. Therefore, the goal of this program is to understand the benefits and risks that alliances create for individual companies and to learn how to form and manage alliances more successfully. This should help participants build their individual alliance skills as well as understand how their company can develop its organizational capability to manage alliances more effectively.
name: Network and Alliance Building

With an increasingly globalized economy, leading and managing employees of different cultural backgrounds becomes imperative in organisations. This module takes the approach of understanding how culture differs and impacts on our interactions at the workplace in Asia and beyond. 

The course is broadly structured to enable an understanding of culture differences with an emphasis on how these similarities and differences impact workplace interactions. Through the course, students will:
(a) gain an understanding of their level of cultural competence at the individual level, 
(b) be given tools to analyze different culture patterns around the world and in particular, Asia, and; 
(c) learn to develop strategies for adapting to cultures with a view to managing in the organisational context. 

The emphasis of the module is on the interplay of cultural competence at the individual level, organisation culture dynamics at the workplace level and societal cultures at the national/country level.

description: Many Global organizations manage their regional and global operations from Singapore. As the business environment is increasingly global, Multi-national corporations need to have staff and talent that understand global issues and possess a global mindset. This course will allow students to develop an understanding on the development of strategy, organizational capabilities, and management challenges faced by Multi-national Enterprises/Corporations (MNE/MNC) for operating in the global economy. We will study business challenges associated with developing strategies, implementing strategies, and managing the operations of companies whose activities stretch across national boundaries through cases, readings and articles. The course will train students to think about the multidisciplinary, multicultural and multilateral issues that are the critical to the management of a Global Enterprise – whether you are the frontline business manager, the country subsidiary manager, the global account manager, or the CEO. Where possible, we will use the Asian context and Asian cases studies that provide an Asian perspective. After this course, students will be more prepared to deal with key global challenges and management issues as Managers and Executives at Multi-national enterprises.
name: Global Business Management

description: This course centers the student on thinking about design with the end market and business in mind.   When we think in terms of design, better products and businesses are launched, and value is more readily created.  Design thinking is individual-centered innovation process that is based on observation, collaboration, learning, visualization and concept and business development.  Tools and frameworks are introduced that allow initial design ideas to be carried through the concept development process to result prototypes and feasibility assessments.  The course is the foundation for the creation of new products, services and businesses.

college: Lee Kong Chian Sch of Business
description:
This course introduces the student to design thinking and an array of design tools for integrating design thinking into an overall design process. Design thinking and tools is a powerful process that can improve product, service and experience concepts (selected applications to products and services will be covered). 

The course is split into two parts, with Part 1 taught by Tschang and Koh, and Part 2 by Dimian.

In Part 1, the design thinking process (based on the IDEO/Stanford Design School process) is introduced. This is a qualitative process consisting of the stages of: the observation of users, ideation, and prototyping. Iteration can occur between any steps, and multiple cycles are typical. Applications of design thinking to product and service innovation will be discussed, along with varying of the design contexts, including the private sector, government and social sectors. Design thinking will be framed against traditional innovation processes and other types of thinking.

In Part 2, design tools and frameworks are introduced that allow the initial design ideas to be further carried through the concept development process to resulting prototypes and feasibility assessments. Value can be more readily created within an organizational context. 

The course is the foundation for the creation of new products, services and businesses.

college: Lee Kong Chian Sch of Business
description:
Welcome to the module on Entrepreneurial Finance & New Business Creation. In this course, we will examine the many and complex issues associated with finance and financial management in entrepreneurial organizations. Specifically, we will consider these four topics: Opportunity Identification, Valuation, Doing Deals and Harvesting. 

Opportunity Identification

We consider the myriad types of opportunities that might be recognized by an entrepreneurial and craft a framework for analyzing the nature of that opportunity.  We consider for example, the type of competitive advantage inherent in the opportunity, the potential cash requirements and returns of the project, its riskiness, its resource (especially human) requirements, and optimal timing.  

Valuation

The value of any project, asset, or organization is influenced by the magnitude, riskiness, and timing of its associated cashflow. In this section of the course, we examine the process of valuation, learning how to effectively project magnitude and riskiness of cashflows, and assess their optimal timing.   

Doing Deals

With the financial need and potential value of the organization clarified, the organization must next consider the source and cost of financing. In this section of the course, we look at the complex world of finance, working to understand the essential sources of finance, the myriad financial instruments available, and how final deals are struck.  

Harvesting

The final segment of the course will consider entrepreneurial exit. An often overlooked segment of the entrepreneurial business plan, defining a harvesting time frame and mechanism is essential for value maximization. We will consider the two most common vehicles for exit:  acquisitions and IPOs.
name: Entrepren'l Fnce & New Bus Cr

college: Lee Kong Chian Sch of Business
description:
Day 1: Reddi
Brief description: How is strategic management different in knowledge intensive industries compared other industries? At first blush, not much. Hence, in session 1 we start with a review of core strategy concepts and frameworks. This review is brief. We will point you to readings should you want to refresh your memory or read more on the foundational concepts. More specifically we will ask: what is strategy; why and how to do industry structure analysis; In session 2 we cover generic strategies and we then turn to specific aspects of knowledge intensive industries like network externalities, the myth of first-mover advantage, consequences of winning the standard wars, the high degree of uncertainty surrounding in these industries that interact with core strategy concepts to provide a more nuanced application of the board core strategy frameworks. Evidence shows that several breakthrough inventions are made by large firms but not commercialized by them. The rigid mental models of managers, scientists in large firms makes them ignore architectural innovation which they dismiss as trivial innovation. The architectural innovation made by new firms end up swapping the market resulting in demise of established incumbents.

Day 2: Reddi
Then in session 3 we will focus on role of unique technology and capabilities of firm in determining resource allocation to new projects and extent and success of corporate diversification. In session 4 We also address why do large firms engage in acquisitions and how do they manage post acquisition IP which is mostly resident in individuals. Does the buyer firm keep the target firm as a standalone unit or does it integrate it? At the end of day 2 your group will have to present the group project.

Day 3: Adel
In the AM session we will discuss turnaround strategy and leadership using the HCA Hospice care case.  It will highlight the issues of leadership in a non profit and underscore leadership issues.
In the PM session we will discuss the innovation strategies of a Singapore firm trying to expand internationally.  Entry strategies and innovation challenges and micro political risk are explored.
name: Managing Strat Innov & Change

college: Lee Kong Chian Sch of Business
description:
The course is designed to guide MBA students to understand and carry out data-driven and data-informed managerial decision-making in business. The course will provide step-by-step guidance on how to execute machine learning methods using computational programming in R, deploying the analytic results into an interactive dashboard, using Shiny.

Students will become able to understand the processes and results of predictive analytics based on supervised (regression and classification) and unsupervised (clustering and dimensionality reduction) machine learning. This will be done in the various contexts of solving business questions: predicting customer attrition, loan default, housing prices, and employee turnover; and housing market and customer segmentation. This eight-week course will provide useful skills in computational data analytics for strategic thinkers in organizations.

The major learning formats will be: (a) the “interactive lecture” where instructors will provide guidance on the principles and executions of predictive analytics, with examples (applications), and (b) “hands-on programming” where students will use their fingertips and modify parts of a given script. (The instructor will provide a template script, so that participants can fill in the blanks as they learn the processes of predictive analytics.)

As there will be discussion of cutting-edge science and technology used in business analytics, the course will be both conceptual and technical (experiential). The experiential (hands-on) learning is the critical component—the course will employ hands-on (learn by doing) approaches. To fully understand what can be done and should be done, and so students can use what they learn during the course in their workplaces (or at least envision what could be done, and what questions to ask their organizations’ data analytics teams), it is vital to undertake hands-on programming for predictive analytics.

To maximize the speed at which they gain knowledge and skills, enrolled students will receive a pre-course note from the instructor, giving guidance on pre-course reading and preparations from Week 1. There will also be weekly exercise questions, where students will receive a set of structured questions (starting in Week 3), using R and Shiny. Upon completion of each exercise there will be a review session on the exercise questions.


NOTE: The course is designed for students new to data analytics and in an MBA program. It is a hard-skill course in which students will learn about R programming language for predictive analytics. 

Again, it is expected that students will have no experience of R programming. In order to fully grasp the course content it is essential for students to practice, both during and after the eight-week course, the programming skills they have learned. Learning R programming is like learning to play the piano—practice is of critical importance.
name: Bus. Analy for Decision Making

college: Lee Kong Chian Sch of Business
description:
Business Analytics refers to the use of data and statistical and quantitative analysis to support and drive business decisions. Business Analytics is quickly becoming a survival capability for organizations. The combination of an increasingly complex world, the vast proliferation of data, advanced technology at affordable prices, and the pressing need to stay one step ahead of the competition has rendered the application of analytics within organizations indispensible. Companies all over the world are looking to use their growing sources of data as their competitive advantage: retailers use customer purchase data to target promotions and drive recommendation engines; airline industries change prices hour by hour in response to changing demand; and credit card companies are creating suites of financial products customized to different customer risk profiles.

This course provides an introduction to the field of business analytics. In particular, this course will develop the foundation of business analytics by developing proficiency in its three basic pillars: 1) understanding how business analytics can be used to improve decision making in organizations, and how to integrate analytics across all business functions in a company; 2) acquiring a practical, hands-on experience with the tools and techniques used in business analytics, with emphasis on application of those tools to real data; and 3) developing the skill of translating analytical results into actionable business insights.
name: Business Analytics

college: Lee Kong Chian Sch of Business
description:
The course is designed to guide students in understanding and implementing data-driven decision-making in business contexts. It offers a step-by-step tutorial on constructing and applying machine learning algorithms for business problem-solving, utilizing Python.

Throughout the course, students will develop a comprehensive understanding of predictive analytics through both supervised (regression and classification) and unsupervised (clustering and dimensionality reduction) machine learning techniques. The course's real-world applications span a variety of business questions, from market segmentation to personalization, algorithmic trading, and portfolio management. Over eight weeks, it aims to make machine learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI) Accessible, Actionable, and Interpretable (AAI), turning these concepts into powerful tools for business problem-solving.

The course employs an interactive lecture format, where principles and applications of predictive analytics are explored, and a hands-on programming approach, where students engage directly with the material by completing parts of provided script templates.

This blend of conceptual and technical (experiential) learning is crucial. The hands-on aspect is particularly emphasized, encouraging students to learn by doing. This approach is essential for understanding and applying the course material in real-world scenarios, enabling students to effectively interact with data science teams within
their organizations.
name: Mach. Learnin for Deci Making

The course employs an interactive lecture format, where principles and applications of predictive analytics are explored, and a hands-on programming approach, where students engage directly with the material by completing parts of provided script templates.

This blend of conceptual and technical (experiential) learning is crucial. The hands-on aspect is particularly emphasized, encouraging students to learn by doing. This approach is essential for understanding and applying the course material in real-world scenarios, enabling students to effectively interact with data science teams within their organizations.
name: Mach. Learnin for Deci Making

college: Lee Kong Chian Sch of Business
description: The primary topic of this course is strategic management in the Chinese context, including that of both local Chinese companies and foreign companies operating in China, but with a somewhat greater focus on the former. The course has two primary features. First, it broadly encompasses three levels of strategies of companies competing in the Chinese context: business strategies, corporate strategies, and cross-border competitive strategies. Second, in analyzing the strategies of companies competing in the Chinese context, the course will take a comparative perspective. The key frameworks in strategic management are mostly developed in the West. Since there are fundamental differences in macro national environment, competitive industry, and firm strategic issues between China and the West, whether the existing frameworks are applicable to the Chinese context is thus a key concern. We shall discuss throughout the course the similarities and differences between strategic management issues in the West and in China.

college: Lee Kong Chian Sch of Business
description: This course introduces design thinking and its application to developing new products, services and the organization of businesses. Design thinking is a way of thinking and a structured set of techniques for creating innovations. Design thinking is a hot area which has the aim to help companies large and small (e.g. startups) to change and innovate. Design thinking as practiced in this course partly follows from the IDEO approach (see for example, www.ideo.com, but which also connects to other variants of design thinking. This blends creative thinking and logical or rational thinking, and involves a process consisting of the inspiration, ideation, and implementation sequence. It also involves underlying methods such as brainstorming, prototyping and systems thinking. Students will learn design methodologies and frameworks, and apply them through exercises and projects. The course is logically divided into five interconnected parts, but which we also separately emphasize. They are: (1) the design domains, including the artifacts to be designed (i.e., products, services, or the business itself), (2) the design methodologies (e.g. human-centered or ethnographic observation, brainstorming, the design process, systems thinking, design roles, team composition), and (3) the design contexts. Design contexts refers to the broader emerging context for designs and business, specifically, society (including different cultures and the poor), and the physical environment. Learning will be done primarily through case analyses, exercises, and a team project. Prototypes using paper or other easily accessed materials will be expected.
name: Design Thinking for Innovation

college: Lee Kong Chian Sch of Business
description:
This seminar consists of 5 special innovation sharing sessions:

Innovation in Asia - The Big Picture:
The main purpose of this innovation seminar is to shed light on Asia's innovation challenges ahead with special reference to Singapore and selected Asian nations.

Fostering a Creative Environment Through the 'Medici Effect' Game:
This hands-on seminar helps students to understand how to discover ideas at the intersection of different fields and introduces them to cross-disciplinary thinking. The workshop uses a practical hands-on tool to introduce the concept of intersectional innovation.

The Entrepreneurial Journey of Local Internet Entrepreneur Arrif Ziaudeen & Chope.com.sg:
\"Internet Entrepreneur\" has become a sexy title, but the reality of an entrepreneur's life is far from this. Using the lens of my own journey through the first two years of Chope.com.sg, I will attempt to illustrate the personal qualities that I think are important or harmful in the early stages of starting a company, some of the challenges you can expect to face, and what you can realistically hope to come away with if you succeed. I will also deep-dive into fundraising, which is one of the most important but difficult aspects of entrepreneurship in Singapore.

Creating a Culture of Innovation:
Based on the concept of business model innovation, an explanation of its design elements and value drivers, this session will outline what it takes in terms of senior leadership and performance governance to create a sustainable culture of innovation in larger organizations. 

The Innovator's Mindset:
This workshop helps students become more effective creators and communicators. We begin with a brief tour of techniques that help unleash and strengthen our natural creativity. Then, since creative ideas must be communicated to become effective, we will explore where barriers to communication might arise and how to overcome those barriers so that we can sell our creative ideas to key stakeholders. The workshop consists of lecture plus interactive activities (read: playing games) that operationalize the key concepts to be practiced.

college: Lee Kong Chian Sch of Business
description:
In this day and age, it is no longer sufficient for managers and leaders in organizations to be simply transactional or simply transformational. They also need to be fair, just, ethical, moral and responsible. This course is designed to explore, inform, and stimulate thinking on issues related to behavioural ethics and responsibility as encountered in the corporate world. To create this intellectual exchange, this course will focus on how individual and organizational behaviour is shaped by context as well as by biases, why these factors make it difficult for managers to be responsible leaders, and what can be done about the influence of these factors. 

It is important to emphasize that the goal of this course is not the ethical or moral transformation of students but to develop a set of tools and frameworks (where possible) that allow us to manage effectively in a world increasingly characterized by stakeholders with competing needs and responsibilities.
name: Ethics & Corp. Responsibility

college: Lee Kong Chian Sch of Business
description:
This course is an interactive, activity-based exploration of the contemporary corporation.  It’s goal is to foster ethical leadership in the corporate world by enabling students to recognise and negotiate different spheres of value in society.  The course begins with an exploration of the history of the modern corporation, and continues week by week with investigations of contemporary corporate sectors, including energy, finance, retail, and food.  Students will first learn to make visible the implicit values of the sphere of business, but rather than critique those values as is typical in most business ethics classes, instead students will learn to lead ethically by coming up with strategies to advance amongst competing and sometimes contradictory value spheres in society.

The course will continue with advanced multi-player role-playing cases each week as students devise strategy for corporations in contact with different spheres of value, develop practical analysis of the balances of forces in each context, and invent new ways to harness social value amidst a pluralism of spheres in society.  By moving through different spheres of value in actities, debates, and role-playing students will develop expertise in ethical leadership for the 21st century.  The ultimate objective of this course then is the transformation of our values in order to make ourselves valuable. As Albert Einstein said, ‘Try not to become a man of success. Rather become a man (or woman) of value.’

college: Lee Kong Chian Sch of Business
description:
The course is part of a multi-year collaboration between the MBA programme and Philips. It provides students with a framework of strategic management consulting as grounded in theory and applied by consulting firms globally. Philips will challenge participants to an actual and current strategic issue and student teams will apply structured problem solving approaches in an iterative and competitive process coached by Prof Thomas and representatives from a leading consulting firm (tbc).\\

Students will go through the steps of the consulting process, generating data, analysis, ideas and strategic recommendations for Philips. They will then present these recommendations to a group of Philips executives in the format of a case-competition. Two top teams will be given the opportunity to present to Philips’ senior leadership. 

Grading will be completed exclusively by the faculty responsible for the course, and is decoupled from Philips’ decision about the winners of the consulting competition.

Course size is capped at 36 participants.

The curriculum covers effective problem-solving approaches with hands-on practice and cultivates top-tier management communication skills through both written and verbal mediums.

For students who discover that consulting isn't their ideal path, or for those with broader career aspirations, this course provides essential frameworks for identifying critical management questions and navigating complex business challenges in any future role. Furthermore, the course includes targeted case interview simulations and guidance on crafting compelling CVs.

college: Lee Kong Chian Sch of Business
description: The main topics of this module centre on the challenge of business acceleration and what management needs to do in order to manage rapid growth and value creation (scaling), e.g. in the context of cross-border / global expansion. Students will be introduced to relevant (growth) management concepts and the requirements of developing an integrated growth and value creation strategy towards a fully-thriving large-scale business (scaling tactics). After this module, students will appreciate what it takes to grow a business to the next level in the corporate life cycle (e.g. a planned increase in firm production ahead of anticipated increases in product demand), including the widening of one’s customer base, business model refinement and cementing one’s innovative brand leadership position.
name: Bus Acceler & Growth Strategy

college: Lee Kong Chian Sch of Business
description: This short module introduces students to core concepts in risk management, with a focus on volatility, uncertainty, complexity and ambiguity. These so-called VUCA environments (the VUCA acronym was arguably first used by the US Army War College to describe the unpredictable security environment in the late 1990s) mean that traditional strategic plans may not always be applicable, and additional tools must be considered. In the first session, tools including decision trees and scenario planning will be introduced to handle somewhat straightforward cases. In the second session, the importance of crafting solution from ambiguous spaces, as well as well as the notions of commitment and flexibility will be highlighted. In the third and fourth sessions, strategic options and technology-related challenges for specific companies will be examined. You will be asked to position yourself to analyse Apple’s current options and innovatory strategic positioning. Using another case on the pharmaceutical industry as background, we will examine the technological waves of change and attempt to foresee the future managerial challenges of Merck and Pfizer.
longName: Risk Management for an Uncertain World: Focus on Volatility, Uncertainty, Complexity and Ambiguity
name: Risk Mgmt for Uncertain World

description: Business success in Asia requires an understanding of the country context, unique business drivers, and management tools. Differences in social, political, environmental, technological, legal, and economic development have led to the emergence of different business systems across the region. By exploring the context in the Asian nations along with the unique business drivers, this course helps students to explore and understand the formation of a variety of business systems in Asia, and how differences in business systems could lead to different outcomes.

college: Lee Kong Chian Sch of Business
description: Differences in social, political and historical development could lead to the emergence of different business systems in the economy. Major Asian economies including China, India, Japan, South Korea, Hong Kong, Singapore, Taiwan, Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand will be analysed and compared.

college: Lee Kong Chian Sch of Business
description: Important emerging innovation trends are identified and their implications for innovation management and developmental entrepreneurship are further explored. The course looks at the trends to open information/open source rather than protected intellectual property, the distribution of innovation over many independent but collaborating actors, and toolkits that empower users to innovate for themselves.  The course emphasises various kinds of internal ventures and multiple external collaborative approaches that include corporate venture capital investments, licensing and different types of alliances and formal joint ventures.  It then concentrates on developmental entrepreneurship via case examples of both successful and failed businesses, and generally grapples with deploying and diffusing products and services through entrepreneurial action.  By drawing on current and historical cases, especially from South Asia, Africa, Latin America, Eastern Europe, China and other developing regions, we seek to cover the broad spectrum of challenges and opportunities facing developmental entrepreneurs.

description:
This course is a blend of theory and practice where the focus is on understanding concepts and frameworks for conducting qualitative research, and using those concepts and frameworks to analyse and formulate action plans to address central theoretical and empirical questions related to ethical and sustainable business practices. 

In addition, this course will also give the students an overview about how to undertake business research for the real world where, very often their first assignment is to produce a report. Research for business or the corporate world warrants the need to be organised, systematic and most importantly resourceful, both in time and money, as very often the output is used for decision making and strategic purposes. Within the larger framework of basic applied research methods and techniques, students will learn the N-C-P: need, context and process of doing or undertaking business research. The rigour of the literature review and information gathering is contextualised by undertaking research using both library resources and the Internet where the importance of critical thinking is fundamental.  With information overload, there is need to manage information, present and communicate it effectively using the appropriate medium to different audiences.

The dramatic rise of India as an economic superpower has been one of the most significant results of globalization. With a strong knowledge workforce, rising income level, an open regulatory environment and a consistent GDP growth, India is now positioned to be at the fore-front of both supply-side efficiency as well as new market opportunities.

However, it is imperative to have a first-hand understanding of the Indian business scenario, regulatory norms and diverse culture to effectively tap into this market. This course on Inside India: Discovering the New Realities will give participants an insider’s view of the dynamic markets of India, its business environment, socio-cultural norms, and emerging opportunities.

description: This course focuses on the increasingly important non-market business environment – the political, regulatory, social, and ecological context in which contemporary global business operates. The nonmarket environment poses significant challenges to managers, whilst offering tremendous opportunities for the development of competitive advantage. You will learn to analyse political environments, discern systematic differences in the business environment across countries and cultures, and formulate nonmarket strategies in a global context.
