college: School of Social Sciences
description:
The heart of the course lies in the science of the natural environment. Summative evaluation of all major topics will be drawn towards two laws of nature: conservation and transformation. Two concepts will persist: interconnectedness and sustainability; confirming the former and questioning the latter. As diverse and varied environmental matters are, this course shall focus on the earth’s resources. Embedded in the module are societal-technological issues relevant and peculiar to an environmental concern. “The earth is our life-support system.”  This is the crux statement that would validate your taking this course. 
This course is part of the General Education (GE) curriculum focused on a science-based study of the environment. It is part and parcel of the SMU's holistic thrust to produce dynamic business leaders and creative entrepreneurs with a solid foundation in all curricular undertakings.

This course is part of the General Education curriculum that focuses on a science-based study of the environment. It is part and parcel of the University’s thrust to produce dynamic business leaders and creative entrepreneurs with solid foundation in all curricular undertakings.

The heart of the course lies in the science of the physical environment. Summative evaluation of all major topics will be drawn towards two laws of nature: conservation and transformation. Two concepts will persist: interconnectedness and sustainability; confirming the former and questioning the latter. As diverse and varied environmental matters are, this course shall focus on the earth’s resources. Embedded in the module are societal-technological issues relevant and peculiar to an environmental concern. 

“The earth is our life-support system.”  This is the crux statement that would validate your taking this course. 

At the end of the course, the learner is expected to grasp the implications of three scenarios: nature working for us, men working for nature and men working with nature.
name: Environmental Science

description:
This course explores some of the physical concepts that have come to shape our current view of the physical universe, a view that is still emerging. Readings will include expository material on the physics topics as well as some biography, history, philosophy, literature, and current scientific events. 

The course will focus primarily on five themes: (1) Conservation of Energy, (2) The Second Law of Thermodynamics, (3) Special Relativity, (4) Quantum Mechanics, and (5) String Theory.
name: Physics for Managers

description:
This is a course under the General Education (GE) curriculum which covers a survey of the physical sciences. Congruent with the University’s Vision, this curricular undertaking upholds the need to create world-class citizens - hence the inclusion of a medium that would pave the way to such status.

This course introduces basic scientific concepts in the areas of Chemistry, Physics, Astronomy, Meteorology and Geology. The course storyline begins at the micro level so as to understand systems at the macro level. A unifying theme runs through the five sciences:  MOTION.  This is an attempt to depict the dynamism of our physical world.

At the end of the journey through five physical sciences, the students are expected to:
• discard hindsights about the old notion that science is static;
• gain insights about causality (cause and effect)  and 
• use foresights  from the knowledge and skills learned in making informed decisions to thrive in this fast, changing world.
name: Intro to Phy Science

description:
This course aims to develop a holistic awareness of science.  It is designed to (a) keep participants abreast of the development in science & technology, and (b) to encourage participants to appreciate the impact of science and technology on our society.

The course’s primary focus is on modes of inquiry rather than knowledge content.  Participants will be using Science Centre facilities such as the Observatory and the DNA Learning Lab to perform hands-on activities, including the opportunity to extract and analyse their own DNA.  By the end of the course, participants will be able: (a) to appreciate the interdependency between science and society and the impact of science and technology on society, (b) to have a basic understanding of the scientific principles and practices, and (c) to judge for themselves the value of contemporary science and the importance of science literacy.
name: Science Explorat'n & soc.

description: This course adopts the framework of Science, technology, society and environment (STSE) education. description:
The business world and the world of living beings – biology – resemble each other fundamentally. In both these systems, numerous self-interested independent actors interact spontaneously to form complex and dynamic, yet ordered systems. And in both biology and business, we ask: How can we understand the workings of these systems? How do we make them work for us?  

This course explores the many similarities and analogies between business, and the various disciplines of biology, such as ecosystem theory, evolutionary biology, and genetics. We will examine how thought in biology has influenced economic thought and vice versa. We will study the tools and models developed for biological problems, and examine whether we can draw valid analogies for economic problems. We will make specific comparisons between situations found in business and biology.

The course includes insights into hot topics in the study of biological systems – fitness landscapes, complexity theory, fractals, and chaos theory – and how they may apply to business problem solving.
name: Biological Models for Biz Apps

This course provides further understanding of Biotechnology with specific reference to its applications in the field of Medical Biotechnology, Bioremediation, Plant Biotechnology, Aquatic Biotechnology, Microbial Biotechnology and Biotechnology Regulations. description: This module will look at the technologies of the Internet, and the e-Commerce markets. It will look at the technology and strategic choices for enterprises, including the B2B and B2C markets. Payment systems, trading applications, transactions handling and other pricing and financial issues will be examined. The implications and impact of the Internet technology and e-Commerce on capital markets, financial transactions and institutions will be discussed. The role of e-CFO and e-Treasury will also be examined for students who wish to pursue the specific areas of applied finance.

description:
This course introduces students to different modes of formal writing that will be useful to them in many academic disciplines. In this academic year, Academic Writing has two tracks: the existing Research Paper (RP) version and a pilot Business Research (BR) version. Both versions of Academic Writing cover core skills: writing a critique, synthesizing relevant information and producing an extended paper.

In Academic Writing (RP), students wrestle with, challenge and refine the great ideas of our times through intellectual debate, expressed in written and oral communication.  As students explore ideas, weigh alternative viewpoints and develop original positions in their own thinking and writing, they will learn to write thoughtful papers substantiated by solid evidence and well-reasoned, persuasive argumentation.

In the pilot version of Academic Writing (BR), students are equipped with the skills to write cogently in academic, business and professional settings. Students will explore topics from a business perspective by reading critically, formulating convincing positions, and conveying their ideas persuasively by crafting clear, concise and coherent analytical reports that are effectively supported by appropriate evidence.

description:
Academic Research Writing is about the writing of research papers in line with the expectations of the academic community that you are now part of. It is for those assigned research on any topic, whether technological, political, or commercial. By definition a research paper combines primary and secondary information, guided by a thesis or claim, to arrive at a new or enlightened conclusion about a topic. The emphasis on research means quite simply that you must go beyond what you know and think personally to find information from a variety of sources and then incorporate the ideas and words of others into your document. You will also learn formal documentation of research sources – attributions, in-text citations, and source lists – in line with APA guidelines.

This course is applicable to students in the University Scholars Programme only.

description:
In this course, students will work in virtual global teams, with students from other universities, to develop a proposal for a corporate client. Students will develop essential skills to thrive in the modern workplace – they will explore virtual collaboration tools, hone their interpersonal and intercultural competence, and employ data storytelling principles to craft persuasive narratives for business proposals.

In the first half of the course, students work in SMU teams to communicate their recommendations persuasively through corporate documents like executive summaries and Slidedocs. Through whole-class and small-group discussions, students explore theories on virtual communication and working in remote teams, and familiarize themselves with tools for cultural analysis and virtual collaboration.
 
In the culminating capstone project in collaboration with the University of Southern California (USC), students will work in global teams comprising students from universities across Asia, Europe and America to develop a proposal for a corporate client. Past industry partners of the VBP project included companies such as Google, Starbucks, Netflix, Tesla and SpaceX. Over 6 weeks, students collaborate virtually with their global counterparts to craft a report to the client of their choice, recommending strategies to enhance the client’s corporate reputation. In the course of the project, students use social and AI-driven collaboration tools, navigate cross-cultural team processes and learn to collaborate effectively across borders and time zones. 
 
The deliverables in this course can be included in students’ portfolio of written and reflective work to showcase their ability to produce industry and discipline-specific communication outcomes. USC will award certificates of achievement to all participants.

college: Ctr for English Communication
description:
Global project teams, aided by digitization and technology, have become an urgent necessity in a world reshaped by geopolitical, economic and pandemic disruptions. Such teams largely function on virtual platforms while still needing to juggle the human skills that occur in face to face environments: effective intercultural communication, the interpersonal complexity of collaboration and conflict; and the need to transform data into communications that spur action. 

In this course, students will explore and use available virtual collaboration tools, hone their interpersonal and intercultural competence, and learn how to translate data into actionable insights in order to communicate them professionally and persuasively.  

In the first half of the course, students begin by preparing individually and in local SMU teams for the capstone global team project in the second half of the course. The course begins with the conceptual cornerstones of intercultural communication, virtual communication, interpersonal theories on collaboration and conflict, and data storytelling. Students familiarize themselves with tools for cultural analysis, appraise available virtual collaboration tools, and learn to communicate their proposed solutions persuasively through corporate documents like executive summaries and slidedocs. 

In the culminating capstone project in collaboration with the University of Southern California (USC), students will work in global teams, alongside students from other universities, on a project for a corporate client. The industry partners for 2020 are Google, Amazon and Audi. The project focuses on creating a context for students to learn how to communicate effectively in virtual work environments, use social and AI-driven collaboration tools, navigate cross-cultural team processes, and develop solutions for the corporate client. The team writes a proposal to the client of their choice, giving the industry partner an opportunity to evaluate and offer professional feedback. The client selects the top 3 proposals for their own brief. 

The deliverables in this course are suitable for inclusion in a portfolio of written and reflective work that the students will be able to use to showcase their ability to produce industry and discipline-specific communication outcomes.
name: Virtual Business Professional

college: Ctr for English Communication
description:
Professional Writing will expand and deepen students’ ability to write effectively in civic and corporate contexts. Such writing skills emerge in leaders who not only know how to analyze and articulate complex problems but also know how to envision and express written solutions that reveal solid decision-making on public policy, and business and societal trends.
 
While the Writing & Reasoning course, taken by most SMU students in their first year, focuses on breadth, here the students will be deepening their skills by exploring and writing about more complex issues in society and business. Students will engage with the need for deeper research, better audience analysis, and more structured writing, with a more nuanced adaptation to the context appropriate to their intended publications.
 
Students will consider and respond to meaningful real-world issues and situations in each of the three written projects. They will explore not only what other people have said about the issues that they confront, but also develop and communicate their own responses. The finished pieces will form the basis of a portfolio of written work to showcase their ability to think critically, conduct appropriate literature research, analyse their findings, argue their case, and produce professional communication outcomes. This portfolio will be a valuable addition to their resumes when they graduate. 

The final project will be an in-depth feature piece written for either Rice Media (https://www.ricemedia.co/) or the Skeptic Magazine (https://www.skeptic.org.uk/).

Rice Media, and Skeptic Magazine editors advise the students during the Week 10 presentations, and students will have the chance to have their work published by the media outlet that they write for after the term finishes.

description: This course examines how a small, globally connected city-state designs and recalibrates key policies in a changing regional and global context. We do so by tracing Singapore’s evolution from postcolonial developmental state to a maturing city-state, focusing on how technocratic, communitarian and state-led approaches have evolved to shape policy in areas such as public housing, meritocracy, multiculturalism, immigration, social protection, regional diplomacy, and social compact. With an eye to Singapore’s Chairmanship of ASEAN in 2027, students explore how regional agendas on economic integration, digital and green transitions, and the pursuit of a rules-based order both influence and are influenced by Singapore’s domestic policymaking. Situated within Global Asia, the course equips students to critically analyse the ideas, institutions and power relations that underpin policy changes in Singapore and its wider regional dynamics in ASEAN.
name: Changing Policyscapes in SG

description: This master's level course offers an exploration of the principles underpinning recent climate change, and is structured around the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) work themes of the physical science of climate change; the impacts, vulnerability and adaptation of climate change, and also approaches to mitigate the causes of climate change aligned with sustainable development. This course will provide students with a deep understanding of the multifaceted aspects of climate change; in particular, how each thematic aspect is linked with each other. The interdisciplinary curriculum bridges the gap between scientific research, policy-making, and practical implementation strategies, as well as looking at enabling conditions from other non-governmental agencies e.g. business and communities that can effect successful climate action.

description: This course explores the Agentic Revolution—the emerging paradigm where AI systems act as interactive, adaptive agents shaping and responding to human needs. Students will engage with the principles of building intelligent agents, with emphasis on learning, reasoning, and adaptation, while critically analyzing the challenges of ethics, alignment, and trust in human-AI interaction. The course will also survey future frontiers and applications, preparing students for the design and responsible deployment of next-generation intelligent systems.

description: This course provides a general introduction to the applications of AI in user-facing domains, exploring the transformative potential of AI systems in everyday life. Key considerations and guidelines for Human-AI interaction will be covered, focusing on the principles of effective design and ethical deployment. Students will also examine interaction design for AI applications and explore the dynamics of Human-AI teaming, preparing them to create collaborative, user-centered intelligent systems.
name: Human-AI Interaction Design

description: This course introduces the essentials of financial decision-making. The main objective of this course is to help students gain an in-depth knowledge of the major theories in corporate finance and their practical implications for thinking about real world issues.  Participants will be provided with a rigorous introduction to the foundations of business finance in competitive financial markets. The course is designed to equip managers and leaders with the basic tools that are necessary for managing a firm in a dynamic global financial environment. Emphasis will be placed on applying these tools to arriving at optimal decision strategies that will maximise the value of the firm. The course also discusses empirical research and relevant case studies and real world examples to enable students to develop a further appreciation of the field of corporate finance.
name: Corporate Finance

description: This is a centrally-coordinated shared course, which can be considered as an open course to count towards your graduation requirement, when applicable.This interdisciplinary course examines the global challenge of climate change and its local manifestations, with a particular focus on Singapore and the tropical region. Students will explore both the scientific foundations and the socio-political dimensions of climate change, including key concepts such as risk, resilience, mitigation, and adaptation. Emphasizing the connections between global processes and local impacts, the course equips students with analytical tools to understand climate dynamics, evaluate policy responses, and navigate the complex governance and communication challenges involved in building a sustainable future.
name: Clim Change & Sustainability

college: Sch of Computing & Info Sys
description: Managers often need to make important decisions related to different business challenges including ESG (Environment, Social and Governance) concerns. Understanding how to build models to represent the business situation, analyse data, perform computations to obtain the desired outputs, and analyse the trade-offs between alternatives, will support good decision making. This course focuses on using Microsoft Excel as a spreadsheet tool to build such decision models and to do business analysis. Students will be able to analyze trade-offs and understand the sensitivity impact of uncertainties and risks. The key emphasis of this course is on developing the art of modeling, rather than just learning about the available models, in the context of managing IT, operations, financial and ESG related decisions.The primary focus is on using personal computers as platforms for soliciting, consolidating, and presenting information (data, assumptions and relationships) as a model for a variety of business settings; consequent use of this model to drive understanding and consensus towards generating possible actions; and finally, the selection of a final course of action and assurance of execution success.
name: Spreadsheet Model. Dec. Making

college: Sch of Computing & Info Sys
description: Recent technological advances have enabled more seamless ways of generating and collecting larger volumes and varieties of data. Statistical Thinking, a crucial branch of Mathematics, serves as the cornerstone for visualising, analysing, interpreting, and predicting outcomes from the data. Students will be introduced to both Frequentist and Bayesian approaches to statistical reasoning. While Frequentist Statistics focuses on drawing conclusions from data through sampling, estimation, and hypothesis testing, Bayesian Statistics provides a probabilistic framework for updating beliefs and making decisions in the presence of uncertainty.Descriptive Statistics forms the foundation of the course by providing fundamental tools for summarising and exploring data. Building on this, Inferential Statistics empowers students to make evidence-based conclusions using sampled data, leveraging both Frequentist and Bayesian perspectives.In this course, students will learn to explore and present data using Python to discover underlying patterns and trends, apply statistical thinking to analyse data, and convert data into meaningful insights for Data Science and real-world problem statements, along with Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) considerations.
name: Stat Thinking for Data Science

college: Lee Kong Chian Sch of Business
description: This new MSc in Management (MiM) course Innovating for Sustainable Futures rests on the assumption that there is a powerful synergy between sustainability and innovation in business and society. The term ‘sustainable innovation’ refers to the creation of new market space, products and services or processes driven by social, environmental or sustainability concerns. Just like general innovation, sustainable innovation goes way beyond incremental improvements of products, services, or processes. The challenge is to proactively embrace risk management and sustainability considerations (environmental, social, financial) aimed at aligning (novel) business strategies with the Sustainable Development Goals to create and capture new value. If governed well by results-oriented, socially aware sustainability leaders embedded in a ‘good’ governance structure, sustainable innovation governance results not only in greater effectiveness at (intra)organisational levels but also helps to create a cleaner, healthier, fairer (and hopefully more stable) world as envisaged by the circular economy. The urgent need for enhanced sustainability innovation governance has never been greater as evidenced by rapid population growth, pollution, (toxic) waste, plastic accumulating in our oceans, limited natural resources, climate change etc. This course will introduce students to the dos and don’ts of integrating sustainability into business practice based on effective policies, processes and frameworks, board governance, senior management strategy, and stakeholder management. Several case studies of for-profit and nonprofit organisations such as City Development Limited (CDL), DBS, SIA, Eco Ark, and others will be featured based on published materials and guided site visits to appreciate what it takes to make sustainable innovation governance work.
name: Innov for Sustainable Futures

description: This course is designed to equip Master in Management (MiM) students with practical knowledge and skills fordata-driven decision-making in managerial contexts. Through step-by-step tutorials, students will learn how tobuild and apply machine learning (ML) algorithms using Python to address various business challenges.Over ten weeks, the curriculum emphasizes both supervised and unsupervised ML techniques, demonstrating real world applications such as user/customer segmentation, recommendation systems, churn/turnover analysis, anduser/customer lifetime value (CLV) prediction. A key objective is to make machine learning (ML) and artificial intelligence (AI) Accessible, Actionable, and Interpretable (AAI) so that students can leverage these tools for effective managerial decision-making and problem-solving.In addition, students will learn as to how AI/ML-driven decision aids can help overcome systematic and predictablebiases in human judgment and managerial decision-making. By understanding why, how, and when to apply machinelearning, students will be able to strategically select and implement the right analytics methods for different business contexts.The instruction includes interactive lectures on predictive analytics principles, complemented by hands-onprogramming sessions where students work with partial script templates in Python. This experiential learningapproach ensures that students develop both a strong conceptual understanding and technical proficiency, enabling them to collaborate more effectively with data science teams in their organizations and ultimately lead ML-powered products and ML-driven organizations.To solidify learning, the course offers weekly bite-sized Python exercise problem sets beginning in Week 2. There is no expectation of advanced Python fluency at the outset; rather, students will develop practical programmingskills through consistent practice. This course is best suited for those who wish to go beyond surface-level discussions of AI/ML and experience firsthand how these techniques underpin strategic, data-informed managerial decisions.
name: Decision Architecture for Mgrs

You will learn how to use data visualisation software and how to code in a programming language. This is a hands-on course that will prepare you for jobs in marketing analytics, marketing technology, marketing intelligence, and data science.

This course focuses on the hands-on application of AI technologies—ranging from synthetic market research and dynamic pricing to agentic workflows—supported by a critical analysis of industry successes and failures. Students will acquire the technical literacy and strategic foresight necessary to implement integrated AI marketing initiatives and evaluate AI-related risks.

This creates a host of new business models, such as online marketplaces, platforms, and omni-channel retailing, that require new sets of skills and concepts to manage. The objective of this course is to provide students with these necessary skills and concepts. Topics that will be discussed include online retailing, online marketplaces and platforms, analytics and AI, logistics and technologies for online retailing, and omni-channel retailing.

This course is divided into two distinct but complementary sections designed to ensure that students are not only literate in standard economic theory but also equipped with the critical lenses required to engage with real-world sustainability challenges. The first section of the course focuses on the basics of environmental economics, introducing students to core analytical tools, methods, and their application. The second section challenges this conventional approach, empowering students to adapt economic thinking to complex sustainability problems.

They also need to be fair, just, ethical, moral and responsible. This course is designed to explore, inform, and stimulate thinking on issues related to behavioural ethics, responsibility and sustainability as encountered in the corporate world. To create this intellectual exchange, this course will focus on how individual and organizational behaviour is shaped by context as well as by biases, why these factors make it difficult for managers to be responsible leaders, and what can be done about the influence of these factors. It is important to emphasize that the goal of this course is not the ethical or moral transformation of students but to develop a set of tools and frameworks (where possible) that allow us to manage effectively in a world increasingly characterized by stakeholders with competing needs and responsibilities.

description: The World Health Organization has projected a shortfall of 18 million health workers by 2030. Singapore is facing a similar scenario of healthcare workforce shortfalls, exacerbated by a fast-aging population. In order to future-proof and ensure the continued accessibility, quality and affordability of healthcare, the Singapore government has made three key shifts to move beyond hospital to the community, beyond quality to value, and beyond healthcare to health. In order to achieve this goal, analytics and data science can play a key enabling role to alleviate the increasing burden in our healthcare systems.Health systems worldwide have embarked on the drive towards digitalization for over the past 20 years. The ability to capture, analyze and synthesize data for high priority and impactful health service delivery and clinical processes is an important precursor to development of efficacious evidence-based interventions. The growth in volume, speed and complexity of healthcare data necessitates the effective use of data analytic tools and techniques to derive insights for improving patient outcomes, ensuring the sustainability of care, improving population health and ensuring the well-being of service providers. In this course, we will introduce the characteristics of healthcare data and associated data mining challenges. We will cover various algorithms, systems and frameworks to enable the use of healthcare data for the improvement of care outcomes. The focus will be on the application of these knowledge to deal with real-world challenges in healthcare analytic applications across the entire data analytic value chain from data preparation, descriptive, predictive and prescriptive modelling techniques. We will also look at the evaluation of analytic solutions in real-world implementation.
name: Appl Data Sc in Healthcare

description: COMM334 – an overseas project experience - is an advanced elective module with an overseas study component designed for students majoring in communication management. With Asia’s economic ascendancy and modernisation, corporate strategic communication in Asia has taken on a new importance in the past two decades. Home to over half of the world’s population, unprecedented political, economic, media, social and technological forces in an age of discontinuities are creating a new world order for Asia. The importance of communicating strategically and the need for greater cross-cultural understanding, including being innovative and enterprising have never been more critical for organisations struggling to effectively communicate with diverse stakeholder groups across different geographies in this new multi-polar business environment.An SMU-XO module, this course is divided into two segments – Singapore and China (Hong Kong). The overseas experience aims to equip communication students to better understand the unique geopolitical dynamics which affect communication in a one country and two systems nation. Students will be equipped with the ability to apply theory and understand how strategic communication has evolved to influence the integration of paid, earned, shared and owned media which are vital to unearthing unique characteristics that drive communication practice in countries in Asia. In addition to gaining insights from top Asian practitioners in the region, students will also acquire in-depth knowledge of the socio-political-cultural-economic factors that underpin the practice that influence business outcomes in the world’s most populous continent. This course will prepare students in communication management to readily transit and take on responsibilities to manage communication for businesses operating across Asia.

description: No organization can afford to ignore the importance of corporate reputation in a hyper-connected digital world of the century where companies are under attack 24/7. A favourable reputation is an intangible prized asset and its contribution to a company’s value is indisputable in today’s crisis-prone business environment. This course will introduce participants to the discipline of reputation management by examining the role of strategic communication in building, enhancing, and repairing corporate reputation. It will emphasize the importance of stakeholder management in a constantly evolving media landscape starting with the need to build trust in the workplace. The course will also discuss the significance of media management as companies struggle with challenges brought on by the rise of a stakeholder society in highly digitized economies in Asia and the damages it is capable of inflicting in times of crises, as well as delve into recovery efforts to restore reputation after crises. Through lectures, case studies, guest speakers, and discussions, participants will become familiar with the concepts, strategies, and tools vital to understanding why leveraging on corporate reputation is critical in ensuring the long-term survivability of businesses today.
name: Managing Corp Reputation & Com

description: Should you eat meat? Should you fly on planes? Does a forest have value beyond what it can offer us? What, if anything, do we owe to future generations or to the non-human animals with whom we share this planet? Are wealthy nations obligated to help those most affected by climate change? These are among the most pressing ethical questions of our time. Answering them requires careful thought about the nature of the environment and our obligations to it. This course introduces students to the central debates in environmental ethics. We will ask who, or what, deserves moral concern, and why, as well as whether nature has value in itself or only in relation to us. We will also consider how our answers to questions like these should shape the choices we make as individuals, citizens, and members of institutions. Along the way, students will develop the analytical tools needed to reason clearly and rigorously about these questions, tools that can prove useful well beyond the seminar room.
name: Environment Ethics

This course examines major political issues facing contemporary Southeast Asian countries. We’ll consider diverse topics such as the state’s role in economic development, legacies of history in state formation, nationalism and ethnicity, variations in authoritarianism, transitions to democracy, and the role of Islam in politics. These topics will be studied through the lens of a few specific countries rather than a survey of every country in Southeast Asia. The course provides a broad foundation for understanding politics in the region, and after the course, students will be prepared to apply that knowledge in further study or in their careers.

description: Urban sustainability challenges are rarely \"tame\" problems with simple technical fixes; they are wicked problems defined by complex causalities, competing stakeholder values, and inescapable policy trade-offs. This course uses an interdisciplinary framework to equip students with the analytical tools needed to navigate urban complexity and design actionable solutions.Across three integrated sections, students will:(1) Master foundational concepts, establishing the wicked problems framework and introducing interdisciplinary lenses to understand complex urban systems;(2) Analyze key urban dimensions, examining economic, technological, cultural, spatial, and resource dilemmas across real-world contexts like electric mobility, hawker food infrastructure, high-density green space, and the water–energy–food nexus;(3) Navigate urban resilience, exploring how cities overcome public complacency, maintain political trust, and stress-test infrastructure against extreme climate adaptation.

This interdisciplinary course introduces students to the foundations, capabilities, and limitations of AI while examining its wider implications for individuals, organisations, and society.Students will explore how AI systems work, from machine learning to agentic AI systems that can use tools and take multi-step reasoning. Rather than treating AI simply as a technological development, the course examines AI through multiple disciplinary lenses, including the humanities and sustainability. A central emphasis of the course is problem-centred AI, where students learn to frame a societal challenge and build an AI agent to address it. Ultimately, this course aims to nurture future ready professionals who can work confidently with AI while exercising human judgment, creativity, empathy, and ethical responsibility in shaping how AI is used in their organisations and society.

description: This course introduces students to two highly connected and increasingly important topics: Smart Cities and Artificial Intelligence (AI). It provides a broad and accessible overview of how cities are being transformed by emerging technologies and how AI is shaping the future of urban life. The course begins by introducing the Smart City concept — how cities around the world are using digital and data-driven solutions to improve quality of life, enhance urban sustainability, and optimize infrastructure and services. Students will explore how smart city technologies are being applied in domains such as:•	Transportation Management: Using AI to optimize traffic flow, improve public transport systems, and reduce congestion.•	Smart Energy Grids: Applying intelligent systems to manage energy distribution, efficiency, and renewable integration.•	Waste Management: Leveraging sensors and automation to improve recycling and resource management.•	Smart Homes: Smart buildings powered by IOT devices and managed by AI. •	Intelligent Healthcare Systems: Using AI for diagnostics, patient care, and public health monitoring.As the course progresses, students will explore a range of AI application areas that power smart cities, including:•	AI in Smart Mobility: Autonomous vehicles, ride-sharing algorithms, and real-time route optimization•	AI in Smart Homes: Personal assistants, energy-saving systems, and aging-in-place support•	AI in Energy and Sustainability: Monitoring consumption, predicting energy demand, and enabling green cities•	AI in Robotics: Urban service robots, maintenance drones, and delivery bots•	Digital Twin Technology: Creating real-time, data-driven virtual replicas of cities to simulate and test urban policies and development scenariosThe course emphasizes systems thinking, civic innovation, and real-world problem solving, not programming or math. Through lectures, global case studies, interactive discussions, and student-led projects, students will develop a practical understanding of how AI technologies are integrated into urban infrastructure and how they shape everyday life. No technical background is required. This course is designed for students from all academic majors, especially those interested in the future of cities, technology, and society.During this class, students will be required to form group to design and propose one AI powered smart city solution/start up idea to the class. Students group will present firstly pitch their ideas at the midterm and then pitch it again at the end of the semester. Feedback will be provided to students during both presentations. Then students’ group will be required to submit a final term paper to show case their AI powered Smart City solution/start-up idea.

description:
Trustworthy Machine Learning (TML) explores how to design, evaluate, and deploy machine learning systems that can be relied upon to behave safely, robustly, and transparently in real-world environments. With ML models now influencing critical domains such as healthcare, finance, and security, understanding their vulnerabilities, biases, and uncertainties has become essential. The course builds a structured understanding of the four pillars of trustworthiness:

• Adversarial robustness: ensuring that models resist intentional or unintentional perturbations to their inputs.
• Interpretability: enabling humans to understand, trust, and diagnose model decisions.
• Privacy: safeguarding sensitive data and promoting privacy-preserved learning.
• Uncertainty: quantifying and managing confidence in model outputs.

The first half of the course introduces these principles and their algorithmic foundations. Students will learn how to generate and defend against adversarial examples, build interpretable and privacy-preserved models, and measure uncertainty and calibration in their predictions and decisions.

In the second half, the course transitions to foundation models (FMs) such as large language models (LLMs) and vision-language models (LVLMs). Students will examine new challenges that emerge at scale, such as jailbreaks, prompt injection, hallucination, and data privacy issues.

Students will gain both theoretical understanding and hands-on experience evaluating the trustworthiness of ML models, reinforcing this in a group project that analyzes or improves one dimension of trustworthiness in an ML or foundation model.

The intended audience for this course is graduate students. In addition to regular lectures, students are exposed to the academic literature via critical reading and class presentations. The objective is to provide students with sufficient foundation to evaluate and learn from academic articles on TML.
name: Trustworthy Machine Learning

description: This course is the first part of a two-course Macroeconomics sequence. The aim of the sequence is twofold. First, it is to introduce students to modern macroeconomic theory, in particular formal macroeconomic models built on microfoundations. Second, it is to develop a deep understanding of macroeconomic phenomena such as business cycles, long-term economic growth, and the process of economic development, as well as macroeconomic policy issues, such as the impact of fiscal and monetary policy on the economy and the design of a social security system or an unemployment insurance scheme.This first part of the sequence first covers the topic of measurement of macro-economic variables, before easing students into micro-founded macroeconomics by developing a static general equilibrium model with production and using it to analyze a number of fiscal policy issues. The course then moves on to a dynamicframework and covers the mechanics of long-term economic growth and the role of policy in economic development. Students are then introduced to dynamic decision problems when considering consumption and savings decisions of households and investment decisions of firms, and these building blocks are combined with a Walrasian approach to the labor market to complete the development of a dynamic macroeconomic model, which is then used to consider fiscal policy questions like the role of the timing in taxes and government expenditures.

The course emphasizes research output: a well-defined question, a defensible empirical design, reproducible analysis, clear visual evidence, and a polished paper.AI is used throughout the research workflow: understanding and comparing papers; mapping the literature; developing and stress-testing research questions; finding, extracting, cleaning, and documenting data; visualizing patterns; writing, debugging, and testing code; interpreting results; and improving exposition. description: Undersea cables, semiconductor fabs, data centres and language models are not merely technical infrastructures. They are instruments through which states project power, firms capture value, and citizens are governed. This course asks how Southeast Asia (a region of small and middle powers bound economically to China and strategically to the United States) navigates the continuing rivalry between the world’s two largest powers.The course is deliberately interdisciplinary, and the readings are drawn from across the disciplines rather than from a single field. Students use international relations theory to ask when interdependence becomes coercive; political economy to trace who captures value as supply chains reconfigure; law and regulation to compare competing models of data governance; and urban studies and science and technology studies to ask how infrastructure reshapes cities and everyday life. No one discipline answers these questions adequately, and part of the purpose of the course is to expose the limits of each.Part I establishes a shared analytical vocabulary: theories of geoeconomics and economic statecraft, weaponised interdependence, infrastructure as a form of power, and the technology strategies of the major powers. Part II tests that vocabulary against eight cases, several of them original materials prepared by the instructor: Southeast Asian responses to U.S. semiconductor export controls; the politics of 5G network choices; the data centre boom and the political economy of compute; sovereign AI strategies and regional large language models; cross-border data governance; submarine cable routes; digital platforms and e-commerce regulation; and smart city technologies.Teaching is discussion-led throughout. Students are expected to argue, to revise their positions in light of evidence, and to defend conclusions that reasonable people contest. Assessment rewards the quality of reasoning rather than the recovery of settled fact, culminating in a substantial individual research essay in which students develop and sustain an argument of their own.
longName: The Geopolitics of Technology: Southeast Asia in an Age of U.S.-China Rivalry
name: Geopolitics of Technology

The course also covers difference-in-differences, panel data, synthetic control and regression discontinuity, followed by heterogeneous treatment effects and causal machine learning. Throughout the course, students connect each estimator to its target population and identifying assumptions, assess statistical uncertainty, and examine how violations affect conclusions. Lectures combine mathematical arguments with empirical examples and Python demonstrations. By the end of the course, students should be able to design a causal study, implement suitable methods and communicate a reproducible analysis with clearly stated limitations.

The curriculum covers core banking and delivery channels (branch, IVRS, ATM, internet and, with particular emphasis, mobile), and situates them in Singapore's current market — including the five MAS-licensed digital banks now in operation.Contemporary topics are treated as central rather than peripheral: FINTECH and digital business models, generative and agentic AI in banking, tokenisation and central-bank digital currency, real-time and cross-border payments, embedded finance, customer and credit analytics, banking security, fraud and scams, and data-privacy and AI-governance compliance.

description: This course will introduce students to the world of Mergers and Acquisitions (M&A) in legal practice. The focus will be on the practicalities of conducting a deal, particularly the lawyer’s role in these transactions.  To start off, we will discuss the general regulatory framework for such deals, with focus on the Singapore/UK vs the US approach. We will then discuss key considerations in structuring a deal (both public and private), how to run a deal, and common practice issues. Case studies from Singapore and other jurisdictions will be used.  There will also be a number of workshops with a partner law firm, which will cover certain key M&A issues in practice. These issues will be further discussed in later class sessions as well. Students will also engage in hands-on practice, simulating assignments that junior M&A lawyers will work on (including due diligence and redlining). At the end of the course, students will engage in a mock M&A negotiation. description: China is the second largest economy in the world and the largest one in Asia. In this course, we will introduce the key areas of business and commercial laws in China. Starting from contract law, we will scout corporate law, securities law and the rules regulating mergers and acquisitions. The business laws in China reflect a mixture of its civil law tradition, British law influence through Hong Kong, and American law impact as a result of the bulk of Chinese scholars and regulators studying in the U.S. So this course will also take a comparative approach, exploring Chinese laws in comparison with American and common laws in general. The purpose of the course is threefold. First, we will learn the basic rules of business laws in China. Second, we will understand the social and economic rationales underlying the rules and practices in China. Finally, using law as a gateway, we will explore some important business and financial activities in the world’s second largest economy.

description: This course examines the ethical and legal questions raised by the design, deployment, and governance of artificial intelligence. It is built on a simple premise: that responsible reasoning about AI requires three things in sequence – a grounding in ethical theory, a working understanding of the technology itself, and the ability to bring both to bear on the concrete domains where AI now operates. The course is structured to build these capacities in turn.It opens with two foundational sessions on normative ethics. Before any claim can be made about whether a particular use of AI is right, harmful, fair, or just, students need a vocabulary for moral reasoning and an appreciation of the major traditions that have shaped it. These sessions introduce consequentialist, deontological, and virtue-based approaches, alongside religious and Eastern ethical traditions, equipping students to recognise that disagreements about AI are often, at root, disagreements about competing ethical commitments.The course then turns to the technology. Two sessions provide a non-technical but rigorous account of how machine learning systems and large language models actually work – what they can do, how they are built and trained, and where they characteristically fail. No prior knowledge is assumed. The aim is to dispel both the hype and the mystery that surround contemporary AI, so that subsequent ethical and legal analysis rests on an accurate understanding of the systems in question rather than on metaphor or speculation.With these foundations in place, the remaining six sessions investigate AI across a series of high-stakes domains: business, the professions, justice, warfare, truth, and power. Each domain is examined as a site where the ethical frameworks and technical realities established earlier collide with real institutions, interests, and harms. Students consider how AI reshapes commercial and professional life, how it intervenes in the administration of justice and the conduct of armed conflict, how it destabilises shared notions of truth and authorship, and how it redistributes power between states, corporations, and individuals – including the deeper questions of moral status, personhood, and religious authority that AI now forces into view.Throughout, the course emphasises the speed at which these technologies are advancing and the gap between that pace and the capacity of existing ethical and legal frameworks to respond. By the end, students should be able to move fluently between abstract principle, technical detail, and applied judgment – and to articulate clear, well-reasoned positions on the most pressing questions AI poses for law and society.
name: AI, Law and Ethics

description: This course aims to introduce PLE students to how law operates in Singapore. We will explore the role of law in Singapore in the management of both public power and the sphere of private dealings between persons. This will be done through a study of the various sources of law and their nature; the legal institutions and the relations between them; and foundational principles and values.We will begin by exploring the concept of law and the ideals of constitutionalism, democracy, the rule of law, and the separation of powers – all of which pertain to the ways in which power is defined and limited by law. Besides studying what law is, we will study tools and concepts which have some degree of formality but are not law, such as policies and decisions by those who hold discretionary powers.Having inquired into these ideas, we will go on to explore the various institutions of the state and their roles, as well as the values that animate them. This is important because law does not put itself into action; legal institutions breathe life into laws by interpreting them, executing them, and serving as sites of contestation as to how they are to be interpreted and executed. We will discuss matters such as different modes of lawmaking and their relative advantages and disadvantages; the role of the state in controlling its own power; and the limits to law as a means of governing society. Finally, we will apply all this knowledge by focusing our attention on a few discrete areas of law as case studies.While this course will focus on Singapore, comparisons will be drawn with other legal systems, particularly the UK’s, when appropriate.
longName: Governance Through Law In Singapore: Institutions, Jurisprudence, And Values

description: Visa and Mastercard are among the most profitable companies in the world – yet most people never think about what happens after they tap their card. In China, Ant Financial built Alipay into a financial ecosystem serving over a billion users, fundamentally reshaping how an entire economy transacts. When Epic sued Apple over a 30% payment “tax,” it wasn’t a side dispute – it was a fight over who controls the most valuable infrastructure in the platform economy. How does Shopee afford free shipping while still growing? Why is gaming more profitable than Hollywood? The answer, in every case, lies in how money moves through these platforms – and the payment systems that make it possible.This course explores how digital payment systems work and why they sit at the centre of the platform economy. Students will learn how payments flow end-to-end – from card networks like Visa and Mastercard, to mobile wallets like Alipay and GrabPay, to cross-border settlement and real-time payments – and how this infrastructure powers the monetisation strategies of platforms across e-commerce, gaming, entertainment, and super app ecosystems. The course examines how companies like Grab, Shopee, Spotify, and Epic Games design their payment and revenue systems, how payment choices shape competitive strategy and business model innovation, and how emerging technologies are transforming both payments and the platform economy. Through Harvard Business School case studies, hands-on business model workshops, and guest speakers from multiple industries including payments, e-commerce, gaming, and entertainment, students will develop practical skills in strategic analysis, business model design, and digital transformation – preparing them for roles in the fast-growing digital economies of Asia and beyond. The course is designed to serve students across business majors. Marketing students will deepen their understanding of how payment design shapes conversion, customer acquisition, and loyalty in digital channels. Operations and information systems students will examine the technology stack, data flows, and partnership decisions that determine how payment infrastructure is built and scaled. Finance students will analyse the unit economics, take-rate dynamics, and capital allocation choices behind payment-driven business models. For students from strategy and entrepreneurship in particular, the course develops the core capability of identifying where value is captured in a digital ecosystem and how strategic choices around payment infrastructure, platform governance, and ecosystem partnerships create defensible competitive advantage – skills that translate directly to careers in strategy consulting, corporate strategy, venture capital, and founding or joining early-stage digital businesses.

description: The rapid advancement of digital technologies, especially artificial intelligence, is redefining competition across virtually every industry, fundamentally transforming how organizations create value, make decisions, and organize work. From generative AI to intelligent automation and autonomous agents, digital technology becomes a core driver of productivity, innovation, and strategic advantage. Firms that fail to harness the full potential of digital transformation risk rapid erosion of their competitiveness in operational efficiency, product and service innovation, talent capabilities, customer engagement, and ecosystem positioning.This MBA course equips students with an integrated strategic and managerial perspective on digital transformation in two interconnected parts. First, through rigorous analyses of real-world business cases, students will develop a deep understanding of the key levers of transformation—including automation, augmentation, and amplification of human capabilities—and how leading organizations deploy data, algorithms, and intelligent systems to reshape their business models and competitive strategies. Second, through hands-on exercises, live cases, and simulations, students will apply these concepts to redesign value propositions, embed AI into core decision processes, reengineer organizational workflows, and build operating models that support human–AI collaboration. The course culminates in the development of actionable transformation strategies and roadmaps for both established firms and emerging industries. By the end of the course, students will be equipped not only to evaluate new technological opportunities and risks but also to lead organizational change and long-term strategic renewal. Students will inherit the fundamental insight: the ability to transform into an intelligent enterprise is not the technology's capability - it is the quality of human judgment and expertise in setting the boundaries within which AI and all relevant technologies operate.

description:
We negotiate every day. We negotiate with potential employers, co-workers, roommates, landlords, parents, bosses, merchants, service providers, spouses, and even our children. What price we want to pay, how much we want to be paid, who will do the dishes...all of these are negotiations. Yet, although people negotiate all the time, most know very little about the strategy and psychology of effective negotiations. Why do we sometimes get our way whereas other times we walk away feeling frustrated by our inability to obtain the agreement we desire?

Negotiation is the art and science of securing agreements between two or more interdependent parties. This course is designed to be relevant to a broad spectrum of negotiation problems that are faced by managers and professionals. It is also designed to complement the technical and diagnostic skills that are learned in other courses at the SMU. A basic premise of this course is that while managers need analytical skills to develop optimal solutions to problems, they also require a broad array of negotiation skills for these solutions to be accepted and implemented. Successful completion of this course will enable you to recognize, understand, and analyse essential concepts in negotiations.
name: Negotiating in Business

description: Management consultancy has grown exponentially in the last 60 years with the consequence that management consultants have come to occupy a key role in modern organizations and society as agents of change. Few people will have avoided encountering either directly or indirectly the outcome of some kind of management consultancy intervention in an organization or wider society. Over the latter part of the 20th Century management consultants have emerged as indispensable advisors deeply involved in a wide spectrum of significant decisions that private and public sector clients make. Such decisions can involve specialist expertise, new knowledge, or the need for external legitimation. The implications of these decisions can influence the clients’ size, shape, strategic positioning, presence in markets, its implementation and use of Information Technology (IT), as well as the nature of the delivery of key services to citizens. Fundamentally consultants have established themselves as the purveyor par excellence of complex, esoteric and valuable knowledge.At the same time the industry has attracted public scrutiny and criticism as a purveyor of “some sort of black art”. The public discourse of consulting highlights the uncritical over-use of consultants. It questions whether clients achieve value for money from their use of consultants because they frequently lack the information, skills and strategies to manage them effectively and therefore cannot drive delivery successfully and achieve expected outcomes.This course will equip participants with knowledge of the practice of consulting from a client and consultant perspective. It will examine the nature of consulting skills, the consulting process, dynamics of the client-consultant relationship, commissioning consultants, and responding to a request for proposals (RFP). Through lectures, case studies, exercises, guest speakers and interactive discussions, participants will have an opportunity to use highly specialised and advanced critical, evaluative and communication skills in order to understand the issues involved in the application of management consultancy models to real business situations.
name: Mgmt Consultancy and Lead

Financial services provide especially consequential examples because the industry is built on information, trust, risk assessment and transactions.This course examines how data analytics, machine learning, large language models, generative AI and blockchain enable new business models and reshape established organisations. Financial services are the principal application domain, with cases spanning platform finance and crowdfunding, digital lending, robo-advisory, digital wealth management, crypto assets and tokenised finance.The course combines managerial frameworks, technology fundamentals, executive cases and hands-on work with approved AI tools. The emphasis is not on coding; it is on asking the right questions, evaluating evidence and economics, designing customer and operating models, and governing deployment responsibly.Participants will leave with a decision-ready proposal for an AI-enabled or digital transformation initiative relevant to an established organisation or a new venture.

description: This elective is designed as a leader-development course with an embedded international experiential component. It asks students to examine how they understand leadership, how others experience their leadership behaviour, how context shapes what leadership requires, and how they can continue developing through deliberate practice.The course begins with a brief pre-departure assessment and feedback session. Students then participate in a three-day immersion in an international location selected to fit the learning purpose of the course. The location will be chosen based on whether it offers a meaningful contrast with Singapore and enables students to engage with place, pace, community, nature, uncertainty, systems and leadership practice in ways that cannot be replicated adequately in a normal classroom.Upon return, students continue the course in Singapore. These sessions help students interpret the evidence generated during the international immersion, design their own leadership experiment, practise a specific behaviour in a real setting, and reflect on the impact of that experiment. The course is therefore organised around a developmental arc: place, context and uncertainty, system, experiment, reflection and transfer.The international location will be selected by the instructor and MBA Office based on pedagogical fit, partner availability, student safety, affordability and operational feasibility. The unit outline therefore refers to an international location rather than naming a specific destination.
name: Leadership Development

description: Artificial Intelligence (AI) has bloomed this year, entering the lives of many students and the general public’s use. We will begin with a survey of the current AIs and their basis in neural networks, and will summarily distinguish AI from human intelligence. Since AI is now used to process and output a variety of forms of symbolic and written, language and images. The basics of large language models are introduced. We will use a variety of the more popular generative AIs, such as ChatGPT and Claude (including visualization features), and introduce other apps for creativity. Fundamental terms and models of creativity and innovation are used to discuss how human work transpired before and after AI. We examine and employ AI for a variety of application areas, including idea generation, visual concepts, narratives, future scenarios, and AI-coded prototypes (called no code or vibe coding). The design thinking innovation technique will be used as a framework to understand how human work occurred before the use of AI, and how AI can be applied effectively to augment various phases in iteration and testing. A group project will be employed to integrate the various AI and non-AI tools to create novel concepts. The course does not employ mathematics or computational work, but AI applications are used and explored. We employ higher levels of reasoning, and multi-disciplinary approaches.

description: Japan offers a rare vantage point for Asian business leaders: it is the developed economy that confronted — decades ahead of its neighbours — the conditions many of their home markets are now approaching, including a rapidly aging population, a mature domestic market, prolonged low growth, and intensifying pressure from global capital markets. Yet within these constraints, Japanese enterprises have built some of the world's most durable competitive positions in advanced manufacturing, intellectual property and content, retail innovation, and urban development. This week-long immersion examines how Japanese firms and institutions drive innovation, navigate structural economic shifts, and capture emerging opportunities — and what their experience means for leaders building, investing in, and internationalising businesses across Asia.The segment combines faculty lectures and case discussions with lectures by professors from the University of Tokyo and Waseda University, senior-management dialogues at leading Japanese companies spanning industrial robotics, consumer electronics and content, retail, financial markets, urban design, and the social welfare sector, and a fireside chat and networking dinner with entrepreneurs and executives at the front line of Chinese enterprises' expansion into Japan. Cultural immersion experiences, including a guided visit to Meiji Jingu and an introduction to the discipline of kendo, ground the week in the values — craftsmanship, continuity, and practice — that underpin Japanese management.

description: The development of new digital technologies has fundamentally changed how consumers interact with brands and each other.  Marketing is no longer about pushing a sales message to a potential buyer. Businesses have to enable conversations with consumers to engage prospects with relevant content that will lead to positive actions for commercial impact.To be effective, marketers need to employ a rigorous and holistic marketing methodology across both traditional and new-emerging techniques. This course will provide students with the relevant knowledge, perspectives, and practical skills required to develop marketing strategies that leverage the opportunities inherent on digital platforms, including social media and consumer-to-consumer social interactions. The emphasis of this course is on understanding the various digital platforms available, how to build social marketing strategies, and how to track their effectiveness.The course utilizes applicable theory, empirical analysis, and practical examples to develop the key learning points. The class format will include a combination of lectures, case study discussions, and guest speakers with relevant industry experience.
name: Digital Marketing

description:
In the era of new digital technologies, the focus of marketing has shifted. It's no longer about selling a product or service but engaging with customers through relevant content and encouraging interactions that positively impact business. This advanced course recognizes this shift and is designed to equip students with a comprehensive understanding of digital marketing, incorporating established and emerging strategies.

This advanced course is delivered using an SMU-X learning approach. SMU-X is an experiential learning framework that calls for students to take on real-world challenges by collaborating on projects with corporations, non-profits, and government organizations. The framework represents a paradigm shift in the traditional teaching and learning approach, from teacher-centered to students taking ownership of their learning.

The course offers a comprehensive blend of theory, empirical analysis, and practical examples to reinforce key concepts related to digital marketing. Students will apply their knowledge to develop a digital marketing strategy for a real industry partner. We will collaborate with a real industry partner and offer consultancy services to recommend relevant digital marketing strategies for a real business problem.

With engaging seminars, case study discussions focusing on global brands, insights from industry experts with rich international business experience, and hands-on real business projects, students will sharpen their problem- solving skills to tackle real-world business problems through interdisciplinary approaches and activities. They are guaranteed an interactive learning experience that is informative and relevant to working for global businesses.

Do note that MKTG236 Digital Marketing Strategy follows the SMU-X experiential learning framework. It combines academic with experiential learning through the use of a project from an industry partner. Students need to take ownership of their learning. It is not designed to offer any software development training sessions and does not cover any IT programming. It is a contemporary marketing module to prepare students to join the marketing industry as a marketer.
name: Digital Marketing Strategy

description: AI is revolutionising how organisations grow and compete—and marketing sits at the epicentre of this shift. McKinsey & Company found that marketing and sales is where organisations across all sectors are most likely to deploy generative AI, fundamentally changing how marketers plan, create, measure, and execute.The real challenge is not about learning more tools but knowing how to use them together. AI marketing is about developing the fluency to connect people, data, and technology into a system that drives business impact. L'Oréal and Coca-Cola, amongst others, have already moved in this direction, designing integrated marketing systems that deliver measurable performance gains.This shift towards integration defines the emerging AI marketing system. It connects identity, data, orchestration, and experimentation within a unified infrastructure, designed to operate continuously, adapt in real time, and compound its value over time. Used strategically, it becomes the invisible engine powering everything marketing does.This course builds on foundational marketing principles and equips you to move beyond the hype. You will learn where to focus first, how to design effective workflows, and how to integrate AI capabilities, new or existing, into your organisation's technology stack. From there, you will design and build integrated AI marketing systems that connect workflows, data, and technology into a unified, continuously operating infrastructure that drives strategic growth. You will also explore how AI can be applied across the full customer journey, how to deploy AI agents within your marketing system, and how to do so within responsible AI governance frameworks.The outcome is not a collection of siloed tools, tactics, and campaigns. It is a system, one that works continuously, scales intelligently, and delivers measurable impact.
name: AI-Powered Marketing

description:
We negotiate every day. We negotiate with potential employers, co-workers, roommates, landlords, parents, bosses, merchants, service providers, spouses, and even our children. What price we want to pay, how much we want to be paid, who will do the dishes...all of these are negotiations. Yet, although people negotiate all the time, most know very little about the strategy and psychology of effective negotiations. Why do we sometimes get our way whereas other times we walk away feeling frustrated by our inability to obtain the agreement we desire?

Negotiation is the art and science of securing agreements between two or more interdependent parties. This course is designed to be relevant to a broad spectrum of negotiation problems that are faced by managers and professionals. It is also designed to complement the technical and diagnostic skills that are learned in other courses at the SMU. A basic premise of this course is that while managers need analytical skills to develop optimal solutions to problems, they also require a broad array of negotiation skills for these solutions to be accepted and implemented. Successful completion of this course will enable you to recognize, understand, and analyse essential concepts in negotiations.
name: Negotiating in Business

description: How did ZARA become one of the fastest growing and most profitable brands in fashion retailing?  How did Wal-Mart grow to be the world’s largest retailer?  Largely the answer is that ZARA and Wal-Mart view their operational capabilities as an important and integral part of their competitive advantage.  As do other successful companies, such as Procter & Gamble, Toyota, and Coca Cola, they invest strategically in physical plants and facilities, in process and information technology, in employees, suppliers, and distributor relationships, and perhaps most importantly, in organizational practices and know-how.  The objective of this course is to provide students with a set of qualitative frameworks and quantitative tools to analyze and guide the long-term, strategic decisions for a company’s operations function. This course caters to those interested in management and business consulting, general management, and operations careers.  Finance specialists interested in assessing the risks, the opportunities, the competitive advantages, and ultimately the value embedded in a company’s operations will benefit from the course as well.
name: Operations Strategy

description: International shipping and ports are fundamental to the achievement of world sustainable development. However, the challenges to shipping and ports in providing high-quality, safe, secure, energy-efficient, environmentally and climate-friendly services that, at the same time, promote connectivity and trade and enable economic growth are complex and substantial. These challenges call for a multi-stakeholder approach involving shipping companies, port authorities, regulators, financial institutions, research institutions, and other relevant partners. They also require effective maritime governance, involving both public and private actors in setting, implementing and promoting standards for quality and sustainability. This course addresses the sustainability imperative for shipping and ports and the various solutions available to different industry stakeholders. The shipping and ports industries have started to respond to the growing environmental and social concerns of regulators, customers and the local communities in which they operate, while at the same time increasingly recognizing that quality and sustainability can provide opportunities for innovation, resilience, competitiveness and value creation.
name: Sustainable Shipping and Ports

description:
Stochastic models deals with the modelling and analysis of the behaviour of systems that evolve randomly over time.  This Ph.D.-level course will survey the important tools of stochastic processes to understand and control the behavior of systems under uncertainty. Applications to business problems related to managing inventory, waiting lines, reliability and others will be discussed.

On successful completion of the course, students should be able to 
- Define Poisson Process and explain its characteristics; model and analyse 
situations using Poisson Process.
- Define Markov Chain and explain its characteristics; model and analyse situations using Markov Chains.
- Define continuous time Markov Processes and explain its characteristics; model and analyse situations using Markov Processes.
- Define and explain Renewal processes and Renewal reward processes; model and analyse situation using Renewal processes
- Define and explain Brownian motion and its uses
- Use the techniques learned to model and analyse situations relating to queues, reliability and inventory and other application areas in business.
name: Stochastic Models

Topics may include but are not restricted to distribution, fairness and justice as they relate to politics and policies.  Understanding politics and public policies is crucial for participation in modern society. This course facilitates this understanding by discussing crucial questions such as why states go to war, why some states have become democratic while others have not, how does culture affect politics, and why various countries are ruled in such different ways.

name: Intro to Pol & Policy Studies

description: What are the ideal ways to arrange our political institutions? What are the ideal relations between our society and ourselves? What does “ideal” even mean here? Moreover, in a world where there always seems to be a regrettable contrast between the lofty ideal and the nasty real, how have different ideals shaped our perceptions of political and social reality, and how have changing perceptions of reality informed our ideals in turn? These questions are fundamental to the study of normative political theory. In this course, we critically examine influential formulations of as well as responses to these questions found in the Western history of political theory. In doing so, we aim to gain a preliminary understanding of (1) the theoretical and practical significance of diverse values (such as justice, liberty, equality, and order), (2) how their meanings have changed over time, and (3) how these values have characterized conflicting political and social ideals. This course paves the way for us to formulate, justify, and strive for political and social ideals particularly suitable for the reality of our own.
name: Political Theory
