description: Immigration is one of the most salient and contentious political issues around the globe today. More people than ever — more than 300 million, or one in every 27 worldwide — live outside their country of birth. This course examines the political and economic questions migration raises. Do immigrants compete with natives for jobs and depress wages, or fuel the innovation that ageing societies need? Is opposition to immigration driven by economic self-interest, cultural concerns, or mere prejudice? Does immigration erode social trust and cohesion? Do immigrants face discrimination in hiring, in housing, in access to public services — and if so, how do we prove it, and why does it persist? Which interventions actually reduce prejudice and xenophobia? And may a state rightfully turn people away at all?Throughout the course, we draw on research and examples from different immigration regimes and contexts around the world, including the United States, Europe, Asia, and the Gulf states. On each question we engage the most credible quantitative research and the debates it has sparked, pairing accessible foundational readings with one research frontier study. While these papers use modern statistical methods — natural experiments, field experiments, large-scale data — no statistical background is required: we will digest each one together in class, learning to weigh what the evidence can and cannot establish.
longName: The Politics of Immigration: Who Gets In, Who Belongs, and the Future of Citizenship
name: The Politics of Immigration

description: This course introduces students to the theoretical and empirical literature on the sociology of sex and gender. We begin with the foundational frameworks sociologists use to understand sex, gender, and sexuality as social constructions—doing gender, social structure, hegemony, and embodiment. We then turn to how gender is produced and contested across social identities and institutions: masculinities, the family and socialization, intersecting inequalities of race and class, globalization and care, the body and medicine, economic markets, as well as cutting edge topics such as generative AI and emerging technologies. Drawing on cases from Asia, North America, and beyond, and on both qualitative and quantitative research, the course treats sex and gender as both a social identity and a social institution.

description: With mandatory sustainability reporting pushed out by different countries and regulators, stakeholders will need to have greater confidence in these reports. Assurance on sustainability reporting will narrow the expectations gap between the users and its preparer, and build trust in this new ecosystem of sustainability reporting. In Singapore, limited assurance on sustainability reporting is compulsory from FY2029 onwards for SGX-listed companies. Even though it is only compulsory for listed companies as of now, non-listed companies may also volunteer to get assurance on their sustainability reporting due to various requests by their different stakeholders. This course will be looking at both internal review of sustainability reporting disclosures (by internal auditors) and the external assurance (by external auditors) of aforementioned disclosures.  By the end of this course, students will learn the processes for conducting (a) an internal review of sustainability disclosures and (b) a sustainability assurance engagement.
name: Sustainability Assurance

description: This course develops students' ability to design, deploy, supervise, and evaluate agent-based AI systems that automate and augment accounting, auditing, taxation, and finance workflows. Students will learn common agentic AI architectures—including tool-using large language models (LLMs), Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), multi-agent systems, workflow orchestration, and enterprise AI integration—and how to translate accounting requirements into reliable, auditable, and scalable AI-enabled processes.The course emphasizes human-in-the-loop supervision, responsible AI deployment, and enterprise implementation, reflecting industry practice that AI accelerates complex tasks while professional judgment and accountability remain with human experts. Through hands-on projects, students will develop AI agents for applications such as audit working-paper review, financial reporting support, valuation and meeting summarization, accounting research, exception detection, and workflow automation, while considering performance, evaluation, cost (e.g., token usage), scalability, security, and operational constraints.
name: Agentic AI for Accounting

college: School of Accountancy
description: This course equips students with the knowledge and practical skills to evaluate the reliability, robustness, and trustworthiness of AI systems and AI agents used in accounting, auditing, taxation, and finance, and to design governance mechanisms and internal controls suitable for regulated environments.Topics include AI risk management, model risk and assurance, AI evaluation methodologies, bias and fairness, explainability, privacy and confidentiality, cybersecurity, vendor and platform risk, auditability and documentation, human oversight, and emerging AI regulations and governance frameworks. Students will learn how to evaluate AI systems using techniques such as benchmarking, test suites, red-teaming, monitoring, and drift detection, and how to operationalise accountability through governance policies, review checkpoints, documentation, and escalation protocols for responsible enterprise AI deployment.

description: COMM334 – an overseas project experience - is an advanced elective module with an overseas study component designed for students majoring in communication management. With Asia’s economic ascendancy and modernisation, corporate strategic communication in Asia has taken on a new importance in the past two decades. Home to over half of the world’s population, unprecedented political, economic, media, social and technological forces in an age of discontinuities are creating a new world order for Asia. The importance of communicating strategically and the need for greater cross-cultural understanding, including being innovative and enterprising have never been more critical for organisations struggling to effectively communicate with diverse stakeholder groups across different geographies in this new multi-polar business environment.An SMU-XO module, this course is divided into two segments – Singapore and China (Hong Kong). The overseas experience aims to equip communication students to better understand the unique geopolitical dynamics which affect communication in a one country and two systems nation. Students will be equipped with the ability to apply theory and understand how strategic communication has evolved to influence the integration of paid, earned, shared and owned media which are vital to unearthing unique characteristics that drive communication practice in countries in Asia. In addition to gaining insights from top Asian practitioners in the region, students will also acquire in-depth knowledge of the socio-political-cultural-economic factors that underpin the practice that influence business outcomes in the world’s most populous continent. This course will prepare students in communication management to readily transit and take on responsibilities to manage communication for businesses operating across Asia.

description: In today's rapidly evolving technological landscape, artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative force with profound implications for society, industry and governments. This course delves into the opportunities as well as the key legal, policy, regulatory, ethical and governance challenges presented by AI technologies, equipping law students with the knowledge and skills to analyse latest developments and navigate this fast-growing and promising field.The primary objective of this course is to provide students with the fundamental building blocks to: (a) understand and appreciate current and emerging opportunities and risks about AI, (b) critically analyse the complex factors to be considered in regulating AI, and (c) constructively participate in the globally-evolving discourse on AI governance, regulation, policymaking, ethics and related issues that will shape the collective endeavour of AI regulation. Consequently, the course structure is designed so that students will be exposed to concepts and perspectives from the technical, legal, and policymaking and regulatory spheres. Students will:•	First, understand the policy and societal impact and concerns of AI systems, including their opportunities and benefits, as well as their concerns.•	Second, understand and appreciate the ethical principles that have been developed to address these concerns, and how these in turn form the foundations of today’s AI regulations. •	Third, gain an appreciation of the range of considerations that governments and international organisations must consider in AI regulation, including questions about the “who”, “why”, “what”, “when” and “how” of regulating. •	Fourth, learn about the current state of regulations for AI, including an exploration of the regulatory approaches of the EU, US, China and Singapore (among other jurisdictions). •	Fifth, learn about other laws and regulations that impact AI, including privacy and data protection laws, and criminal and civil laws. Students will learn through a mix of lectures (including from guest speakers), active class participation, collaborative group projects, and research papers. These will be supported by recommended texts and readings chosen to reflect the local / common law environment within which the class is situated.
longName: Artificial Intelligence Law, Policy and Ethics
name: AI Law, Policy & Ethics

description: Should you eat meat? Should you fly on planes? Does a forest have value beyond what it can offer us? What, if anything, do we owe to future generations or to the non-human animals with whom we share this planet? Are wealthy nations obligated to help those most affected by climate change? These are among the most pressing ethical questions of our time. Answering them requires careful thought about the nature of the environment and our obligations to it. This course introduces students to the central debates in environmental ethics. We will ask who, or what, deserves moral concern, and why, as well as whether nature has value in itself or only in relation to us. We will also consider how our answers to questions like these should shape the choices we make as individuals, citizens, and members of institutions. Along the way, students will develop the analytical tools needed to reason clearly and rigorously about these questions, tools that can prove useful well beyond the seminar room.
name: Environmental Ethics

description: This course will provide a detailed coverage of the most important works of classical Chinese philosophy from the Spring and Autumn period to the end of the Warring States Period, that is from roughly 722 until 221 BCE. We will look extensively at the two major philosophical schools, Confucianism and Daoism, and relate these two to the other important thinkers of the era. The course will include close readings of the major texts of the time, in selected passages from English translations of The Analects, Mencius, Laozi/Daodejing, Zhuangzi, as well as passages from the Xunzi, Mozi, and Hanfeizi. From these readings we will endeavour an understanding of the most important differences between Western and Chinese philosophy, the differences in interpretation and worldview, how classical Chinese thought has contributed to what China is today, and relate these ways of thought to thinking about current affairs.Near the end of the course we shall take a closer look at the Sun-tzu: The Art of Warfare, a philosophical/military work from the classical Chinese era, popular in Business and Management practices, and relate this work to the philosophical background of the major texts studied. From this we will learn how and why the combination of politics/warfare and philosophy was a natural one in the Classical Chinese worldview, and explain the philosophy behind this combination with a view to the continued popularity of this work in business and management.
name: Intro to Classical Chin Phil

description: Machine Learning is one of the fundamental subjects in the field of Artificial Intelligence. Machine Learning is concerned with computer programs that automatically improve their performance through experience (e.g., learning to recognize images, classify text documents, detect fraudulent credit card transactions, or drive autonomous vehicles).  This course covers both fundamental principles and practical algorithms for machine learning. It includes in-depth introduction of the techniques and algorithms in two major machine learning paradigms – supervised learning and unsupervised learning. For supervised learning, it covers both linear and non-linear models for two supervised tasks: classification and regression. For unsupervised learning, it covers three major unsupervised tasks: clustering, dimension reduction, and anomaly detection. The course also includes deep learning approaches for each of the aforementioned five tasks, highlighting the principles of making different “shallow” models “deeper”. The course is intended to prepare students for a good understanding of principles, challenges, and opportunities in ML. It aims to equip students with the capability of applying machine learning techniques to address real-world applications and building the foundations of doing research in machine learning. To this end, the course highlights the following five key features: * Systematic treatment of ML techniques. It covers shallow and deep algorithms and techniques for five popular ML tasks. * Understanding of commonly used mathematical foundations in ML. The course introduces principled mathematical foundations behind diverse ML techniques, such as least squares optimization, Lp regularization, maximum likelihood estimation, gradient descent optimization, and backpropagation. * Introduction to emerging topics and current ML challenges. The course includes an overview of emerging topics including semi-supervised learning, self-supervised learning, and interpretability, security, privacy, and safety in ML. * Progressive ML model development. CS421 includes a Kaggle-competition-style group project to shape the capability of developing effective models to address a real problem with data progressively made available. * Model implementation. One assignment and diverse lab sessions are designed to support the development of capability in implementing different ML models using existing libraries. It is a course recommended for those who have some ML experience/skill and want to achieve a more systematic and comprehensive understanding of ML, as well as for beginners who are not familiar with ML but have very strong curiosity to explore. Extensive coding is expected for this course. Students are strongly encouraged to have proficiency in IS103 Computational Thinking prior to reading this course. NOTE: While this is an introduction course, it is a technical course and it is highly recommended that students are proficient in programming, probability, statistics and linear algebra (e.g., CS103 Linear Algebra for Computing Applications, CS105 Statistical Thinking for Data Science, CS201 Data Structures and Algorithms and CS202 Design and Analysis of Algorithms). Previous course code & title: IS449 Introduction to Machine Learning

The purpose of this course is to introduce students to formal statistical reasoning. Its focus is on the analysis of data. The theory is motivated by examining real-world problems with real-world data. Emphasis is placed on the central role played by computers in modern statistics. The Python programming language is used for the labs. No prior knowledge of Python is required to enroll.

description: Limiting global warming to 1.5°C, the more ambitious goal of the Paris Agreement, requires global CO₂ emissions to reach net zero around 2050. Most emissions come from a handful of sectors: energy, heavy industry, transport, and agriculture and land use. Many are hard to abate, with emissions built into chemical processes, long-lived assets and fuels with no ready substitute. Decarbonising them means rebuilding the industrial core of the global economy — an Industrial Revolution 2.0 requiring investment estimated at US$3–4 trillion a year, much of it in Asia.Energy transitions are long and uneven; they ebb and flow. Multilateral agreements, targets and frameworks set the direction, but on their own do not make a transition happen. Change happens when firms shift sectoral norms, standards and practice, and when the investors, lenders and governments who fund and regulate them help reshape the economics behind them.The course works sector by sector, and each one starts with where the emissions actually come from — fossil carbon in fuels and feedstocks, carbon held in trees and soils, methane from livestock, nitrous oxide from fertiliser use. That physical picture decides which levers exist, who can pull them, and when. From there we examine sector business models, the technologies and policies that could change them, and how the transition is being financed.Students leave with a toolkit rather than an answer: frameworks to judge what a company can do, when it can do it, whether the numbers work, and whether its reported emissions reflect real change. The course draws on lectures, case studies, guest speakers from industry and finance, and a term-long group project on a single company. It is aimed at students heading into sustainable and transition finance, corporate strategy, energy and infrastructure investing, policy or consulting — and at anyone who will have to form a view on what a company can actually do about its emissions.
name: Sectoral Decarbon Know

description: Insolvency and debt restructuring law is concerned with debtors who are unable to repay their debts. This course will consider the rules and processes which the law has developed to address this ever-present problem, with a focus on debtors which are companies. In particular it will cover, in more depth than in LAW201, the formal processes available in Singapore for the liquidation and restructuring of companies – winding up, receivership, schemes of arrangement, and judicial management. In those contexts, the substantive policies and principles of the law will be addressed – e.g. , the pari passu principle, the concept of set-off, and the avoidance of suspect transactions entered in the run-up to insolvency. In addition, the course will consider informal debt restructurings (work-outs), and also introduce the issues and developing law relating to cross-border insolvencies. As well as providing a theoretical grounding in corporate insolvency principles, aspects of the course may involve the participation of specialist insolvency lawyers from private practice, with the aim of providing a more practical perspective.

description: The Law of Armed Conflict (LOAC), also known as International Humanitarian Law (IHL) or the Law of War is the aspect of international law that applies during armed conflicts and regulates the means and methods of warfare. It prescribes how military operations may be conducted in order to minimise the suffering caused by war to the extent possible, in particular by protecting non-combatants such as civilians, wounded soldiers, prisoners of war and the natural environment. While much of LOAC is, given the history of its development, Eurocentric, this course approaches LOAC from the perspective of a young developing Asian nation, focusing on Asian experiences during armed conflicts such as the numerous struggles against colonial powers; the Vietnam War, the invasions of Iraq and Afghanistan, the situation in Myanmar and the War against Iran. It will examine how major international events such as the Holocaust; the World Wars and the many conflicts in the past century have shaped LOAC today. Additionally, given recent advances, this course will examine the impact of new technologies such as the use of AI, robotics, drones new biological and genetic weapons and cyberwarfare in armed conflicts today. Students will be encouraged to critically assess the effectiveness, limitations, and future development of LOAC in a rapidly evolving environment with a focus on Asia and the Pacific.
name: Law of Armed Conflict

description: Physics has gravity. Biology has evolution. What does a manager or entrepreneur have to guide decisions about how to build and grow a company? Data matters. But data necessarily tells us about what has already happened. Managers and entrepreneurs must make decisions about what will happen — often in situations where the evidence is incomplete, circumstances are changing, and there is no obvious precedent to follow. This course explores how well-developed theories and principles can help. Drawing on academic research, real-world cases, and the thinking of influential entrepreneurs and practitioners, Leading New Ventures to Growth equips students with frameworks for reasoning about some of the hardest problems involved in building a successful enterprise: finding opportunities and understanding customer needs, getting an early venture off the ground, setting strategy, responding to established competitors, motivating people, and building an organisation and culture capable of growing. The course does not present these ideas as a collection of “best practices.” Instead, students will learn to ask why something works, under what circumstances it works, and when apparently good advice should be ignored. They will test theories against business cases, challenge their assumptions and limitations, and learn to apply them to unfamiliar situations. Finally, students will put these ideas into practice by working with a real venture on a real growth problem. The aim is not to give students a playbook for building a company. It is to develop the judgment to build their own.
name: Leading New Ventures to Growth

description: In an era of product commoditisation and widely available technology, user experience has become the competitive advantage that is hardest for competitors to copy. Designed for business owners and senior managers, this course uses design thinking as its methodological backbone and user insight as its core discipline, covering the theory, frameworks and tools of experience-driven innovation. A live team project runs across all three days: participants apply each module to a real challenge drawn from their own organisations, culminating in a pitch on Day 3. Two threads run throughout. The first is overseas expansion, where unfamiliar markets become the ultimate stress test of a leader’s user insight. The second is artificial intelligence, examining how AI compresses the cost of each stage of the innovation process and how leaders should govern its use. description:
This course examines why employees withdraw from work, why they stay in or leave organisations, and what happens after they exit. Employee withdrawal encompasses both changes in participation at work, such as lateness, absence, and reduced effort, and the termination of organisational membership. The course critically evaluates these behaviors as distinct outcomes and as potentially connected processes, with attention to their consequences for employees, work groups, and organisations.

The course introduces major theories, empirical approaches, and current debates across five domains: the unfolding model and job embeddedness; relationships among forms of withdrawal; proximal withdrawal states and the timing of turnover; post-exit destinations, boomerang employment, and prior work experience; and collective turnover. Five reading-based seminars, with four assigned papers each, lead to a final session devoted to research proposal presentations.
name: Emp Withdrawal, Turnover, & Mo

description: Immigration is one of the most contentious political issues around the globe today. More people than ever, more than 300 million, live outside their country of birth.This course examines the political, economic, and ethical questions migration raises. Do immigrants compete with natives for jobs and depress wages, or fuel the innovation that ageing societies need? Is opposition to immigration driven by economic self-interest, cultural concerns, or mere prejudice? Do immigrants face discrimination in hiring and housing, and if so, how do we prove it? Which interventions actually reduce prejudice? And may a state rightfully turn people away at all?We weigh the arguments on all sides, with cases from Singapore and around the world, and read studies at the frontier of current research. Together, we work through the available evidence on some of the most pressing of these questions. You will learn to judge what a study can and cannot show, and to argue your own position. No background in political science or statistics is needed.
name: The Politics of Immigration

description: Economic sociology examines the social foundations of markets, firms, and work – how real people buy, sell, hire, invest, and organize work. It is a course about people, power, trust, status, and institutions and we still study how corporations emerged, how networks shape hiring, how markets signal prestige, and how technology will reshape the future. Conventional economics often treats individuals as isolated calculators of self-interest. This course starts from a different claim: economic action is social action. Markets, firms, and jobs are built from relationships, trust, status, power, and history. Across the term, we ask questions that are concrete and, frequently, unexpected. Why do large corporations dominate modern life? Who actually controls them? How do friendships and relationships help people get jobs? Why do some companies have higher status than others? Will artificial intelligence make our jobs obsolete in the future? We read classical arguments by Smith, Marx, Weber, and Polanyi alongside modern work on social networks, institutions, labor markets, and technology and accelerationism. Economics knowledge and quantitative skills are not required. All foundational ideas will be covered from a sociological perspective.
name: Economic Sociology: Capitalism
